title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Executive Summary ii Executive Summary Hazard mitigation helps reduce or eliminate potential losses from future disasters. Hazard mitigation planning helps establish and maintain a process that leads to the implementation of hazard mitigation actions. The State of Tennessee is familiar with the hazard’s impacts on its residents, visitors, infrastructure, environment, and economy. This 2023 update to the State Hazard Mitigation Plan (State Plan, or SHMP) reaffirms the state’s commitment to making continual improvements to its statewide mitigation strategy and program. The 2023 hazard mitigation planning process began when the Tennessee Emergency Management Agency (TEMA) assembled an inclusive State Hazard Mitigation Planning Committee (SHMPC) representing a cross-section of stakeholders that supported TEMA in developing this State Plan update. The composition of the group was designed to foster FEMA’s Whole Community doctrine, which is based on the premise that both the government and its residents are responsible for implementing mitigation initiatives, as well as activities to support the other three phases of emergency management--preparedness, response, and recovery. The State Plan shows Tennessee’s commitment to pursue risk-reduction initiatives for assets exposed to natural and technological hazards. It also guides decision makers in their efforts to prioritize mitigation actions and commit resources to reducing the effects of known hazards. The first task of the SHMPC was to identify the natural, technological, and human-caused hazards of concern that affect the state. In doing so, the committee assessed the: • Vulnerability of populations • Vulnerability of state-owned and leased natural and built assets • Risk presented by these hazards to the assets The next step involved conducting a thorough evaluation of the state’s current mitigation capabilities and updating the state’s mitigation strategy. The strategy identified seven overarching mitigation goals and related objectives that underpin the Mitigation Action Plan developed to implement hazard mitigation initiatives. The SHMPC identified seven goals and related objectives, which are fully discussed in Section 5 (Mitigation Strategy). The goals and objectives provide the framework for the committee’s review of ongoing mitigation actions included in the 2018 SHMP, and to identify new mitigation actions developed by state agencies to further increase community resiliency during the five-year period covered by this plan, 2023 to 2028.

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Assurances of Continued Compliance with Federal Requirements vii Assurances of Continued Compliance with Federal Requirements The Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan (SHMP) was prepared pursuant to the requirements of the Disaster Mitigation Act of 2000 (DMA or DMA 2000) (Public Law 106-390) and the implementing regulations outlined in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) set forth by the Interim Final Rule published in the Federal Register on February 26, 2002 (44 CFR Sections 201.4 and 201.5) and finalized on October 31, 2007. (Hereafter, these requirements and regulations will be referred to collectively as the Disaster Mitigation Act, or DMA 2000.) The Disaster Mitigation Act emphasizes the need for mitigation plans and coordinated mitigation planning and implementation between state and local authorities, new regulations established requirements that hazard mitigation plans must meet for a state to be eligible for certain federal disaster assistance and hazard mitigation funding under the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (Public Law 93-288). The Tennessee SHMP falls under the assurances proclaimed in this plan: Tennessee assures that it will comply with all applicable federal statutes and regulations in effect with respect to the periods for which it receives grant funding in compliance with 44 CFR Part 13.11(c). The state will amend the SHMP whenever necessary to reflect changes in state or federal laws and statutes, as required in 44 CFR Part 13.11(d). The adoption of this SHMP demonstrates the state’s commitment to fulfilling the mitigation objectives outlined in the SHMP. Likewise, the state authorizes the agencies identified in the SHMP to execute their responsibilities associated with implementing this plan.

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Letter from the Director viii Letter from the Director The State of Tennessee faces many naturally occurring statewide atmospheric, geologic, hydrologic, and seismic hazards; and a range of human-caused and technological hazards occur across the state. These hazards affect vulnerable state assets, the built and natural environments, and populations who may experience injury or death. The Tennessee Emergency Management Agency (TEMA) is empowered by state law and by the governor’s executive authority to protect the public from disasters and emergencies. Underlying this authority is Tennessee Code Annotated (TCA) 58-2-101 through 58-2-104, which charges TEMA with overseeing the development of a Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) approved standard state hazard mitigation plan (HMP). The plan’s risk and vulnerability assessments were conducted using advanced geographic information systems (GIS) technologies; included a review of comprehensive regional hazard studies and incorporated streamlined analysis methodologies. The assessment integrates new and updated data made available by federal and state agencies and used data-gathering scientific modeling methods that have become available since the 2018 SHMP was written. The 2023 SHMP details the state’s mitigation strategy for targeting all natural, technological, and human-caused hazards affecting residents, their property, and community assets. It also discusses TEMA’s efforts to provide an ever-increasing level of technical assistance to support local hazard mitigation plan (LHMP) development and further state and local mutual planning coordination. This Plan is a dynamic document designed to evolve and keep pace with changing hazard concerns; technology; best practices; lessons learned; and applicable state and federal laws, statutes, and orders. The Plan will continue to comply with applicable federal statutes and regulations during the period covered by the plan, 2023 to 2028. To remain compliant with statutes listed in 44 CFR 13.11(c), the Plan will be amended as needed to reflect changes in state or federal laws and statutes as required by 44 CFR 13.11(d). Patrick C. Sheehan, Director Tennessee Emergency Management Agency 3041 Sidco Drive Nashville, Tennessee 37204

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Background ix Background The Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan (SHMP) documents the state’s effort and intention to reduce the vulnerability of the state to all hazards. The plan is organized using a “top-down” approach based on reviewing an updated community profile; conducting risk, vulnerability, and capability assessments; and developing a mitigation strategy based on identified community needs and the state’s capacity for implementing mitigation actions that strengthen community resiliency. Today’s residents benefit from a series of legislative measures passed starting in 1950, when the U.S. Congress first passed the Federal Disaster Relief Act (Public Law 81-875). The Act authorized the President to provide supplementary federal assistance when a state Governor requested help beyond what the state could manage on its own in responding to a major disaster. This law also established the process by which the nation’s Executive Branch of government would approve the request by declaring a presidential disaster declaration after severe hazard events affecting one or more states. The passage of the Disaster Relief Act (DRA) of 1974 and the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (Stafford Act) on November 23, 1988, amended earlier legislation by providing additional federal guidance and support to communities recovering from a major hazard event. The Stafford Act constitutes the statutory authority for most federal disaster response activities, particularly those related to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and its programs providing funding for disaster relief, recovery, and hazard mitigation planning. These and other legislative milestones that set forth mitigation planning-related policies and procedures are shown in Figure 1.

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Background x Figure 1: Historical Legislation Affecting Hazard Mitigation Planning and Tennessee Hazard Mitigation Planning Milestones On October 17, 2004, the State of Tennessee officially adopted its initial Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan in response to the requirements of DMA2K and CFR Section 201.4(a). Initial federal mandates included the requirement for states to update their HMP every three years, but the planning cycle was changed to every five years in 2014. The updates are required “to reflect changes in development, progress in statewide mitigation efforts, and changes in priorities.” The first Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan (SHMP) was approved by FEMA on October 19, 2003. The 2023 version of this plan is the fifth update produced to meet DMA2K requirements. To comply with 44 CFR 201.4(7), Tennessee will continue to follow all applicable federal statutes and regulations related to hazard mitigation planning. Further, as required in 44 CFR 201.4(7), the state will amend its plan as necessary to reflect changes in state or federal laws and statutes. Showcasing its elevated level of professionalism, the state pursued, and received, accreditation from the Emergency Management Accreditation Program (EMAP) in 2007 and was reaccredited in 2013 and 2019. Having an updated SHMP that meets the EMAP Standard is a requirement for maintaining accreditation. As such, the state also adheres to the higher-level programmatic standards required by EMAP, including that of developing a mitigation plan that addresses both natural and human-caused hazards.

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Background xi The need for an accreditation program was recognized in 1997, when the federal Department of Emergency Management, FEMA’s predecessor, submitted a white paper to the National Emergency Management Association (NEMA) that discussed the importance of community preparedness. Even then, experts in the emergency management field recognized that disasters were causing an ever-higher level of destruction that required federal, state, and local governments to increase their level of pre- and post-disaster services and planning. In 2003, the first programs were accredited. Tennessee’s program was accredited in 2007, making it among the states to adopt the standard shortly after the EMAP standard was established.

The program focuses on disaster resilience. The SHMPC and TEMA updated their list of existing hazard mitigation goals to support this vision by adding a new goal to meet the new FEMA planning requirement to address high-hazard potential dams. TEMA led the planning process, including identifying stakeholders, providing input on completing the plan update, and reviewing the draft plan. TEMA was the grant applicant and received the award in 2021. 1.1.2.2 Establishing the Planning Team TEMA was designated as the lead planning agency for the 2023 Tennessee SHMP update, with a core planning team established to guide and support the process. Members included representatives from TEMA, ETSU, IEM, and numerous state agencies. The team was responsible for the day-to-day process of updating the plan. The team also identified and engaged a diverse group of stakeholders based on FEMA’s “whole community” approach to planning. The whole community approach refers to the belief that emergency management is a shared responsibility. By incorporating a wide range of knowledge, perspectives, and experiences, this plan intends to assess the state’s current initiatives and develop strategies that reflect the whole community. The State Hazard Mitigation Planning Committee (SHMPC) also guided the plan update. The committee works to enhance and promote effective multi-hazard mitigation planning at the state level of government in partnership with public and private stakeholders. Its focus is on developing and implementing the SHMP, policies, tools, or processes that lead to safer and more resilient communities. The overall goals of the committee include the following: • Promoting and facilitating the coordination of mitigation efforts across the state • Assessing the effectiveness of mitigation core capabilities • Securing information about mitigation opportunities, programs, and benefits into the hands of local decision makers • Coordinating policy recommendations on state-level issues • Overseeing the maintenance and successful implementation of the National Mitigation Framework (NMF) and the National Mitigation Investment Strategy (NMIS)

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 1: The Planning Process 8 One element the new guidance expands upon is the section on High Hazard Potential Dams. Dams are considered critical infrastructure and benefit the state in various ways, such as by supplying water, reducing flood damage, creating recreational opportunities, producing energy, and more. Maintaining these benefits is an important goal for the state. However, dams are not without risk. The risks they present to life and property are classified in terms of High Hazard, Significant Hazard, and Low Hazard. Tennessee’s Safe Dams Program actively participated in this plan update and shared dam safety information with the team. In order to be eligible for FEMA’s HHPD Grant Program, this plan met all the requirements outlined in Section 3.8, High Hazard Potential Dams, of the State Mitigation Planning Policy Guide. The Emergency Management Accreditation Program (EMAP) guidance was also considered. Tennessee was first accredited in 2007. Since then, it has been reassessed twice and has met EMAP standards both times. The 2018 SHMP was written to meet EMAP standards, as was the 2023 plan. ETSU is the entity responsible for the EMAP update in the 2023 plan. 1.1.2.3 Coordinating with Other Agencies and Stakeholders One of the first steps of the planning process was to identify and invite key agencies and stakeholders to participate in the plan update. For this plan update, “stakeholders” refer to state, local, and tribal agencies; colleges and universities; private entities, including private nonprofit organizations; and quasi-governmental authorities like special districts that perform critical functions. Organizations with mitigation capabilities were identified and invited to participate. This includes agencies and stakeholders responsible for the following: • Emergency management • Economic development • Land use and development • Housing • Health and social services • Infrastructure • Natural and cultural resources

text: Great Smoky Mountains National Park, located in eastern Tennessee, is the most visited national park in the United States.12 Clingmans Dome is the highest point in Tennessee and in the Great “Smokies,” and it is the third highest mountain peak east of the Mississippi River.13 Figure 6: Tennessee Topographical Map and Legend14 There are six land regions in Tennessee: the Blue Ridge, the Appalachian Ridge and Valley, the Cumberland Plateau, the Highland Rim, the Nashville Basin, and the Gulf Coastal Plain. • The Blue Ridge region is in the eastern part of the state and borders North Carolina. This area of Tennessee includes the Great Smoky Mountains, the Chilhowee Mountains, and the Snowbird Mountains. The average elevation of this area is 5,000 feet above sea level, with its highest point at Clingmans Dome, found in the Great Smoky Mountains, at 6,643 feet above sea level. • The Appalachian Ridge and Valley region is a moderately low-lying area situated along the banks of the Tennessee River and is west of the Blue Ridge Mountains within the Great Smoky Mountains National Park, the Nantahala Forest, and the Cherokee National Forest. This area stretches west from the Blue Ridge Mountains, is 55 miles long, and is blanketed by valleys and wooden ridges. The Great Valley is in the western section of the Appalachian and Valley region, where the basin widens, and the ridges are lower. • The Cumberland Plateau is west of the Appalachian Ridge and Valley area, also called the Appalachian Plateau. The Cumberland Plateau’s elevation is 1,500–1,800 feet above sea level. This region is described as having flat-topped mountains separated by sharp valleys. Lookout Mountain, southwest of Chattanooga, offers hang gliding, paragliding, and the Incline Railway that takes you up the steep mountainside to the top of Lookout Mountain. • The Highland Rim is west of the Cumberland Plateau, also known as the Pennyroyal region. Pennyroyal receives its name from a branched annual plant in the mint family that was used to repel insects, relieve headaches, and treat pneumonia. This area

The Great Smoky Mountains National Park is the most biodiverse national park in the United States. More than 19,000 species have been identified and documented in the park, with 10,000 species not previously known and many not seen anywhere else in the world. Scientists believe an additional 80,000–100,000 species may live there that have yet to be identified.18 Areas of the Blue Ridge Mountains, Cherokee National Forest, and Tennessee watersheds were identified as areas of exceptional biodiversity recommended as priorities for protection.19 2.3.1 Forests Tennessee’s forests cover 13,881,540 acres, or 53% of the state, with the five major forest types being oak-hickory, oak-pine, bottomland hardwoods, cove hardwoods, and pine. Because Tennessee is the number one producer of hardwood flooring, it has been called “the hardwood capital of the world.” Tennessee also has several cloud forests, the Southern Appalachian spruce-fir forest, which is a temperate forest located in the highest elevations of the eastern part of the state.20 2.3.2 Wetlands Tennessee has more than 787,000 acres of wetlands covering 3.0% of Tennessee with most located within the western area of the state. The most widespread wetland system, the Bottomland Hardwood, is primarily located in Weakley, Fayette, Shelby, and Lauderdale Counties21 -and is the largest forested wetland system in North America. Bottomland hardwoods are described as river swamps found along rivers and streams that provide important habitats for birds and many other water-loving species of plants and animals.22 2.3.3 Species The state’s enormous biodiversity contributes to many native and rare species of plants, amphibians, fish, and birds. The state currently has documented 543 rare plants, with 153 of those considered state endangered.23 The state has 21 species of frogs and 56 species of salamanders, ranking Tennessee as the third-most amphibian-diverse state. Rising temperatures increase the speed at which water evaporates from the land and bodies of water and decrease the amount of rain flowing into rivers and aquifers. Average annual rainfall increased by 5%, with much of the additional precipitation falling on the four wettest days of the year. Increasing rainfall is detrimental to crop yields, damages aquatic ecosystems, and poses an increased risk to the health of the population due to degrading water quality. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 2: Tennessee Overview 33 2.5 Demographics 2.5.1 Population Tennessee is vulnerable to natural hazards because of its large population, economic assets, widespread infrastructure, and natural and built environment, which may all be exposed to disasters. This section outlines the current conditions across each of these sectors and highlights areas of potential or inherent vulnerability. The estimated total population of Tennessee is 7,051,339 (U.S. Census Bureau, July 1, 2022), which is an increase of 10% since the 2010 census.33 As of the 2020 census, it was the 16th most populous state in the nation.34 The average population density of the state is 167.6 persons per square mile. This figure fluctuates throughout the state between rural, urban, and suburban areas. A map displaying population density per county is shown in Figure 11. Young children who are unable to care for themselves may not be able to communicate their needs during a disaster or catastrophic event. Such barriers may also limit the ability of those for whom English is not their native language to participate in the mitigation and planning processes. Of those foreign-born, 33.0% of naturalized citizens and 57.0% of noncitizens speak English less than “very well.”38 The racial composition of Tennessee, for those who self-report their race, is as follows: • 78.0% White alone • 19.0% Hispanic or Latino • 17% Black or African American alone • 2.0% Asian alone • 0.5% American Indian and Alaska Native alone • 0.1% Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islanders alone • 2.0% two or more races39 Consideration may be needed to address language and cultural barriers that impede participation and implementation of limited English-speaking households during the mitigation process.

Driving on these deteriorating roads costs the average Tennessee driver around $227 per year for repairs, increased vehicle depreciation, heightened fuel consumption, and wear and tear on tires. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 2: Tennessee Overview 47 Figure 19: Map of Tennessee Aviation System Plan Airports66 2.7.2 Railroads Thirty-four freight railroads cross Tennessee, including six Class I rail lines that cover 2,133 miles and 23 Class II rail lines that cover 806 track miles. Memphis Intermodal Facility is home to the third largest freight rail hub in the United States. Rail transportation in Tennessee is expected to grow by 130% between 2012 and 2040. However, the state has added supplemental track mileage because current lines do not provide enough track mileage to support the population increase and growth in demand for rail freight movement. One study showed differing infrastructure conditions. Class I and II track operators respectively estimated 64% and 26% of rail capacity is sufficient, but the same study showed that 41% of inspected rail lines need to be upgraded to accommodate heavier rail cars. Tennessee’s railroads employ 2,816 individuals with an average wage per person of $136,140 annually.67 Rail transportation is the most fuel-efficient method to move freight over land. By comparison, the 14.7 million tons of freight that originated in Tennessee in 2021 and were shipped by rail would have taken 815,000 trucks to transport.68 The National Railroad Passenger Corporation, more commonly known as Amtrak, provides service to three stations in Tennessee: the Memphis station, Riverfront Station69 and the Newbern-Dyersburg station, which houses a railroad museum. After the bipartisan infrastructure package was passed in November 2021, $66 billion was set aside for improvements to Amtrak services. State lawmakers want Tennessee to study the cost and feasibility of installing an Amtrak rail line that would connect Chattanooga, Knoxville, Nashville, and Memphis and include the construction of rail stations in Murfreesboro and Tullahoma. Currently, Nashville is the thirdlargest U.S. city not serviced by Amtrak.70

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 2: Tennessee Overview 48 2.7.3 Other Transportation Services There are transit services in every Tennessee county. Services include bus services on fixed routes, express buses, dial-a-ride, local shuttles, and paratransit services for individuals with qualifying disabilities. In April 2022, statewide transit ridership rebounded to only 60% of preCOVID-19 levels. Tennessee’s Department of Transportation learned through community feedback that more public transit services are needed on weeknights and weekends to make essential trips. Individuals with flexible options are choosing to use private vehicles over public transportation, which leads to increased traffic, increased exhaust emissions, and added stress on and deterioration of roadways.71 2.8 Dams According to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) National Inventory of Dams (NID), there are 1,238 dams in Tennessee, and 67% of these are privately owned. Of the 1,238 dams, 274 are classified as having high hazard potential under NID, meaning that if the dam fails, it causes severe damage and/or loss of life and property; 208 are classified as having significant hazard potential; and 282 are classified as having low hazard potential. The state regulates 147 of the 247 dams classified as having high hazard potential, and 85% of the 147 are in satisfactory condition. Emergency action plans (EAPs) are mandatory for all state-monitored dams. However, since only a small percentage of private dam operators have high hazard potential, the number of those with an EAP in case of an emergency is limited.72 Table 15 lists dams that were rated as less than satisfactory. Tennessee ranks among the top one-third of states in total energy use and ranks in the middle of the 50 states in per capita energy use. Contributing factors in energy consumption include the need for residents to travel long distances to reach dispersed locales, the state’s role as a logistics hub, and its location as a popular tourist destination. Manufacturing accounts for one-fourth of Tennessee’s energy consumption, but industrial activities also contribute the most to Tennessee’s GDP, including the manufacture of food, beverages, and tobacco products, motor vehicles and automotive parts, chemicals, fabricated metal products, and electrical equipment. The average electricity cost in Tennessee is below the national average, and the average cost for residents is among the lowest ten states.76 2.10 Drinking Water, Stormwater, and Wastewater Having safe and plentiful drinking water is imperative to maintaining the vitality of Tennessee’s communities. The Environmental Protection Agency’s Drinking Water and Infrastructure Needs Survey and Assessment report that $8.7 billion is needed over the next 20 years to maintain and improve Tennessee’s drinking water infrastructure. Funding from the 2021 American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) has facilitated the construction of utility and drinking water infrastructure projects across the State of Tennessee. Forty percent of 43 utility companies have reported struggling with treated water loss rates. Admirable public safety records and increases in investment suggest the state is seeing improved drinking water infrastructure conditions. In 2019, 12 systems were under a sewer tap moratorium due to combined sewer overflows, meaning that water from the sewer system was leaking into systems processing drinking water.

After 46% of waterways were assessed, 56% of streams and rivers were found to be contaminated with at least one pollutant, and 38% of the state’s reservoir acreage was (and remains) listed as impaired. An increasing number and level of harmful chemicals found in stormwater runoff are indicative of the need to adjust surface and catch-and-release systems to the growing population. The ARPA has provided Tennessee with $1.35 billion to go toward Tennessee’s water, wastewater, and stormwater projects.77 With an ever-increasing residential population and stress added to water systems during the tourist season, the challenge will be to update and repair these systems so as not to contribute to human health challenges.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 2: Tennessee Overview 51 2.11 Natural Environment 2.11.1 Rivers and Watersheds Figure 20: Tennessee Lakes, Rivers, and Water Resource Map78 Tennessee may rightfully boast of its extensive network of rivers and streams. These waterways span approximately 60,000 miles, with the state’s 13 major river systems representing much of this mileage. The state includes over 570,000 acres of lakes and reservoirs, 55 watersheds, and 17,000 miles of warm-water streams, with temperatures ranging from 70 degrees Fahrenheit to 90 degrees Fahrenheit in the summer.79 There is only one natural lake, Reelfoot Lake, which is recognized by the U.S. Department of the Interior as a National Natural Landmark. Reelfoot Lake, an 18,000–acre natural area in Lake and Obion Counties, was created in 1811–1812 by a series of earthquakes along the New Madrid Faultline. This area includes 10,900 acres of marshes and open water, and 7,100 acres of hardwood forests, cypress bottoms, and bogs. 2.11.1.1 Aquifers Nine principal aquifers in western Tennessee produce 200–2,000 gallons per minute of highquality groundwater. Water flow from middle and eastern Tennessee varies in yield from 50 to 2,000 gal/min. Output there is reduced because water flows through karst systems comprised of eroded rock materials, such as limestone, dolomite, or gypsum, which affect the hardness of groundwater. Tennessee’s largest underground water systems lie in western Tennessee and are part of a larger geologic structure called the Mississippi Embayment. The water in the Mississippi Embayment is between 2,000 and 3,000 years old, flows through quartz sand bodies, and is of excellent quality. Other than water used for thermoelectric purposes, 21% of the water withdrawn in Tennessee is groundwater. In 2015, 298 million gallons per day (MGD) of groundwater were provided for public and rural-domestic supplies; 52 MGD for self-supplied industries; and more than 60 MGD for irrigation and livestock uses. text: 4 4 2.15 2.1 Severe Storms 4 3 4 1 3 2.35 3.0 Terrorism 1 4 1 4 2 1.7 2.2 Tornado 4 3 2 4 1 2.2 2.8 Wildfire 4 2 2 4 2 1 2.3 No Risk Low Risk Moderate Risk High Risk The FEMA National Risk Index81 provides a composite risk score for 18 natural hazards at the county and Census tract level. These include avalanche, coastal flooding, cold wave, drought, earthquake, hail, heat wave, hurricane, ice storm, landslide, lightning, riverine flooding, strong wind, tornado, tsunami, volcanic activity, wildfire, and winter weather. The National Risk Index (NRI) is an easy-to-use, interactive tool that shows which communities are most at risk to natural hazards. It includes data about the expected annual losses to individual natural hazards, social vulnerability, and community resilience at the county and census tract levels. The risk equation behind the national Risk Index includes three components: a natural hazards risk component, a consequence enhancing component, and a consequence reduction component. Expected annual loss (EAL) is the natural hazards risk component, measuring the expected loss of building value, population, and/or agriculture value each year due to natural hazards. Social Vulnerability is the consequence enhancing component and analyzes demographic characteristics to measure the susceptibility of social groups to the adverse impacts of natural hazards. Community Resilience is the consequence reduction component and uses demographic characteristics to measure a community’s ability to prepare for, adapt to, withstand, and recover from the effects of natural hazards. The Social Vulnerability and Community Resilience components are combined into one Community Risk Factor (CRF) which is multiplied by the EAL component to calculate risk.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 63 Figure 25: Reference Map of Tennessee with the Grand Divisions Displayed East Tennessee’s dominant feature is the Appalachian Mountains, including the Great Smoky Mountains, and the eastern half of the Cumberland Plateau. This area is characterized by rugged terrain, deep valleys, and numerous rivers and streams. The highest point in the state, Clingmans Dome, is located here, offering breathtaking panoramic views. East Tennessee is known for its lush forests, waterfalls, and outdoor recreational opportunities, attracting visitors from around the world. Middle Tennessee is bordered by the Cumberland Plateau to the east and Tennessee River to the west and is a region of rolling hills and forested plateaus. The Cumberland Plateau is characterized by a mix of uplands and deep gorges, carved by rivers such as the Cumberland River. This region is known for its scenic beauty, with waterfalls, caves, and many state parks. The city of Nashville, the state capital, and a cultural hub is located in Middle Tennessee. West Tennessee is characterized by flatter terrain and fertile agricultural land. The Mississippi River forms the western boundary of the state and has played a significant role in the region's history and economy. Memphis, the second largest city in Tennessee, is in the southwest corner of the state and known for its rich musical heritage, including blues, rock 'n' roll, and soul. 3.2.2 Climate Tennessee experiences a diverse climate characterized by generally mild winters and hot, humid summers. The state's climate is influenced by several factors, including its latitude, elevation, and the Cumberland Plateau and Appalachian Mountains in the eastern part of the state. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 64 Temperature: Tennessee has a relatively moderate climate, with variations between its regions. In general, summers are warm to hot, with average high temperatures ranging from the upper 80s to low 90s Fahrenheit (30–35 degrees Celsius). Winters are generally mild, with average high temperatures ranging from the upper 30s to low 50s Fahrenheit (3-10 degrees Celsius). Figure 26: Annual Average Temperature in Tennessee, 1991–2020 Climate Normals Precipitation: Tennessee receives a significant amount of rainfall throughout the year. Annual precipitation varies across the state, ranging from around 45 inches (114 cm) in the northern Tennessee Valley to over 100 inches (254 cm) in the highest elevations of the Great Smoky Mountains National Park. The following steps were used to define the risk of each hazard: • Profile and describe each hazard ▪ Geographic areas most affected by the hazard ▪ Previous occurrences with probability and frequency estimates at the state, TEMA region (East, Middle, Southeast, and West), and county levels ▪ Impacts of climate trends and variations • Determine exposure to each hazard (community vulnerability) ▪ Exposure was determined by overlaying hazard maps with inventory of structures, facilities, and systems to determine exposure to the hazard 3.3.1 Data Limitations The primary source of historical data used throughout the risk assessment is the National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) Storm Events Database86, which provides natural hazard event data from 1950 to the present. In staying consistent with climatological studies, the NCEI Storm Events Database was evaluated for the last 27 years (1996–2022) to determine future probability and frequency of a hazard occurring. Throughout the planning process, every effort was made to use the best available data. A significant portion of data showing the historic occurrences of natural hazards was obtained through the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI). The NCEI Storm Events Database contains data from January 1950 to 2022, although storm events were recorded differently prior to 1996. From the years 1950 to 1954, the NCEI Storm

From the years 1950 to 1954, the NCEI Storm Events Database only contains information on tornado events, and thunderstorm, wind, and hail events were added to the database for the period between 1955 and 1992. All event types identified in the NWS Directive 10-1605 (48 in total) are recorded from 1996 to the present. Additionally, property damage and crop damage estimates from the NCEI Storm Events Database are a “best guess” estimate based on all available data at the time of the event publication. The NCEI Storm Events Database does not record all events, only occurrences that have sufficient intensity to cause loss of life, injuries, significant property damage, and/or disruption to commerce. The Storm Prediction Center (SPC) National Weather Service Database87 examines convective/thunderstorm-related winds only and does not include wind data from hurricane or non-thunderstorm wind damage. This data contains measured and estimated wind gusts, and associated wind damage, without estimated wind speeds. Many observed instances identify a severe thunderstorm wind event with no estimated or actual wind speed estimates. 3.4 Vulnerability Analysis Overview A Vulnerability Analysis enables the planning team to quantify and/or qualify exposure of assets to a given hazard determines how various threats and hazards impact life, property, the built environment, the natural environment, and the state’s critical operations of Tennessee. Vulnerability may be defined as the manifestation of the inherent states of the system (e.g., physical, technical, organizational, cultural) may adversely affect (cause harm or damage to) that system. Examples include identifying geographic areas that suffer damages disproportionally as compared with other locales, or the overall exposure of the entire state to terrorism. Identifying and understanding vulnerability to each threat and hazard provides a solid foundation for developing and implementing effective mitigation actions. 3.4.1 Data Limitations The Vulnerability Analysis element of each hazard profile is based on the information provided in the Risk Assessment that shows the potential impact and amount of damage that may be caused by the given hazard. The assessment was developed using the best available data collected from a variety of sources, including local, state, and federal agencies. Multiple qualitative and quantitative analyses were

The assessment was developed using the best available data collected from a variety of sources, including local, state, and federal agencies. Multiple qualitative and quantitative analyses were performed. The estimates provided in the Vulnerability Analysis enable the community to understand the relative risk to each hazard and the potential losses that may be incurred. However, loss estimation methodology deals with uncertainties stemming from incomplete scientific knowledge about a given hazard, its effects on the built environment, incomplete datasets, and approximations and simplifications necessary to provide a meaningful and complete analysis. Further, most datasets used in the assessments include records covering a relatively short periods of time, which increases the uncertainty of any statistical analysis. 3.4.2 Vulnerability Analysis Methodology To direct the vulnerability analysis effort for the state of Tennessee, two distinct methodologies were applied. The first includes a quantitative analysis that relies upon the best available data and technology, while the second methodology includes a qualitative analysis that relies more on local knowledge and rational decision making. Upon completion, the methodologies are

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 72 combined to create a Vulnerability Analysis that allows for some degree of quality control and assurance. The quantitative assessment focuses on potential hazard loss estimates, while the qualitative assessment is comprised of a scoring system built around values assigned by the Planning Team as to the likelihood of occurrence, spatial extent, and potential impact of each hazard studied. 3.4.2.1 Quantitative Methodology The quantitative methodology consists of utilizing Hazus (version 6.0),88 a FEMA geographic information system (GIS)-based loss estimation software, as well as a detailed GIS-based approach independent of the Hazus software. These two GIS-based studies together help form a quantitative vulnerability analysis. GIS technology allowed for the identification and analysis of potentially at-risk community assets such as people and infrastructure. This analysis was completed for hazards that can be spatially defined in meaningful manner (i.e., hazards with an official and scientific determined geographic extent) and for which GIS data were readily available. 3.4.2.2 Qualitative Methodology The qualitative assessment relies less on technology, but more on historical and anecdotal data regarding expected hazard impacts. The qualitative assessment completed for the state of Tennessee is based on the Priority Risk Index (PRI)89. The purpose of the PRI is to prioritize all potential hazards, and then group them into three categories of high, moderate, or low risk to identify and prioritize mitigation opportunities. For the state of Tennessee, an additional category (Vulnerability) was utilized that measured each of the Tennessee Emergency Management Agency (TEMA) region’s (East, Southeast, Middle, and West) vulnerability to a hazard based on the impact each hazard would have on the public; responders; continuity of operations; property, facilities, and infrastructure; the environment; the economic condition of the jurisdiction; and public confidence in the jurisdiction’s governance. The PRI is a good practice to use when prioritizing hazards because it provides a standardized numerical value for hazards to be compared. With the addition of Vulnerability, adapted PRI scores were calculated using six categories under the Enhanced Priority Risk Index (EPRI): • Probability • Impact • Spatial Extent • Warning Time • Duration • Vulnerability

text: Development in the TEMA regions (East, Southeast, Middle, and West) has significantly impacted the state’s assets, leading to economic growth, improved transportation infrastructure, and advancements in education and healthcare. Since the last plan update, there have been over 130 new constructions of state assets in Tennessee and over 300 state assets have been renovated. New state asset construction accounts for over $1.3 billion in state asset values with renovations adding an additional $573 million in state asset values. 3.5 Land Cover and Land Development Trends Over the years, Tennessee has undergone significant land cover and land development changes. Urbanization has been a prominent trend, with major cities like Nashville, Knoxville, and Chattanooga experiencing rapid growth. As urban areas expand, agricultural land and natural landscapes have given way to residential, commercial, and industrial zones. The state's forests, which once covered around 52% of the land area, have faced gradual loss. Forest fragmentation, urban development, agriculture, and timber harvesting have contributed to the reduction in forest cover. This loss of forests raises concerns about habitat fragmentation and the potential impacts on biodiversity. Agriculture has long been an important land use in Tennessee, with activities such as livestock farming, crop cultivation (including corn, soybeans, tobacco, and cotton), and poultry production. However, the conversion of agricultural land into urban areas has impacted the agricultural sector. The construction and expansion of transportation infrastructure have also shaped land cover changes in Tennessee. The state has an extensive network of highways, railways, and airports. The following examples illustrate how vulnerabilities can change rapidly: • Uncontrolled residential growth can expose a population to hazard-prone areas. • Rapid population growth can surpass a community's capacity to protect itself, such as ensuring sufficient water resources during a drought. • Swift development can strain a community's vulnerable resources, including the energy infrastructure. • Residential development that prioritizes quick and inexpensive construction to meet consumer demand often lacks long-term mitigation measures and resilience. • Fast-tracked development, driven by consumer demand, can alter the landscape in ways that affect urban runoff, drainage, and other environmental factors, leading to significant effects on floodplains. • Increased businesses can result in a higher transportation volume of hazardous materials throughout the state, either for production or maintenance purposes. • The presence of businesses engaged in producing chemicals and managing hazardous materials may elevate the community risk because stockpiles are located there, and/or chemicals/hazardous materials are transported to or from a site. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 91 Development in Tennessee is not limited to urban areas. The state has also seen the establishment and expansion of various industries across the state, including manufacturing, healthcare, finance, and tourism. These sectors have contributed to job creation and economic growth across the state, which promotes development of both urban and rural areas. Moreover, Tennessee's natural landscapes and recreational assets have attracted investment in the tourism and hospitality sectors. The state's music heritage, outdoor activities, and historical sites have made it a popular destination for visitors. Population and development trends can vary across different regions of the state. While urban areas have experienced substantial growth, rural areas have faced challenges such as population decline and limited economic opportunities. Efforts are in place to address these disparities and promote balanced development across the state. Overall, Tennessee's population growth and development trends highlight the state's appeal as a place to live, work, and visit. The ongoing efforts to manage growth, enhance infrastructure, and promote economic diversification will continue to shape the future trajectory of the state's population and development. The extensive nature of these threats, coupled with the usual involvement of multiple agencies in responding to even isolated incidents, underscores the critical significance of protocols and prompt dissemination of public health information. Moreover, it is crucial to recognize that communicable diseases, even those not typically considered major public health risks, can propagate swiftly within confined spaces or through contaminated public resources following emergencies and the subsequent relocation of large populations. Consequently, well-established procedures are imperative to ensure appropriate sanitation measures, timely triage, and comprehensive reporting of cases during periods of overcrowding in temporary housing, shelters, or residential facilities. The recent COVID-19 pandemic is a good example of how disease outbreaks can rapidly evolve into much larger-scale incidents that have wide-ranging effects on the health of the population, the economy, and the supply chain of many different services and materials. Several primary diseases of concern in the state of Tennessee have been identified, along with the potential impact of climate trends and variations, and other possible risk factors for communicable diseases. Pandemic Refers to an epidemic that has spread over several countries or continents, usually affecting a large number of people. 3.7.1.1.1 COVID-19 COVID-19, or coronavirus disease 2019, is a disease caused by the virus SARS-Co-V-2. It is considered a respiratory illness but can affect other areas of the body besides the respiratory system and lungs. Respiratory symptoms can range from mild to severe. COVID-19 was declared a public health emergency of international concern (PHEIC) on January 30, 2020, and identified as a global pandemic by the World Health Organization on March 11, 2020. The United States declared COVID-19 a national emergency on March 13, 2020, and the United States ended the public health emergency declaration on May 11, 2023. The state of Tennessee declared COVID-19 a public health emergency on March 11, 2020. Additional guidance and recommendations on gatherings and closure were issued in the weeks following and are detailed in the Tennessee Department of Health’s (TDH) COVID-19 timeline. 3.7.1.1.2 Influenza Influenza is a seasonal acute respiratory illness caused by the influenza virus. Globally, there are four types of influenza: A, B, C, and D. Types A and B circulate regularly among people and cause seasonal epidemics. Type A is further classified based on the proteins on the surface of the virus (hemagglutinin and neuraminidase). Currently, subtypes H1N1 and H3N2 are circulating in humans. Historically, influenza A is the

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: D. Types A and B circulate regularly among people and cause seasonal epidemics. Type A is further classified based on the proteins on the surface of the virus (hemagglutinin and neuraminidase). Currently, subtypes H1N1 and H3N2 are circulating in humans. Historically, influenza A is the only type of influenza that has been known to cause a pandemic. Type B is not broken into subtypes but is broken down into lineages. Currently, influenza B/ Yamagata and B/ Victoria lineage are the two circulating. Type C occurs less frequently and causes relatively mild illness and is not considered an influenza type of public health importance. Type D is not known to cause infection or illness in humans and is primarily found in cattle. 3.7.1.1.3 Vector-Borne Diseases Vector-borne diseases are human illnesses caused by parasites, viruses, and bacteria that are transmitted by a vector, often through the bite of an infected organism. Global examples include Malaria, dengue fever, Lyme disease, and others. Prevention of these diseases requires multiprong efforts to mitigate the disease and vector populations. Tickborne diseases (TBD) are spread through the bite of an infected tick. The pathogens responsible for TBD infections can be bacteria, viruses, or parasites. These pathogens can cause a variety of diseases, however within the state of Tennessee the most common are: Spotted Fever Rickettsiosis, Lyme Disease, Ehrlichiosis, and Anaplasmosis.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 104 Diseases spread by ticks continue to be a growing concern in Tennessee, as tick populations have continued to increase over the past two decades. Ticks prefer to live in grassy, brushy, or wooded areas and are more likely to bite humans during the warmer months of the year. However, the black-legged or deer tick is potentially a threat during colder months as well. Mosquito-borne diseases are spread through the bite of an infected mosquito. Like ticks, infected mosquitos can spread many diseases. While rare, infections of West Nile Virus, Eastern Equine Encephalitis, and La Crosse Encephalitis are of particular concern, as there are no current vaccines available for prevention, infections can be severe and potentially fatal, and the treatment for infection is only supportive. 3.7.1.1.4 Hepatitis A Hepatitis A is a vaccine preventable disease that affects the liver and is spread through the feces of an infected person. It is highly contagious and is transmitted through person to person contact and from contaminated food or drinks. Those who are at high risk for Hepatitis A infection include those who travel internationally, people who use or inject drugs, men who have sex with men, people experiencing homelessness, and people with occupational exposure risk. 3.7.1.2 Risk Assessment – Communicable Disease 3.7.1.2.1 Geographic Extent COVID-19 was a global pandemic with cases and deaths occurring globally. Some studies have found that COVID spreads easier in cooler, less humid climates, so changes in temperature may affect transmission. Conversely, the COVID-19 pandemic had some impacts on the environment. The limitations on travel and other economic sectors due to COVID-19 restrictions decreased air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions within a few weeks of restrictions being put in place. Similar to COVID-19, influenza may be impacted by climate trends. Influenza is already considered to be seasonal in nature and typically vaccines are created based on what circulates during influenza season in the southern hemisphere for the northern hemisphere and vice versa. Changes in seasonal temperatures could influence transmission of influenza and when influenza seasons start. For example, the 2022–2023 influenza season started early in Tennessee, prior to many individuals getting their influenza vaccines. Studies have found evidence that climate trends and variations contribute to the expanding range of suitable tick habitats. As temperatures and humidity rise, it is believed that tick habitats will continue to expand, increasing the risk of exposure to infected ticks. Longer, warmer summers have given

Many infectious diseases are vaccine preventable (e.g., Hepatitis A) entirely or have reduced transmission, extent, and severity (e.g., influenza, COVID-19). Vaccines are a powerful public health tool to prevent and mitigate disease and reduce the potential for outbreaks. Increases in vaccine hesitancy are of concern as herd immunity is necessary to help reduce the likelihood of outbreaks. 3.7.1.3.2 Vulnerable Population Population increases could increase the risk of infectious disease outbreaks and their impact on hazard mitigation for Tennessee. In 2022, the state added 83,000 residents from domestic migration, an increase in population by 1.2% after a .6% increase in 2021. An increase in the population can impact infectious disease risk. For example, areas with higher population densities saw earlier outbreaks of COVID-19. Population density has been found to be a risk factor in infectious disease spread particularly for diseases that spread from person to person and through food and water. Further, vector-borne illnesses can also increase or change patterns with increasing population density. Various populations are vulnerable to communicable diseases, and understanding these groups is crucial for effective public health interventions. title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: communicable diseases, and understanding these groups is crucial for effective public health interventions. One vulnerable population consists of infants and young children whose immune systems are still developing, making them more susceptible to infections. Their close proximity in daycare centers and schools increases the risk of disease transmission. Another vulnerable group includes the elderly, particularly those with pre-existing health conditions or weakened immune systems. Age-related decline in immune function can make them more susceptible to infectious diseases and increase the severity of illness. Long-term care facilities and nursing homes often house a significant proportion of elderly individuals, further amplifying the risk of disease outbreaks. Individuals with compromised immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS, cancer, organ transplants, or autoimmune diseases, are highly vulnerable. These conditions weaken their ability to fight off infections, leaving them more susceptible to communicable diseases. Strict infection control measures and targeted prevention strategies are essential for protecting this group. Homeless populations also face increased vulnerability to communicable diseases due to factors such as crowded living conditions, limited access to healthcare, poor nutrition, and higher rates of substance abuse. These circumstances can contribute to the spread of infections like tuberculosis, hepatitis, and respiratory illnesses within homeless communities.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 113 3.7.2 Dam/Levee Failure 3.7.2.1 Hazard Profile – Dam/Levee Failure Dams are water storage, control, or diversion barriers that impound water upstream and in reservoirs. Dams are a vital part of our nation’s infrastructure, providing drinking water, flood protection, renewable hydroelectric power, navigation, irrigation, and recreation. These critical daily benefits are also inextricably linked to the potential harmful consequences of a dam failure. Dam failure is a collapse or breach in a structure. A dam failure can result in severe loss of life, economic disaster, and extensive environmental damage. While most dams have storage volumes small enough that failures have few repercussions, dams with large storage volumes can cause significant flooding downstream. Dam failures often have a rapid rate of onset, leaving little time for evacuation. The first signs of failure may go unnoticed upon visual inspection of the dam structure. However, continual maintenance and inspection of dams often provides the opportunity to identify possible deficiencies in their earlier stages and can prevent a possible catastrophic failure event. The duration of the flooding event caused by the failure depends largely on the amount of water and downstream topography. Given smaller volumes of water and topography suited for transporting the water rapidly downstream, the event may only last hours. Because of the lack of seasonality and other predictive factors, a predictive frequency or likelihood of dam failures is difficult to determine. However, the National Dam Safety Program (NDPS) produces hazard rankings (high, significant, and low) and definitions of dam structures, based on potential impact. These rankings can be defined as the following: • High:

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: a predictive frequency or likelihood of dam failures is difficult to determine. However, the National Dam Safety Program (NDPS) produces hazard rankings (high, significant, and low) and definitions of dam structures, based on potential impact. These rankings can be defined as the following: • High: Dams assigned the high hazard potential classification are those where failure or mis-operation will probably cause loss of human life. • Significant: Dams assigned the significant hazard potential classification are those dams where failure or mis-operation results in no probable loss of human life, but can cause economic loss, environmental damage, disruption of lifeline facilities, and other various indirect impacts. Significant hazard potential classification dams are often located in predominately rural or agricultural areas but could be located in areas with population and significant infrastructure. • Low: Dams assigned the low hazard potential classification are those where failure or mis-operation results in no probable loss of human life and low economic and/or environmental losses. Losses are principally limited to the owner’s property. Dam failures can result from any one of or a combination of the following causes: • Prolonged periods of rainfall and flooding, which cause most failures; • Inadequate spillway capacity, resulting in excess overtopping flows or a controlled spillway release; • Internal erosion caused by embankment or foundation leakage or piping;

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 114 • Improper maintenance, including failure to remove trees, repair internal seepage problems, replace lost material from the cross-section of the dam and abutments, or maintain gates, valves, and other operational components; • Improper design, including the use of improper construction materials and construction practices; • Negligent operation, including the failure to remove or open gates or valves during high flow periods; • Failure of upstream dams on the same waterway; • Landslides into reservoirs, which cause surges that result in overtopping; • High winds, which can cause significant wave action and result in substantial erosion; and • Earthquakes, which typically cause longitudinal cracks at the tops of the embankments that can weaken entire structures. • Wildfires can alter the landscape around dams, increasing the potential for landslides/mudslides that could cause direct and indirect structural damage. • Sinkholes forming near or under a dam may compromise the dam’s stability. In October 2014, a sinkhole was found next to the Boone Dam in northeast Tennessee and the dam required repairs that took approximately 7 years to complete. The reservoir above the dam did not store water for the duration of the repair project (https://www.tva.com/newsroom/boone-dam-project). • Upstream flooding due to a dam can occur when water accumulates or backs up behind the dam, inundating areas upstream due to excessive reservoir inflow, blockage or malfunction of the dam, reduced reservoir capacity, or ice jams. The environmental impact of a dam failure is multifaceted and can have far-reaching consequences. One of the most immediate and severe effects is flooding, as the sudden breach of the dam releases

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: inflow, blockage or malfunction of the dam, reduced reservoir capacity, or ice jams. The environmental impact of a dam failure is multifaceted and can have far-reaching consequences. One of the most immediate and severe effects is flooding, as the sudden breach of the dam releases a tremendous volume of water downstream. This floodwater can inundate and damage ecosystems, erode soil, and lead to sedimentation in rivers and lakes which can disrupt aquatic habitats and degrade water quality. Additionally, the release of water from the dam can carry contaminants from upstream sources polluting downstream water bodies and posing a significant threat to aquatic life. The destruction of habitats and altered flow regimes resulting from the dam failure can lead to a loss of biodiversity, impacting plant and animal species in the affected areas. In Tennessee there are 1,238 dams with an average age of 54 years, with 274 of them identified as high hazard potential dams (HHPD). TEMA has been highly involved with the Safe Dams Program as well.102 TEMA developed ArcGIS dashboards that have inundation maps of some HHPDs as well as all EAPS. This allows for transparent communication between the EMA Directors and the dam owners (many of which are private). While inundation has been modeled and digitized into a GIS for some HHPDs, modeling and digitization is ongoing for all other

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 115 HHPDs. This presents a data limitation, resulting in an inability to assess overall exposure and state asset exposure in all parts of the state. Additionally, while an EAP is available for all regulated dams on file, many are outdated and have limited value. An EAP update process is ongoing through a grant-funded agreement with Tennessee Tech University and a one-time budget request out of the General Fund for $500,000 to hire a consultant to complete the dam breach analysis for the State Park-owned dams and some other high-risk dams throughout the state. 3.7.2.1.1 Levee Failure Levees and floodwalls are flood control barriers constructed of earth, concrete, or other materials. For the purposes of this plan, levees are distinguished from smaller flood barriers (such as berms) by their size and extent. Berms are barriers that only protect a small number of structures, or at times only a single structure. Levees and floodwalls are barriers that protect significant areas of residential, commercial, or industrial development; at a minimum, they protect a neighborhood or small community. A levee failure involves the overtopping, breach, or collapse of the levee and is especially destructive to nearby development during flood events. The effects of a levee failure on property are similar to that of a flood, as discussed in the flooding section. One major difference is that the velocity of the water is increased in the area of the breach, so the potential for property damage is higher in these areas. Levees are normally monitored during these events and the population in danger is alerted to a possible levee failure. 3.7.2.2 Risk Assessment – Dam/Levee Failure 3.7.2.2.1 Geographic Extent Tennessee currently has 274 high hazard potential dams (HHPD) within its borders. Each dam serves various purposes, including flood control, water supply, hydroelectric power generation, and recreation. The geographic extent of dams in Tennessee spans across different regions of the state. Some notable dams include: • Norris Dam: Located on the Clinch River in northeastern Tennessee, Norris Dam is one of the largest dams in the state. It forms Norris Lake, which stretches across multiple counties and provides recreational opportunities, as well as flood control and hydroelectric power generation. • Chickamauga Dam: Situated on the Tennessee River in Chattanooga, Chickamauga Dam creates Chickamauga Lake, which extends upstream into Tennessee and Georgia. It primarily serves for flood control and navigation purposes. • Watts Bar Dam: Found on the Tennessee River near Spring City, Watts Bar Dam forms Watts Bar Lake. This dam serves as a major producer of hydroelectric power and offers recreational activities such as boating and fishing.

The dam provides flood control and hydroelectric power, along with recreational opportunities. • Pickwick Landing Dam: Situated on the Tennessee River near Savannah, Pickwick Landing Dam forms Pickwick Lake. It serves as a vital component of the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) system, providing flood control, navigation, and power generation. As global temperatures rise and weather patterns become more erratic, the functioning and effectiveness of these critical infrastructure systems are increasingly compromised. One of the major impacts of climate trends on dams and levees is the intensification of precipitation events. Higher temperatures contribute to increased evaporation rates, which, in turn, leads to more moisture in the atmosphere. This results in heavier rainfall and an elevated risk of extreme precipitation events which could overwhelm the capacity of dams and challenge the ability of levees to contain floodwaters. Refer to the Flood/Extreme Precipitation and Extreme Temperatures sections for additional information about projected changes for these hazards that would have a direct impact on potential dam and levee failure. Additionally, climate trends and variations can impact the long-term viability of dams and their water storage capacities. Changes in precipitation patterns can result in more frequent and severe droughts in certain regions, reducing the availability of water resources behind dams. Refer to the Drought section for additional information on the potential impact of climate trends and variations for this hazard. Inadequate water levels not only affect water supply for human consumption and agriculture but also limit the generation of hydroelectric power. Additionally, climate trends can affect the structural integrity of dams and levees. Higher temperatures can

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 137 3.7.2.3.1 Estimated Impact and Potential Losses The failure of dams and levees can have catastrophic impacts on infrastructure, leading to widespread damage and disruption. When a dam or levee fails, it can result in uncontrolled flooding, posing a significant threat to roads, bridges, buildings, and other vital infrastructure components. The immediate impact of dam and levee failures is the inundation of surrounding areas with floodwaters. This can submerge roads, rendering them impassable or even causing their complete destruction. Bridges may collapse under the force of the rushing water, cutting off vital transportation routes and isolating communities. The loss of road and bridge infrastructure severely hampers the movement of people, goods, and emergency services, making it challenging to provide aid and relief to affected areas. The failure of dams and levees also poses a grave risk to buildings and structures. Floodwaters can submerge residential and commercial areas, causing extensive damage to foundations, walls, and electrical systems. The force of the water can weaken or collapse structures, leading to the loss of homes, businesses, and public facilities. This not only disrupts the lives of individuals and communities but also impairs the functioning of essential services such as healthcare facilities, schools, and government offices. Moreover, the failure of dams and levees can have cascading effects on other critical infrastructure systems. Floodwaters can damage or destroy power plants, water treatment facilities, and telecommunication networks. This can result in widespread power outages, compromised water supply, and the loss of communication capabilities. The disruption of these essential services further compounds the challenges faced by affected communities and prolongs

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: Floodwaters can damage or destroy power plants, water treatment facilities, and telecommunication networks. This can result in widespread power outages, compromised water supply, and the loss of communication capabilities. The disruption of these essential services further compounds the challenges faced by affected communities and prolongs the recovery process. The long-term impact of dam and levee failures on infrastructure is significant. Rebuilding and repairing the damaged infrastructure require substantial financial resources, time, and effort. Communities may experience prolonged periods of disruption, economic losses, and displacement. The recovery process involves not only repairing physical structures but also restoring essential services, rebuilding transportation networks, and ensuring the safety and resilience of the infrastructure against future events. Currently, there are no up-to-date emergency action plans for high hazard potential dams in the state of Tennessee that provide the inundation zones. A few inundation zones were previously modeled in Middle Tennessee and these zones were used to identify state assets within these zones, but these zones need to be updated and it may be misleading to provide the size of the population at risk as well as the specific critical infrastructure/facilities and community lifelines that may be in these zones. Therefore, a data deficiency is declared for dam inundation zones for high hazard potential dams in the state of Tennessee and the impacts it could have on specific institutions and critical infrastructure/facilities and community lifelines within the hazard area. The state of Tennessee will continue to work with the United States Army Corps of Engineers and higher education entities to develop emergency action plans for these dams and

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 138 identify specific institutions and critical infrastructure/facilities and community lifelines within the hazard area. 3.7.2.3.2 Vulnerable Population The failure of dams and levees can have devastating consequences on the population, leading to significant loss of life, displacement, and long-term socio-economic impacts. When a dam or levee fails, it can result in uncontrolled flooding, posing a grave threat to the safety and wellbeing of the population living in and downstream of the affected areas. One of the immediate impacts of dam and levee failures is the risk of drowning and physical harm to individuals. The sudden release of a large volume of water can inundate communities, trapping people in their homes or forcing them to seek refuge on rooftops or higher ground. Swift-moving floodwaters can sweep away individuals, making rescue and evacuation efforts extremely challenging. The loss of life due to drowning and other water-related incidents is a tragic consequence of such failures. Moreover, the failure of dams and levees can lead to widespread displacement of the population. Residents in affected areas may be forced to evacuate their homes and seek temporary shelter in emergency facilities or with friends and relatives. Displacement disrupts lives, separates families, and strains the resources and capacities of hosting communities. It can also result in long-term homelessness and the need for extensive efforts to provide adequate housing and support for the affected population. In addition to the immediate physical risks, dam and levee failures can have long-term socioeconomic impacts on the affected population. The loss of homes, businesses, and infrastructure disrupts local economies and livelihoods. Individuals may lose their

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: provide adequate housing and support for the affected population. In addition to the immediate physical risks, dam and levee failures can have long-term socioeconomic impacts on the affected population. The loss of homes, businesses, and infrastructure disrupts local economies and livelihoods. Individuals may lose their jobs, and businesses may be unable to operate, leading to financial instability and hardship. The recovery and reconstruction process can be lengthy, causing prolonged economic disruptions and affecting the overall well-being of the population. Furthermore, the psychological and emotional toll on the affected population cannot be overlooked. Dam and levee failures are traumatic events that can cause immense stress, anxiety, and grief among survivors. The loss of loved ones, possessions, and a sense of security can have long-lasting psychological impacts on individuals and communities. Mental health support and counseling become crucial in helping the population cope with the trauma and rebuild their lives. Populations vulnerable to dam and levee failure encompass various groups that face increased risks. One particular vulnerable group includes communities living downstream of dams or along the path of potential floodwaters caused by dam or levee failure. These individuals and families are at a high risk of sudden, large-scale flooding if the structures fail to hold back the water effectively. Low-lying areas and floodplains are especially susceptible to the impacts of dam and levee failures. These regions, often prone to flooding, face an elevated risk of inundation when these

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 139 structures fail. Consequently, populations residing in these areas are more vulnerable to the devastating consequences of such failures. Urban areas and densely populated regions situated near dams or along rivers protected by levees also exhibit heightened vulnerability. The concentration of infrastructure, utilities, and a larger number of residents in these areas increases the potential impact of dam or levee failures. The risks include widespread flooding, damage to critical infrastructure, and the safety and well-being of a significant population. Socioeconomically disadvantaged communities face greater vulnerability to dam and levee failures. Limited resources, inadequate access to early warning systems, and insufficient evacuation plans or means to evacuate can compound their challenges during such emergencies. These factors further exacerbate their vulnerability and can result in disproportionate impacts on these communities. 3.7.2.3.3 Impact on State Assets The following maps show areas where state assets are located within leveed areas. There are a total of 85 state assets located within leveed areas.
