text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 146 3.7.3 Drought 3.7.3.1 Hazard Profile – Drought A drought is a deficiency in water availability over an extended period. Drought is a unique hazard, in that unlike other natural hazards, no specific threshold of “dryness” exists for declaring a drought. In addition, the definition of drought depends on stakeholder needs. There are four different types of drought and each is defined in Table 51. Table 51: Types of Drought with Definition of Each Type of Drought Definition Meteorological Occurs when observed precipitation has been significantly lower than average or normal levels over a period of time Agricultural Occurs when precipitation and soil water storage cannot satisfy the demand for water in crops. Hydrological Occurs when surface and sub-surface water levels are significantly lower than average or normal levels. Socioeconomic Occurs when water deficiencies begin to significantly impact human population in an area. It is important to note that the lack of precipitation alone does not constitute drought; the season during which the precipitation is lacking has a major impact on whether drought occurs. For example, a week of no precipitation in July, when the solar energy to evaporate water and vegetation’s need for water to conduct photosynthesis are both high, may trigger a drought, while a week of no precipitation in January when evapotranspiration is low may not initiate a drought. Each type of drought can be triggered or ended by different conditions, for instance, the onset (and end) of an agricultural drought tends to be quick, as crops need water every few days; once they get rainfall, they improve. But hydrologic

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: not initiate a drought. Each type of drought can be triggered or ended by different conditions, for instance, the onset (and end) of an agricultural drought tends to be quick, as crops need water every few days; once they get rainfall, they improve. But hydrologic drought sets in (and is alleviated) only over longer time periods. A few dry days will not drain a reservoir, but one week of slightly above normal rainfall cannot replenish it either. Moreover, different geographical regions define drought differently based on the deviation from local, normal precipitation. For example, in the more humid/wet eastern United States, the impacts of drought can happen quicker or be noticed sooner than in the naturally drier areas of the western United States. Drought can occur anywhere, triggered by changes in the local-to-regional-scale atmospheric circulation over an area, or by broader-scale circulation variations such as the expansion of semi-permanent oceanic high-pressure systems or the stalling of an upper-level atmospheric ridge in place over a region. The severity of a drought depends upon the degree and duration of moisture deficiency, as well as the size of the affected area. Periods of drought also tend to be associated with other hazards, such as wildfires and/or heat waves. Lastly, drought is a slow onset occurrence, causing less direct—but tremendous indirect—damage.

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 147 Droughts can have significant environmental, agricultural, health, and economic impacts. Common direct impacts of drought include diminished crop yields or total crop loss, the depletion of aquifers, livestock mortality, soil erosion, dust storms, wildfires, reduced electricity production from hydroelectric dams, and reduced water quality or availability. Drought can impact both surface water and groundwater availability and can potentially have direct, disastrous effects on human populations. The indirect consequences of drought, such as unemployment, reduced tax revenues, increased food prices, reduced outdoor recreation opportunities, higher energy costs as water levels in reservoirs decrease and consumption increases, and water rationing, are not often fully known. This complex web of impacts causes drought to affect people and economies well beyond the area physically experiencing the drought. It can be difficult to determine when a drought begins or ends, but there are several metrics/indicators of drought, such as departure from normal precipitation, departure from normal stream flow, or soil moisture deficits. Researchers have developed several drought indices to help define the onset, severity, and end of droughts; each drought index brings together data related to the supply of or demand for water in the environment. Drought is often measured using the Palmer Drought Severity Index (PDSI, also known operationally as the Palmer Drought Index). The PDSI, first developed by Wayne Palmer in a 1965 paper for the U.S. Weather Bureau, measures drought through recent precipitation and temperature data regarding a basic supply-and-demand model of soil moisture. It is most effective in long-term calculations. Three other indices used to measure drought are the Palmer Hydrologic Drought Index

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: in a 1965 paper for the U.S. Weather Bureau, measures drought through recent precipitation and temperature data regarding a basic supply-and-demand model of soil moisture. It is most effective in long-term calculations. Three other indices used to measure drought are the Palmer Hydrologic Drought Index (PHDI), the Crop Moisture Index (CMI), which is derived from the PDSI, and the Keetch-Byram Drought Index (KBDI), created by John Keetch and George Byram in 1968 for the U.S. Forest Service. The KBDI is used mainly for predicting the likelihood of wildfire outbreaks. As a compromise, the PDSI is used most often for droughts since it is a medium-response drought indicator. The objective of the PDSI is to provide measurements of moisture conditions that are standardized so that comparisons using the index can be made between locations and between months. The U.S. Drought Monitor is a map released every Thursday, showing parts of the U.S. that are in drought using five categories to describe the intensity of drought conditions. The U.S. Drought Monitor relies on experts to synthesize the best available data from drought indices and other sources and work with local observers to interpret the information. The U.S. Drought Monitor also incorporates ground truthing and information about drought impacts, via a network of more than 450 observers across the country, including state climatologists, National Weather Service staff, Extension agents, and hydrologists. While the entire planning area can experience drought, the major impact of a drought occurrence in the state is on the agricultural community, which makes up more than 40% of the land in Tennessee, per the Tennessee Farm Bureau. The mountainous Eastern region of Tennessee produces cattle, hay, goats, vegetables, and tobacco; Middle Tennessee produces wheat, corn, poultry, equine, and nursery crops; and the rich farmland of West Tennessee is responsible for cotton, corn, wheat, sorghum, and soybeans. The worst-case scenario for the state of Tennessee would be an exceptional drought (D4). September 2019–November 2019 – There was an accelerated period of drought over three months. The lack of rainfall and well-above normal temperatures caused drought conditions to expand across the state during September. Tennessee started the month with only 4.24% of the state reporting drought conditions, but by October 1, 100% of the state was in some level of drought. The strongest drought (D3-Extreme Drought) was found in 0.10% of the state, in parts of Franklin and Marion counties at the border with Alabama, while D2 (Severe Drought) covered 15.8% of the state, mainly in East and Middle Tennessee. Above-normal precipitation in October produced weekly improvements in drought conditions. By the end of the month, drought conditions were cleared from West Tennessee and most of Middle Tennessee, but East Tennessee remained in drought consideration due to the lack of rainfall in the area. At the start of November, large areas of East Tennessee and the Cumberland Plateau remained in drought conditions from the flash drought that affected the state earlier in the fall. However, this area of the state also recorded some of the highest precipitation totals over the month, leading to weekly improvements in drought conditions. By the last Drought Monitor release at the end of November, all but a few small areas of D0 had been cleared from the state.

The Fourth National Climate Assessment (2018) states that climate trends are

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 160 expected to increase the average temperature and the number of high-heat days in the southeastern United States and intensify the hydrologic cycle, leading to an increase in both extreme precipitation events and periods of drought in the southeastern United States. This intensification of the hydrologic cycle will likely lead to increasing numbers of flash droughts, which are defined by the rapid onset or intensification of drought conditions. Flash droughts in the southeastern United States are often connected to short periods of time (a couple of weeks or months) with much higher-than-normal temperatures and much lower-than-normal precipitation leading to the rapid depletion of soil moisture and streamflow. September 2019 is a prime example of a flash drought in Tennessee, and more broadly across the southeast. From the September 3 to the October 1 release of the U.S. Drought Monitor, Tennessee went from 95.76% of the state being free of drought or abnormally dry conditions to 0% of the state being free of drought or abnormally dry conditions.

While there is no direct impact on the populace of the state as it pertains to injuries and fatalities, social impacts such as public safety, health, and conflicts between the populace and entities over water rights have the potential to occur due to drought conditions. For instance, anxiety and depression over economic losses caused by drought may occur, health problems related to low water flows and poor water quality may impact the populace, farmers may encounter health issues due to an increase in dust, forest fires may increase, and there may be fewer outdoor recreational activities due to the lack of water. Based on historical records, there have been no reported direct injuries or fatalities a result of drought within the state of Tennessee. Various populations are vulnerable to the impacts of drought, and understanding these groups is important for effective mitigation and support. Agricultural communities and farmers are particularly vulnerable as drought conditions can lead to crop failures, livestock losses, and economic hardships. Their livelihoods heavily depend on water availability for irrigation and sustenance of crops and livestock. Rural populations face increased vulnerability to drought. Limited access to alternative water sources, reliance on rain-fed agriculture, and inadequate infrastructure for water storage and distribution can potentially exacerbate challenges during periods of water scarcity. These

text: water availability for irrigation and sustenance of crops and livestock. Rural populations face increased vulnerability to drought. Limited access to alternative water sources, reliance on rain-fed agriculture, and inadequate infrastructure for water storage and distribution can potentially exacerbate challenges during periods of water scarcity. These communities may experience water shortages for drinking, sanitation, and daily needs. Urban populations are not immune to the effects of drought either. Water supply systems in cities can be strained during droughts, leading to water rationing, reduced availability, and increased costs. Vulnerable urban populations, including low-income communities, may struggle to afford water or face inadequate access to water sources during times of scarcity. Furthermore, ecosystems and wildlife are also highly vulnerable to drought. Aquatic habitats, wetlands, and rivers may experience reduced water flows, leading to habitat degradation and loss of biodiversity. This, in turn, can disrupt ecosystem services and have cascading effects on both human and animal populations. 3.7.3.3.3 Impact on State Assets All state assets are vulnerable to drought and its various impacts.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 172 3.7.4 Earthquake 3.7.4.1 Hazard Profile – Earthquake An earthquake is the motion or trembling of the ground produced by sudden displacement of rock in the Earth’s crust. Earthquakes result from crustal strain, volcanism, landslides, or the collapse of caverns. Earthquakes can affect hundreds of thousands of square miles; cause damage to property measured in the tens of billions of dollars; result in loss of life and injury to hundreds of thousands of persons; and disrupt the social and economic functioning of the affected area. Most property damage and earthquake-related deaths are caused by the failure and collapse of structures due to ground shaking. The level of damage depends upon the amplitude and duration of the shaking, which are directly related to the earthquake size, distance from the fault, site, and regional geology. Most earthquakes are caused by the release of stress accumulated because of the rupture of rocks along opposing fault planes in the Earth’s outer crust. These fault planes are typically found along the borders of the Earth’s ten tectonic plates. These plate borders generally follow the outlines of the continents, with the North American plate following the continental border with the Pacific Ocean in the west but following the mid-Atlantic ridge to the east. Earthquakes occurring in the mid-Atlantic ridge usually pose little danger to humans. Figure 81: National Seismic Hazard Model117 Faults can be defined as boundaries between two areas of rock that form in areas of high stress, for example where the motions of two lithosphere plates force them into one another. title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 173 these areas, extreme stress may cause the rock to break, forming a plane known as a fault. Once a fault has formed, the shearing resistance for continued movement of the fault is less than the shearing resistance required to fracture new intact rock. Thus, faults that have generated earthquakes in the recent past are likely to produce earthquakes in the future. Earthquakes shake the ground because fault rupture releases vibrations that radiate in the form of seismic energy. These earthquake waves, also called body waves, come in two distinct forms: Primary or "P" waves and Secondary or "S" waves. When body waves reach the free surface of the earth some of their energy is converted into complex surface waves that are trapped near the surface of the Earth and produce generally lower frequency ground motions. P waves are compressional waves that do not produce much damage. They can move through any type of material and travel at almost twice the speed of S waves. S waves are shear waves that can often be seen on the ground surface and deform the ground perpendicular to their direction of travel. Unlike P waves, S waves are unable to pass through fluids such as water and magma. When S waves deform the ground, it causes lateral or shear (back and forth) forces on structures. Older buildings were constructed primarily to withstand gravity (vertical forces); therefore, they are more prone to fail due to the strong lateral motions experienced during a big earthquake. Both P and S waves are generated across a broad spectrum of frequencies.

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: forth) forces on structures. Older buildings were constructed primarily to withstand gravity (vertical forces); therefore, they are more prone to fail due to the strong lateral motions experienced during a big earthquake. Both P and S waves are generated across a broad spectrum of frequencies. The higher the frequency, the faster the energy from the earthquake attenuates, or dissipates, with distance. Also, due to this loss of energy or attenuation and geometrical spreading, locations close to the source of the rupture that caused the earthquake will receive more energy (and shaking) than more distant locations. When P and S waves arrive at the surface of the Earth, part of the energy is trapped and guided by the Earth's surface. Their behavior is different than for body waves, so they are identified as surface waves. These waves are classified into two types of surface waves—Love waves and Rayleigh waves. Rayleigh waves behave like ocean waves, with a rolling motion. They travel a little slower than Love waves. Love waves have horizontal back and forth motion that is perpendicular to the direction the wave is traveling. Major damage can occur in earthquakes due to secondary effects triggered by strong earthquake ground shaking. A secondary effect that is often observed in low-lying areas near water bodies is ground liquefaction. Liquefaction is the conversion of water-saturated soil into a fluid-like mass. This can occur when loosely packed, waterlogged sediments lose their strength in response to strong shaking. Liquefaction may occur along the shorelines of the ocean, rivers, and lakes, and it can also happen in low-lying areas away from water bodies but where the ground water is near the Earth’s surface.118 Earthquakes are typically

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: lose their strength in response to strong shaking. Liquefaction may occur along the shorelines of the ocean, rivers, and lakes, and it can also happen in low-lying areas away from water bodies but where the ground water is near the Earth’s surface.118 Earthquakes are typically described in terms of magnitude and intensity. Magnitude is the measure of the amplitude of the seismic wave and is often expressed by the Richter scale, and intensity is a measure of how strong the shock was felt at a particular location, indexed by peak ground acceleration (PGA) percentages and the Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) scale. The

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 174 Richter scale is a logarithmic measurement whereby an increase in the scale by one whole number represents a tenfold increase in measured ground motion of the earthquake (and an increase in energy released of more than 30 times). An increase by two whole numbers represents a 102 (or 100-fold) increase in ground motion, and thus more than 302 (or 900) times the energy released. PGA is a measurement of the largest increase in velocity, or ground acceleration, recorded during an earthquake—ultimately a measure of amplitude. The following table shows the rough correlation between the Richter scale, PGA, and the MMI. The relationship between these is approximate and depends upon such specifics as the depth of the focus (the location of the actual rock movement) and distance from the epicenter (the location on the Earth’s surface above the earthquake focus) of the earthquake.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 176 3.7.4.2 Risk Assessment – Earthquake 3.7.4.2.1 Geographic Extent The Central United States Earthquake Consortium (CUSEC) identifies three major seismic zones which impact the state of Tennessee. These include the New Madrid Seismic Zone and the East Tennessee Seismic Zone which are both located within the state of Tennessee and the Wabash Valley Seismic Zone which is located within proximity of Tennessee. Figure 82: Seismic Zones in Relation to the State of Tennessee120 The New Madrid Seismic Zone and the East Tennessee Seismic Zone have a footprint within the state of Tennessee. The New Madrid Seismic Zone is spatially associated with the Reelfoot rift which is a deep valley that formed bounded by faults within the earth’s crust. Compressive stress related to plate motions within the area causes seismic activity within the New Madrid Seismic Zone. In the winter of 1811/1812, the New Madrid Seismic Zone generated a sequence of earthquakes that lasted for several months and included three very large earthquakes with magnitudes ranging between 7 and 8. Several settlements along the Mississippi River were destroyed with minor structural damage caused to several buildings as far away as Cincinnati, Ohio and St. Louis, Missouri. Shaking from these earthquakes was felt in areas hundreds of miles away and included Hartford, Connecticut; Charleston, South Carolina; and New Orleans, Louisiana. 120 CUSEC, “Central United States Earthquake Consortium,” cusec.org. https://cusec.org/#

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 177 The East Tennessee Seismic Zone and the Wabash Valley Seismic Zone are lesser-known seismic areas which have the potential to impact the state of Tennessee. The East Tennessee Seismic Zone is a midcontinent earthquake zone which encompasses ancient faults with no known faults that reach the surface. The East Tennessee Seismic Zone stretches from northeastern Alabama to southwestern Virginia and is considered one of the most active earthquake zones in the eastern United States. Events ranging from 5 to 6 in magnitude are estimated to occur once every 200 to 300 years in the East Tennessee Seismic Zone. The Wabash Valley Seismic Zone is located in southeastern Illinois and southwestern Indiana. The zone is capable of producing earthquakes with a magnitude of 7 which could impact portions of the state of Tennessee. One of the more recent earthquakes that brought attention to the zone occurred on June 18, 2002. The 4.6 magnitude earthquake occurred near Evansville, Indiana with an epicenter between Mt. Vernon and West Franklin. The earthquake caused only minor damage to the area. The Wabash Valley Seismic Zone also produced a 5.2 magnitude earthquake on April 18, 2008, which could be felt across 16 states and by more than 40,000 people. 3.7.4.2.2 Previous Occurrences/Probability Since the 2018 Hazard Mitigation Plan update, the USGS Earthquake Hazards Program indicates there have been 57 occurrences of earthquakes which have impacted the state of Tennessee. The earthquake was felt as far away as Memphis, Jackson, and Paducah, Kentucky. Gary Patterson, who serves as the center's director of education and outreach, noted that because of West Tennessee's flat geology, the energy of the earthquake travels farther which results in the earthquakes being felt disproportionately. Multiple earthquakes have been recorded in the area, however most of these earthquakes are registered under magnitude 2.5. The zone extends in an approximately 250 km long band that parallels the southern Appalachian Mountains from northeast Alabama through Tennessee to southwest Virginia and possibly northeast Kentucky. Few, if any, earthquakes in the Eastern Tennessee seismic zone can be linked to named faults as it is laced with known faults but numerous smaller or deeply buried faults remain undetected. The USGS received 1,881 responses from people across Southeast Tennessee and the United States who said they felt the earthquake. • January 19–20, 2020126 – Over the Martin Luther King Jr. holiday weekend, two earthquakes of varying magnitudes rocked Fincastle, Tennessee in Campbell County. The first occurred at around 5:19 a.m. on Sunday, while the second occurred at around 1:12 p.m. on Monday. The earthquakes were also felt in the East Tennessee Seismic Zone. There is no known cause for the earthquakes, but they may be linked to a significant transform fault that was active over a billion years ago because they happen at depths well below the mountains' surface. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 187 Figure 85: Total Earthquake Events per Year by Epicenter within the State of Tennessee from 1996 to 2022 3.7.4.2.3 Impact of Climate Trends and Variations The impacts of climate trends and variations on earthquake frequency are largely unknown; however, there are some USGS and NASA scientists who believe melting glaciers could induce tectonic activity due to the tremendous amount of weight that is shifted on the earth’s crust as water melts and runs off. This newly freed crust can experience post-glacial isostatic uplift, which could cause seismic plates to slip and stimulate seismic activity as it returns to its original, pre-glacial shape. Additionally, secondary impacts such as liquefaction may increase due to soils that have been saturated from repetitive precipitation instances. 3.7.4.3 Vulnerability Analysis – Earthquake Risk to earthquakes within the state of Tennessee can be visualized using the hazards risk zones from the USGS Earthquake Hazards Program. Earthquakes can also cause death, injury, destruction of homes, disruption of transportation and communication networks, and water supply contamination. This is all dependent upon the magnitude of the earthquake, the depth of the focus, the distance from the epicenter, the population density, and the mitigation actions in effect to disrupt the impacts of the earthquake. The concentration of infrastructure, including buildings, transportation systems, and utilities, increases the potential for widespread damage and loss of life. The higher population density also poses challenges for evacuation and emergency response efforts. Communities located near major fault lines or in seismically active regions face an elevated risk. These areas often have a history of earthquakes and may experience more frequent seismic activity. Populations living in such zones must be prepared for potential earthquakes and their associated hazards, such as ground shaking.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 199 Fragile infrastructure and informal settlements pose additional vulnerabilities. In developing areas with inadequate building codes and construction standards, buildings and infrastructure may be more prone to collapse during earthquakes. Informal settlements, often lacking sturdy structures and infrastructure, are particularly at risk. Historical and culturally significant sites may also be vulnerable. Heritage structures that were not designed or retrofitted to withstand seismic activity may suffer severe damage during earthquakes. These sites often hold significant cultural and historical value, and their loss can have profound impacts on communities and cultural identity. 3.7.4.3.3 Impact on State Assets Figure 87 shows state assets mapped by seismic risk level zone. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 201 3.7.5 Extreme Temperatures (Heat and Cold) 3.7.5.1 Hazard Profile – Extreme Temperatures Extreme temperatures include both hot and cold occurrences, which can have a significant impact on human health and primary/secondary effects on infrastructure (e.g., burst pipes and power failure). What constitutes “extreme cold” or “extreme heat” can vary across different areas of the country, based on the acclimatization and preparedness of the local population. 3.7.5.1.1 Extreme Heat The National Weather Service (NWS) Instruction 10-1605136 defines extreme or excessive heat as a period with combinations of high temperatures (above normal) and high relative humidity. Depending on the part of the country experiencing high temperatures, the heat effects are modulated by relative humidity, cloud cover, wind speeds, the duration of a hot spell, the time of the year, and other factors, including location and types of housing. FEMA provides a definition that considers extreme heat to be when the temperature and humidity rise to 90 degrees or above for a 2- to 3-day period.137 Other FEMA publications also define extreme heat as the temperature consistently staying 10 degrees or more above a region’s average high temperature for an extended period of time. Extreme heat can affect parts of the state differently with temperatures above 100 degrees in the West and Middle regions not being uncommon each year, while temperatures in higher elevations of the East and Southeast regions less often exceed 100 degrees. Extreme heat can cause damage to buildings and infrastructure, but the main threat is to human health and safety across the state of Tennessee without proper preparation. Health hazards derived

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: temperatures in higher elevations of the East and Southeast regions less often exceed 100 degrees. Extreme heat can cause damage to buildings and infrastructure, but the main threat is to human health and safety across the state of Tennessee without proper preparation. Health hazards derived from extreme heat include heat cramps, heat exhaustion, heat syncope, and heat stroke. Heat disorders are associated with the inability of the body to shed excess heat by circulatory changes and sweating or a chemical (salt) imbalance caused by too much sweating. Table 79: Extreme Heat Illness Symptoms and Aid138 Illness Symptoms Aid Heat Cramps Painful muscle cramps and spasms usually in legs and abdomen with heaving seating Apply firm pressure on cramping muscles or gently massage to relieve spasm. Give sips of water unless the person complains of nausea, then stop giving water and seek immediate medical attention if cramps last longer than 1 hour.

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 202 Illness Symptoms Aid Heat Exhaustion Heavy sweating; weakness or tiredness; cool, pale, or clammy skin; fast, weak pulse; muscle cramps; dizziness; nausea or vomiting; headache; fainting Move person to a cooler environment, preferably a well air-conditioned room. Loosen clothing. Apply cool, wet clothes, or have person sit in a cool bath. Offer sips of water. If person vomits more than once or symptoms worsen or last longer than 1 hour, seek immediate medical attention. Heat Syncope A sudden loss of consciousness caused by a circulatory instability response to excess heat Move the person to a shaded/cool area to decrease body temperatures, sit or lie down the patient as soon as they begin to feel symptoms, monitor vital signs to ensure the person does not acquire another medical condition, elevate legs to promote blood flow to the heart, and rehydrate with water or a sports beverage. Heat Stroke Throbbing headache, confusion, nausea, dizziness, body temperature above 103° F; hot, red, dry, or damp skin; rapid and strong pulse; and fainting or loss of consciousness Call 911 or transport the victim to a hospital immediately. Heat stroke is a severe medical emergency. Delay in seeking medical treatment can be fatal. The NWS created a Heat Index (HI) which includes likelihood of a heat disorder based on temperature and relative humidity. The HI is used as a common guideline for the issuance of excessive heat alerts—when the maximum daytime heat index is expected to equal or exceed 105 degrees and a nighttime minimum HI of 80 degrees or higher for at least two consecutive days.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 204 Figure 89: Wet Bulb Globe Temperature Scale that Can be Utilized Across Tennessee for Exposure to Extreme Heat140 3.7.5.1.2 Extreme Cold Extreme cold occurs when temperatures drop well below normal in an area. In regions unaccustomed to winter weather, near freezing temperatures are considered “extreme cold.” The National Weather Service Instruction 10-1605 defines cold as a period of low temperatures or wind chill temperatures reaching or surpassing locally-/regionally-defined advisory conditions (typical value is -18 °F or colder). Extreme cold can be defined as a period of extremely low temperatures or wind chill temperatures reaching or surpassing locally-/regionally-defined warning criteria (typical value around -35 °F or colder). In situations that do not meet the advisory criteria, the combination of seasonably cold temperatures and low wind chill values (roughly 15 °̊F below normal) may impact human health. Extreme cold temperatures occur throughout Tennessee but vary depending on the region and climate for that region. A significant temperature drop paired with an increased wind speed causes the body’s core temperature to drop rapidly, creating increased possibilities for illness such as frostbite or hypothermia which have the possibility to become life-threatening. The elderly and infants are the most susceptible groups to extreme cold, but it can affect anyone. Extreme cold can also affect infrastructure and housing due to the possibility of bursting pipes in areas with no heat or poor insulation. Per the NWS, cold weather can also affect crops. In late spring or early fall, cold air outbreaks can damage or kill produce for farmers as well as residential plants and flowers. A freeze occurs when the temperature drops below 32 °F. Freezes and their effects are significant during the growing season. Frost develops on clear, calm nights and can occur when the air temperature is in the mid-30s. Each plant species has a different tolerance to cold temperatures.

Its climate is characterized by moderately large variations in temperature and abundant precipitation. For most of the state, summers are warm and humid while winters are cool with occasional episodes of very cold arctic air. Temperatures decrease across the state as elevation increases, averaging 3 °F decline per 1,000 feet increase in elevation. The higher elevations of the state, such as the Cumberland Plateau (average elevation of 2,000 feet) and the Smoky Mountains (peaks over 6,000 feet), have noticeably lower average temperatures compared to the Great Valley of East Tennessee (elevations from ~1,800 feet in the north to ~700 feet in the south) and the lower elevations of Middle and West Tennessee. Average (1991–2020 normals) minimum temperatures in January range from 22 °F in Mountain City to 33 °F in Memphis. Average high temperatures in the summer vary between 85 °F and 90 °F in West and Middle Tennessee and between 80 °F and

text: and West Tennessee. Average (1991–2020 normals) minimum temperatures in January range from 22 °F in Mountain City to 33 °F in Memphis. Average high temperatures in the summer vary between 85 °F and 90 °F in West and Middle Tennessee and between 80 °F and 85 °F in East Tennessee and the Cumberland Plateau. Historical observed extreme temperatures for the state range from -32 °F in Mountain City in the winter of 1917 to 113 °F in Perryville in the summer of 1930. 3.7.5.2.2 Previous Occurrences/Probability Since the 2018 Hazard Mitigation Plan update, the NCEI Storm Events Database indicates there have been 44 occurrences of heat and/or excessive heat that have impacted the state of Tennessee. From 1996 to 2017, there were 89 extreme heat events in the state of Tennessee. The annual chance of occurrence for the state of Tennessee for a heat and/or excessive heat occurrence is calculated at 100%. Several notable events are described below: • July 2019 – Two heat waves occurred during the month with high temperatures in the mid to upper-nineties across the state, and heat index values as high as 110 °F.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 207 Heat advisories and excessive heat warnings were issued for portions of West and Middle Tennessee for July 17 and 18.143 • August 2019 – A strong heat wave hit the state August 12–13 with Heat Advisories issued in many areas across the state, and Excessive Heat Warnings issued for West Tennessee where heat index values topped 110 ˚F. Memphis recorded a heat index value of 115 ˚F on the 12th.144 • October 2019 – The month started out in a continuation of the heat wave from September, with high temperatures in the mid-to-upper 90s during the first week of the month. Daily record high temperatures were set in Memphis (1st -3rd), Jackson (2nd & 3rd), Clarksville (1st 3rd & 5th), Nashville (1st -3rd & 5th), Crossville (1st -3rd), Chattanooga (1st -4th), Oak Ridge (1st -3rd & 5th), Knoxville (1st -3rd), and in the TriCities (1st -4th), with Chattanooga reaching 100 °F on the 2nd & 3rd.145 • June 2022 – A major heat wave impacted the state in the second half of the month sending temperatures into the triple digits from June 21 to 23. The cold temperatures were combined with high winds, and wind-chill warnings were issued for many higher-elevation counties in East TN. • February 2021 – The coldest period of the month occurred from February 10 to 19, when there were 79 broken and 9 tied record-low daily high temperatures and 24 broken and 2 tied record-low daily low temperatures (at weather stations in the state with at least a 30year record). The cold air mass was strongest and most persistent in West Tennessee, with a moderating trend towards the east. This contrast was at its most extreme on February 15, when the high temperature recorded at Memphis International Airport was 15 °F, while the high temperature recorded at the Tri-Cities airport in northeast Tennessee was 55 °F. The length of the cold outbreak was also extreme, with Memphis

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 216 staying below freezing for nine days, which tied the record for longest streak below freezing (it happened previously in 1940 and 1899).152 • December 2022 - Eleven Tennessee counties received federal recovery assistance under a Major Disaster Declaration as a result of the severe winter weather, named Winter Storm Elliot, which impacted the state on December 22-27, 2022.153 A strong cold front swept the state on December 22-23 with temperatures falling over 40-degrees in a few hours into the single digits or sub-zero for many areas of the state. Along with these bitterly cold temperatures winds gusted in the 30-40 mph range after the frontal passage, sending wind chills into the -20 °F range for most areas of the state and prompting a wind chill warning issued for all counties in Tennessee on December 22. Light snowfall and strong winds also occurred as the temperatures plummeted after the frontal passage, with snow totals ranging from a dusting to ~2” across the state. Temperatures on the morning of December 23 were below zero at the airport weather stations in Jackson (-2 °F), Clarksville (-3 °F), Nashville (-1° F), and Crossville (-4 °F). This was the first time these stations have recorded sub-zero temperatures since January 2018 for Clarksville and Crossville, February 1996 for Nashville, and December 1989 for Jackson. Winter Storm Elliott was a cross-country storm that brought subzero temperatures to Tennessee and left over 306,000 customers without power during its the peak of the event.154 As temperatures warmed, burst pipes and loss of water pressure resulted in many boil water advisories across the state. Winter Storm Elliot was referred to as a “once-in-a-generation storm,” by the National Weather Service with its recordbreaking temperatures and high winds. In the Tennessee Valley Region, the average temperature was 3 °F at 8 a.m. CDT on Friday, Dec. 23. This was the coldest system average temp since February 1996.155,156 The following table provides a brief description and impact of each occurrence. Table 88: Statistical Summation of Extreme Temperature (Cold) Occurrences by TEMA Regions TEMA Region Total Number of Events (1996 – 2022) Total Property Damage Total Crop Damage Injuries Fatalities Chance of Occurrence Return Frequency East 2 $0 $0 0 1 7% 1 event every 13 to 14 years Southeast 17 $0 $0 0 2 63% 1 event every 1 to 2 years Middle 16 $0 $0 0 2 59% 1 event every 1 to 2 years West 11 $0 $0 0 18 41% 1 event every 2 to 3 years 3.7.5.2.3 Impacts of Climate Trends and Variations Temperatures in Tennessee have risen by 0.5 °F since the beginning of the 20th century, less than a third of the warming averaged for the contiguous United States. Temperatures were highest in the 1920s and 1930s, followed by a substantial cooling of about 2 °F by the 1960s (see Figure 91). Since that cool period, temperatures have risen by more than 2 °F, and since 2010 they have been near the highs of the 1920s and 1930s. Because of the significant cooling that occurred in the middle of the 20th century, the southeastern United States is one of the few locations globally that has experienced little to no overall warming since 1900, while the United States as a whole has warmed by about 1.8 °F. The United States also cooled from the 1930s into the 1960s, but not by nearly as much as Tennessee. Hypothesized causes for this difference in warming rates include increased cloud cover and precipitation, increased small particles from coal burning, natural factors related to forest regrowth, decreased heat flux due to irrigation, and multidecadal variability in North Atlantic and tropical Pacific sea surface temperatures. However, some recent years have been very warm, including 2012 (2nd warmest), 2016 (3rd warmest), 2017 (5th warmest), and 2019 (7th warmest).

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 225 Data from the NCEI Storm Events Database related to heat, excessive heat, cold, windchill, extreme cold, and extreme windchill was too sparse to be used for statistical analysis of trends and patterns. However, warnings and advisories are archived at the county level and available through the Iowa Environmental Mesonet. Heat advisories, excessive heat warnings, windchill advisories, and windchill warnings were downloaded for every county in Tennessee between 2005 and 2021. There was a total of 3,589 heat advisories and warnings and 1,651 windchill advisories and warnings during this period in Tennessee. Extreme heat events can impact infrastructure sectors such as transportation when infrastructure begins to buckle, with secondary impacts across all sectors from heat-related power outages and health threats to the general population. Below are examples of how extreme heat can impact the state: • Power lines become less efficient from overheating effects. • Concrete degradation from direct heat can cause cracks, dimpling of the material, and expansion of structures.

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 242 • Overheating of materials can permeate buildings and cause greater energy needs for cooling. • Cast iron cannot bend or stretch and will crack to relieve stresses of heat. • Crop decay and increased livestock mortality rates can be expected due to worsening heat, especially when combined with drought conditions. • Local dams, levees, and other water retention structures could see loss in efficiency as cracks and breaks occur from the stressors of heat. Extreme cold events can also have similar impacts on infrastructure as fluctuating temperatures can cause materials to weaken. Extreme cold events can lead to damaged water systems; cracked pipes such as water, oil, and gas; and damaged concrete and steel supports. As temperatures fluctuate, pre-season freezes and shifts in warming can also result in double blooms, premature budding, and early snowmelt which can increase scraggly brush growth and worsen wildfire threats each year. 3.7.5.3.2 Vulnerable Population Extreme temperatures also have a significant impact on the health of human beings. Children, pregnant women, older adults, people with outdoor jobs, and persons with disabilities or with pre-existing health conditions may be disproportionately impacted. Additionally, individuals affected by poverty may be impacted more by extreme temperatures as they may not have the ability to cool or heat their homes. Elderly individuals are highly susceptible to the effects of excessive temperatures. Age-related physiological changes, chronic health conditions, and decreased ability to regulate body temperature make them more prone to heat-related illnesses and complications. Additionally, social factors such as limited mobility, isolation, and inadequate access to cooling facilities may further increase their vulnerability.

Children, especially infants and young children, are also at-risk during periods of excessive heat. Their bodies have a limited capacity to regulate temperature, and they may be less able to communicate discomfort or seek relief. Additionally, their dependency on caregivers and their reliance on appropriate hydration and cooling measures make them vulnerable. Individuals with pre-existing health conditions, such as cardiovascular diseases, respiratory illnesses, and obesity, are more susceptible to heat-related complications. Certain medications or treatments can also interfere with heat regulation, further increasing their vulnerability. These individuals may require additional support and monitoring during periods of extreme temperatures. Socioeconomically disadvantaged populations often face heightened vulnerability to excessive heat. Limited access to air conditioning, inadequate housing conditions, and lack of resources for cooling strategies can amplify the risks. Communities with limited green spaces and high levels of urban heat island effect may also experience more significant impacts.

In such weather conditions, vulnerable populations are at a greater risk. Extreme heat can result in fatal heat stroke and related conditions, while extreme cold may cause hypothermia, frostbite, carbon monoxide poisoning due to improper generator usage, and heart attacks. Power outages and communication disruptions are more likely to occur during these weather events. Additionally, ice accumulation and road buckling may make emergency services and food supplies inaccessible due to road inaccessibility. Rising temperatures can also negatively affect nuclear reactors' efficiency by impacting nuclear equipment or warming the cooling water source, posing a risk to all thermal power plants, including nuclear units.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 246 3.7.6 Floods 3.7.6.1 Hazard Profile – Floods A flood is a partial or complete inundation of normally dry land areas. The National Flood Insurance Program defines a flood as: A general and temporary condition of partial or complete inundation of two or more acres of normally dry land area or two or more properties from overflow of inland or tidal waves, unusual and rapid accumulation or runoff of surface waters from any source, mudflow, or collapse or subsidence of land along the shore of a lake or similar body of water as a result of erosion or undermining causes by waves or currents of water exceeding anticipated cyclical levels that result in a flood as defined above. Factors influencing the type and severity of flooding include natural variables such as precipitation, topography, vegetation, soil texture, and seasonality, as well as anthropogenic factors such as urbanization (extent of impervious surfaces), land use (agricultural and forestry tend to remove native vegetation and accelerate soil erosion), and the presence of flood-control structures such as levees and dams. In Tennessee, the following types of flooding are of main concern: • Riverine flooding is the partial or complete inundation of a normally dry area by an existing water way such as river, stream, or a drainage ditch. It is the result of runoff from heavy rainfall or intensive snow or ice melt. The speed with which riverine flood levels rise and fall depends not only on the amount of rainfall, but even more on the capacity of the river, as well as the shape and land cover

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: runoff from heavy rainfall or intensive snow or ice melt. The speed with which riverine flood levels rise and fall depends not only on the amount of rainfall, but even more on the capacity of the river, as well as the shape and land cover of its drainage basin. Riverine flooding is generally a longer-term event than flash flooding as it may last days to weeks and result in property damage and/or loss of life. • Flash flooding is caused by heavy or excessive rainfall over a short period of time, generally less than six hours. Flash floods are usually characterized by raging torrents after heavy rains that rip through low-lying areas sweeping everything before them. They can also occur even if no rain has fallen, for instance after a levee or dam has failed, or after a sudden release of water by a debris or ice jam. Flash floods are common in urban areas and can lead to loss of life and/or property. • Closed-basin flooding occurs when a lake has no outlet or a relatively small outlet. Seasonal rainfall and storm systems can cause the lake level to rise faster than it can empty. Floodwaters in closed-basin lakes accumulate over long periods of time and may stay for weeks, months, or years. • Ponding occurs when concave areas (e.g., parking lots, roads, and clay-lined natural low areas) collect water and are unable to drain. • Urban flooding is similar to flash flooding but is specific to urbanized areas. It takes place when storm water drainage systems cannot keep pace with heavy precipitation, and water accumulates on the surface. Most urban flooding is caused by slow-moving thunderstorms or torrential

Flood Warning Take Action A Flood Warning is issued when the hazardous weather event is imminent or already happening. A Flood Warning is issued when flooding is imminent or occurring. Flood Advisory Be Aware A Flood Advisory is issued when a specific weather that is forecast to occur may become a nuisance. A Flood Advisory is issued when flooding is not expected to be bad enough to issue a warning. However, it may cause significant inconvenience, and if caution is not exercised, it could lead to situations that may threaten life and/or property. Flood Watch Be Prepared A Flood Watch is issued when conditions are favorable for a specific hazardous weather event to occur. A Flood Watch is issued when conditions are favorable for flooding. It does not mean flooding will occur, but it is possible. It is essential to understand that the magnitude of an X-year flood event for a particular area depends on the source of flooding and the area’s location. The size of a specific flood event is defined through historic data of precipitation, flow, and discharge rates. Consequently, different 100-year flood events (1% annual chance of occurrence) can have very different impacts. The 100-year flood event in two separate locations have the same likelihood to occur,

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: of a specific flood event is defined through historic data of precipitation, flow, and discharge rates. Consequently, different 100-year flood events (1% annual chance of occurrence) can have very different impacts. The 100-year flood event in two separate locations have the same likelihood to occur, but they do not necessarily have the same magnitude. For example, a 100-year event for the Mississippi River means something completely different in terms of discharge values (ft3/s) than for the Cumberland River. Not only are the magnitudes of 100-year events different between rivers, but they can also be different along any given river. A 100-year event upstream is different from one downstream due to the change of river characteristics (volume, discharge, and topography). As a result, the definition of what constitutes a 100-year flood event is specific to each location, river, and time since floodplain and river characteristics change over time. Finally, it is important to note that each flood event is unique. Two hypothetical events at the same location, given the same magnitude of stream flow, may still produce substantially different impacts if there were different antecedent moisture characteristics, different times of day of occurrence (which indicates the population’s probable activities at the flood’s onset), or other characteristic differences.

A watershed can be defined as all the land area that drains into a given body of water. Tennessee has more than 60,000 miles of rivers and streams that sustain our communities, support our economy, provide recreation, and serve as habitat for aquatic species. However, each of these streams have the potential to experience riverine flooding. The most impactful flooding occurs during the winter and early spring when frequent lowpressure systems bring general rains of high intensity. During this period both widespread flooding and local flash floods can occur. During the summer, heavy thunderstorm rainfalls frequently result in local flash flooding. In the fall, while flood-producing rains are rare, a substantial tropical storm system on occasion causes serious floods. The numerous dams constructed along the Tennessee and Cumberland rivers and levees along the Mississippi River are major features in the control of floodwaters in the state. Extreme precipitation is typically assessed for 1-hour and 24-hour time intervals. Figure 124: Observed (1895–2022) Average Annual Precipitation for Tennessee, Compared to the 20th Century Average with Darkening Shades of Brown for Below Average Precipitation and Darkening Shades of Green for Above Average Precipitation Based on NOAA’s Climate at a Glance tool, most of the eastern United States has experienced an increase in precipitation between 1901 and 2021. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 286 Based on information from the Fourth National Climate Assessment Report, the southeastern United States has seen a high number of days with precipitation above 3 inches in recent decades. Specifically in Tennessee, twice as many stations have seen an increase in such heavy precipitation days compared to stations that have seen a decrease. There is no clear spatial pattern based on station-level information. Figure 129: Observed Days with Precipitation above 3 Inches and Percent Change from 1950–2016214 The Fourth National Climate Assessment Report also provides information about observed changes in total annual precipitation that falls in the heaviest 1% of events. Examining the full record (1901–2016), there has been an 18% increase in such events in the southeastern United States, while narrowing the record to 1958–2016 shows an even larger increase (27%). In the same report, projections for such events were also made based on the RCP 4.5 (lower emissions) and RCP 8.5 (higher emissions) scenarios. Based on the higher emissions scenario, all of Tennessee is expected to see a large increase in the total annual precipitation that would fall in heavy precipitation events, with most of the state projected to see an increase of greater than 40%. 214 Fourth National Climate Assessment, Chapter 19: Southeast. https://nca2018.globalchange.gov/chapter/19/.

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 287 Figure 130: Observed (top) and Projected (bottom) Change in the Amount of Precipitation Falling in the Heaviest 1% of Events215 Figure 131, Figure 132, and Figure 133 display the heavy precipitation, flood, and flash flood occurrence trends for the state of Tennessee from 1996–2021 at the county level. There are many counties across the state where 1-year, 2-year, and 5-year heavy precipitation events have seen an increasing trend. A 1-year heavy precipitation event is the heaviest precipitation event that is expected each year, i.e., a 100% chance of exceedance. A 2-year heavy precipitation event is a precipitation event that has a 50% chance of exceedance each year. A 5-year heavy precipitation event is one that has a 20% chance of exceedance each year. Hamilton, Humphreys, and Lauderdale counties have the most significant increasing trends for 1-year heavy precipitation events. Some counties have seen increasing trends in flood events and flood damages, with Davidson County seeing the most significant trend in flood events and Cumberland County seeing the most significant trend in flood damages. Lake County has seen the most significant decreasing trend in flood events while neighboring Dyer and Obion counties 215 Ibid.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 292 Figure 134: Projected Change in Annual Precipitation for Tennessee Based on models and projection data from Multivariate Adaptive Constructed Analogs (MACA), the U.S. Department of Agriculture, and the U.S. Forest Service, most of Tennessee is expected to see an increase in annual precipitation by the late 21st century, with northern and eastern parts of the state projected to experience the largest increase (6–8% increase in extreme northeast Tennessee, see previous figure). Counties in southwest Tennessee are not expected to see a large increase in precipitation. Potential changes in precipitation are not expected to be spread across all four seasons. All counties in Tennessee are expected to see an increase in spring precipitation, especially counties across northern Tennessee. Middle and especially West Tennessee are expected to see a decrease in summer precipitation while parts of the Tennessee Valley and northeast Tennessee are expected to see an increase in summer precipitation. All counties, except those in northwest Tennessee are expected to see an increase in fall precipitation, with the largest increases expected in the mountains of East Tennessee. Most counties, except those along the southern border with Mississippi, Alabama, and Georgia, are expected to see an increase in winter precipitation, with counties in northeast Tennessee expected to see the largest increase.

Flood velocity is important because the faster water moves, the more pressure it puts on a structure and the more it will erode stream banks and scour the earth around a building’s foundation. In some situations, deep and fast-moving waters can push a building off its

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 301 foundation. Structural damage can also be caused by the weight of standing water (hydrostatic pressure). Another threat to property from a flood is called “soaking.” When soaked, many materials change their composition or shape. Wet wood will swell, and if dried too quickly, will crack, split, or warp. Plywood can come apart and gypsum wallboard can deteriorate if it is bumped before it has time to completely dry. The longer these materials are saturated, the more moisture, sediment, and pollutants they absorb. Soaking can also cause extensive damage to household goods. Wooden furniture may become warped, making it unusable, while other furnishings such as books, carpeting, mattresses, and upholstery usually are not salvageable. Electrical appliances and gasoline engines will flood, resulting in major asset losses. Many buildings that have succumbed to flood waters may look sound and unharmed after a flood, but water has the potential to cause severe property damage. Any structure that experiences a flood should be stripped, cleaned, and allowed to dry before being reconstructed. This can be an extremely expensive and time-consuming effort. Using the Hazus Flood Model, the 100-year flood scenario was analyzed to determine losses. The Hazus Flood Model provides a breakdown for seven primary sectors (Hazus occupancy) throughout each county by full replacement cost. The losses for the state of Tennessee for these sectors at the county level are provided in Table 106.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 307 3.7.6.3.2 Vulnerable Population Just as with property damage, depth and velocity are major factors in determining the threat posed to people by flooding. It takes very little depth or velocity for flood waters to become dangerous. A car will float in less than two feet of moving water, and can be swept downstream into deeper waters, trapping passengers within the vehicle. Victims of floods have often put themselves in perilous situations by entering flood waters that they believe to be safe, or by ignoring travel advisories. Major health concerns are also associated with floods. Flood waters can transport materials such as dirt, oil, animal waste, and chemicals (e.g., farm, lawn, and industrial) that may cause illnesses of various degrees when coming in contact with humans. Flood waters can also infiltrate sewer lines and inundate wastewater treatment plants, causing sewage backup and creating a breeding ground for dangerous bacteria. This infiltration may also cause water supplies to become contaminated and undrinkable. Using the Hazus Flood Model, the 100-year flood scenario was analyzed to determine the population impacted from this worst-case scenario. The Hazus Flood Model provides a breakdown for the total population displaced by flood waters and the total amount of the population needing short-term shelter. The impacts on the population for the state of Tennessee for these categories at the county level are provided in Table 108. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 314 3.7.7 Geologic Hazards 3.7.7.1 Hazard Profile – Geologic Hazards Geologic hazards relate to the danger involved in topography, rock formations, and soil. Included in this category are expansive soils, landslides, and sinkholes. 3.7.7.1.1 Expansive Soils Expansive soils are described as a soil/clay that is prone to expansion or shrinkage due directly to variation in water volume. Expansive soils swell when exposed to large amounts of water and shrink when the water evaporates. This continuous cycle of wet to dry soil keeps the soil in perpetual motion causing structures built on this soil to sink or rise unevenly, often requiring foundation repair. Expansive soils are comprised primarily of minerals with little to no organic material and are thus incredibly viscous, proving difficult to drain. In Tennessee, expansive soils may exacerbate flooding, increase damage to infrastructures and homes, and impact crop health. “Clay” is defined as a natural, earthy, fine-grained material that develops plasticity when mixed with a limited amount of water. Swelling clay has high plasticity that is capable of absorbing large quantities of water, thus increasing greatly in volume. The high plasticity clay tends to contract during drying and expand when exposed to moisture. Clay minerals that are 14 Armstrong clays, like montmorillonite, vermiculite, bentonite, and mixed layer clays are responsible for swelling. Variations in moisture content and volume changes are greatest in clays found in regions of moderate to high precipitation, where prolonged periods of drought are followed by long periods of rainfall. Swelling of clays in Tennessee occurs statewide due to the fluctuating climate that occurs in all four regions. There are several ways to identify the expansiveness of clay soils, with the most notable being the plasticity index in Table 114. title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 315 history. These destructive events can result in the loss of lives, destruction of property, and severe environmental damage. Understanding the causes and consequences and implementing effective mitigation strategies are crucial in mitigating the impact of landslides and safeguarding vulnerable communities. Landslides can be triggered by various natural and human-induced factors. Natural causes include geological factors such as slope steepness, soil composition, and the presence of weak or fractured rock layers. Additionally, heavy rainfall, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and slope saturation due to melting snow or glaciers can also contribute to landslide occurrence. Human activities such as deforestation, improper land use, construction on unstable slopes, and inadequate drainage systems further increase the susceptibility to landslides. The most common landslides in Tennessee consist of debris flow, rockslides, and mudslides. Rockfalls and topple failures are localized in steep slopes exposing bedrock. These are outlined in Table 115. Table 115: Landslide Type and Description Landslide Type Description Debris Flow Debris flows are fast-moving landslides that are particularly dangerous to life and property because they move quickly, destroy objects in their paths, and often strike without warning. These often start off as translational slides, but the water and rubble mix as the slide moves downslope. Rockslide A rapid movement of rock fragments down a slope. There are two common types, namely translational slides and block slides. Mudslide Mudslides develop when water rapidly accumulates in the ground and results in a surge of water-saturated rock, earth, and debris. These slides often start off as rotational slides.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 316 Figure 143: Schematic Illustration of Major Types of Landslides in Tennessee221 3.7.7.1.3 Sinkholes Karst topography refers to landscapes that are formed by the dissolution of soluble rocks such as limestone, dolomite, and gypsum. Sinkholes are one of the common features of karst terrain and are caused by the collapse of the ground surface into underground cavities. Karst topography emerges when water interacts with soluble rock layers. Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, which forms a weak carbonic acid solution. As this mildly acidic water infiltrates the ground, it dissolves the rock, creating cavities and intricate networks of underground passages. Over time, these passages enlarge, eventually leading to the formation of sinkholes, caves, underground rivers, and other unique features. Sinkholes, often referred to as dolines, are a defining feature of karst topography. They are bowl-shaped depressions that develop when the roof of an underground cavern collapses, creating a visible opening on the surface. Sinkholes can range in size from small depressions to vast craters, and their depth can vary from a few meters to hundreds of meters. They may appear suddenly or gradually, and their growth and collapse are influenced by factors such as water flow, rock composition, and human activities. 221 United States Geological Survey, “Landslide Hazards Program,” usgs.gov. https://www.usgs.gov/programs/landslide-hazards

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 317 There are several types of sinkholes, each with distinct characteristics: • Dissolution Sinkholes: These form gradually over time as underground water dissolves soluble rock, creating a subsurface cavity. Eventually, the unsupported surface collapses, forming a sinkhole. Figure 144: Dissolution of Processes in Limestone222 (Source: United States Geological Society) • Cover Collapse Sinkholes: These sinkholes occur when a thick layer of sediment or soil covers a cavity. Over time, the overlying material becomes too heavy to support its weight, leading to sudden collapse. Figure 145: Cover-Collapse Process in Karst Topography Cover Subsidence Sinkholes: Unlike cover collapse sinkholes, cover subsidence sinkholes experience gradual subsidence as the underlying rock dissolves and the overlying material slowly settles. 222 United States Geological Survey, “Sinkholes,” usgs.gov. https://www.usgs.gov/special-topics/waterscience school/science/sinkholes#:~:text=What%20is%20a%20%22sinkhole%22%3F,more%20than%20100%20f eet%20deep

All three of these occur within the state of Tennessee, but it is important to note that specific areas within the state may be more prone to certain geological hazards than others. Expansive soils, also known as shrink-swell soils, can cause significant damage to structures and infrastructure. These soils expand when wet and shrink when dry, leading to ground movement and potential foundation problems. Expansive soils are more prevalent in the western part of Tennessee, particularly in areas underlain by clays and shale. Counties like Shelby, Tipton, Fayette, and Hardeman have been identified as having a higher risk of expansive soils. 223 Ibid.

Other factors, such as land use practices and human interventions, can interact with climate to influence the occurrence and severity of geologic hazards. Increased precipitation can result in greater soil moisture content, causing expansive soils to swell more and potentially lead to landslides and damage to infrastructure. Conversely, increased frequency and severity of drought can cause soils to shrink and crack, leading to subsidence and foundation problems in structures. The impacts of climate on landslides would be increased water from intense rainfalls that would weaken the soil’s stability due to an increase in saturation which increases pore water pressure. Landslides and other types of mass wasting events can be triggered by weather events like extreme rainfall or repeated freeze-thaw cycles that destabilize slopes and cause fracturing in exposed rock surfaces. Climate variability is expected to increase the number and severity of extreme precipitation events in the Southeast U.S. (see the Flood section for more details about expected changes in extreme precipitation), which could increase the likelihood of landslides in parts of Tennessee. A study conducted by the USDA and U.S. Forest Service Office of Sustainability and Climate found that the frost-free season (the longest period of the year during which the temperature does not drop below freezing) could increase in length by 40 to 60 days in in counties across Tennessee by 2070–2090 using the ensemble mean of 20 global climate models and the

West Tennessee is predicted to experience the largest increase. Similarly, according to U.S. Climate Resilience Toolkit there may be 35 to 50 fewer days per year with minimum temperatures below freezing across Tennessee based on the higher emissions scenario. The lengthening of the frost-free season and overall decrease in number of days with temperatures below freezing would reduce the amount of time during the year rock surfaces would be exposed to freeze-thaw cycles. This reduction could reduce the number of localized rockfalls in Tennessee. See the Extreme Temperatures section for more information on observed and expected changes to winter temperatures in Tennessee. Climate can also alter vegetation patterns which could drastically impact landslides since vegetation plays a crucial role in stabilizing slopes, and any changes can affect slope stability, potentially leading to increased landslide occurrences. Sinkholes are associated with dissolution of soluble rocks. Changes in precipitation patterns and groundwater recharge rates can alter water table levels. These fluctuations in the water table can lead to the dissolution of soluble rocks, potentially increasing the formation of sinkholes in areas of Tennessee with underlying karst geology. Additionally, there could be an increase in groundwater extraction due to projected increases in Tennessee's population and the intensification of the hydrological cycle which may require more groundwater use for irrigation of agriculture. An increase in groundwater extraction can trigger sinkhole development by causing the collapse of underground cavities. 3.7.7.3 Vulnerability Analysis – Geologic Hazards The National Risk Index (NRI) includes data on the expected annual losses to individual natural hazards, historical

Expansive soils can exert pressure on foundations causing them to crack or heave. Buildings and other structures can experience uneven settlement or tilting, leading to structural damage. Infrastructure such as roads, sidewalks, and underground utilities can be damaged or disrupted by the movement of expansive soils. Expansive soils can also affect agriculture productivity by damaging crop roots, restricting water infiltration, and causing uneven subsidence. Landslides can directly damage or destroy structures in their path, including buildings, roads, railways, and pipelines. Displaced soil and debris can block roads, disrupt transportation, and damage infrastructure. Landslides can have long-term economic impacts on the affected areas. Sinkholes have the potential to cause structural damage, leading to the collapse or compromise of buildings, roads, bridges, and other infrastructure. Utilities such as water and sewage systems, gas lines, and electrical conduits can be disrupted or damaged. Sinkholes can also lead to the formation of sinkhole lakes, impacting the hydrological system of an area. 3.7.7.3.2 Vulnerable Population Geologic hazards have significant impacts on humans and their surrounding environment. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 342 3.7.8 Hazardous Materials Release 3.7.8.1 Hazard Profile – Hazardous Materials Release A hazardous material (also known as HAZMAT) is defined by the U.S. Department of Transportation as, “Any substance that may pose an unreasonable risk to health and safety of operating or emergency personnel, the public, and/or the environment if not properly controlled during handling, storage, manufacturing, processing, packaging, use, disposal, or transportation.”234 The hazardous properties can be combustible, flammable, toxic, poisonous, corrosive/severely acidic, reactive, radioactive, or noxious. Tough U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), U.S. Tennessee Department of Transportation (DOT), U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), and U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) categorize these in different ways, a basic distinction among hazardous substances is their persistence in the environment and respective levels of health risks that these present. The release of a hazardous material can be caused by a spill, leak, explosion, pipeline break, transportation accident, or human action. If the material has escaped its container into the outside environment, a potentially hazardous situation exists. Hazardous material releases can contaminate air, water, and soils possibly resulting in death and/or injuries. Dispersion can take place rapidly when transported by water and wind. While often accidental, releases can occur as a result of human carelessness, intentional acts, or natural hazards. When caused by natural hazards, these incidents are known as secondary events. Materials can include toxic chemicals, radioactive materials, infectious substances, and hazardous wastes. Such releases can affect nearby populations and contaminate critical or sensitive environmental areas. With a hazardous material release, whether accidental or intentional, there are several potentially mitigating or exacerbating

Such releases can affect nearby populations and contaminate critical or sensitive environmental areas. With a hazardous material release, whether accidental or intentional, there are several potentially mitigating or exacerbating circumstances that will affect its severity or impact. Mitigating conditions are precautionary measures taken in advance to reduce the impact of a release on the surrounding environment. Primary and secondary containment or shielding by sheltering-in-place protects people and property from the harmful effects of a hazardous material release. Exacerbating conditions and characteristics that can enhance or magnify the effects of a hazardous material release include: • Weather conditions: affects how the hazard occurs and develops. • Micro-meteorological effects of buildings and terrain alter dispersion of hazardous materials. • Non-compliance with applicable codes (e.g., building or fire codes) and maintenance failures (e.g., fire protection and containment features) can substantially increase the damage to the facility itself and to surrounding buildings. Tennessee requires businesses to adhere to EPA Tier II reporting standards. Tier II is a federal obligation mandated by the EPA, with reporting done on the state and local level. Known officially as Emergency and Hazardous Chemical Inventory Forms, Tier II Reports are submitted annually to local fire departments, Local Emergency Planning Committees (LEPC) and State Emergency Response Commissions (SERCs) to help those agencies plan for and respond to chemical emergencies. Mandated by Section 312 of the Emergency Planning and Community Right-To-Know Act (EPCRA)—also known as SARA Title III—the Tier II form captures information about the types, quantities, and locations of hazardous chemicals at a given facility. The form also lists contact information for the facility’s designated emergency point-of-contact. The Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR) and CDC both keep a list of hazardous materials ranked for hazard planning purposes. But incidents can also happen during transportation, loading and unloading, and pipeline transport. Contributing and/or causal factors include human error; natural hazards such as earthquakes, tornadoes, floods, and lightning strikes; automobile and railroad accidents; power outages; electrical fires; computer malfunctions or server breakdowns.
