text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 346 3.7.8.3 Vulnerability Analysis – Hazardous Materials Release Hazardous materials releases can have significant and wide-ranging impacts on the environment, human health, and the economy. They can contaminate air, water, and soil, posing serious health risks to both humans and wildlife. Exposure to hazardous substances can lead to acute or chronic health effects, including respiratory problems, organ damage, cancer, and even death. The release of hazardous materials can also result in the loss of biodiversity, destruction of ecosystems, and long-term contamination of land and water resources. Moreover, these incidents often require costly cleanup and remediation efforts, leading to economic burdens for affected communities and businesses. 3.7.8.3.1 Estimated Impact and Potential Losses Hazardous material releases can have a severe impact on infrastructure, resulting in significant damage and potential losses. Infrastructure, such as roads, bridges, pipelines, and buildings, can be affected by the release, leading to structural damage or even collapse. Corrosive or toxic substances can erode or weaken infrastructure components, compromising their integrity and stability. In the case of pipelines, a hazardous material leak can result in pipeline failures, leading to environmental contamination and disrupting the transportation of resources. The cleanup and remediation efforts following a hazardous material release can also impact infrastructure, as extensive decontamination measures may be required. Additionally, the economic consequences of infrastructure damage can be substantial, including costs associated with repairs, reconstruction, and loss of functionality. Disruptions in transportation routes and utilities can hinder economic activities, affecting businesses, trade, and local economies. 3.7.8.3.2 Vulnerable Population Hazardous material releases pose a significant risk to human populations, resulting in various impacts and

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: substantial, including costs associated with repairs, reconstruction, and loss of functionality. Disruptions in transportation routes and utilities can hinder economic activities, affecting businesses, trade, and local economies. 3.7.8.3.2 Vulnerable Population Hazardous material releases pose a significant risk to human populations, resulting in various impacts and potential losses. The exposure to toxic substances released into the environment can lead to acute and chronic health effects on individuals residing in affected areas. Inhalation of hazardous fumes or contact with contaminated water or soil can cause respiratory problems, skin irritations, neurological disorders, and other serious illnesses. Depending on the severity and duration of exposure, the consequences can range from temporary discomfort to long-term health complications or even death. Hazardous material releases may also necessitate evacuations to ensure the safety of the population, leading to disruptions in daily life, displacement, and potential psychological distress. The economic impact on individuals can be significant, with medical expenses, loss of income due to illness or evacuation, and property damage or loss. Additionally, the long-term consequences of a hazardous material release, such as the stigma associated with contaminated areas, can affect property values and community well-being. Populations residing in close proximity to industrial areas or transportation routes where hazardous materials are transported are at an increased risk of exposure to hazmat releases. These communities may face higher levels of pollution and have limited resources to protect

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 347 themselves or evacuate in the event of a release. The lack of access to adequate healthcare and limited awareness of the potential hazards further exacerbates their vulnerability. Disadvantaged populations, including low-income communities and marginalized groups, are often disproportionately affected by hazmat releases. These communities are more likely to live near industrial facilities or hazardous waste sites, where the potential for releases is higher. Socioeconomic factors, limited access to healthcare, language barriers, and reduced resources for emergency response and evacuation can make it challenging for these populations to effectively respond and recover from hazmat incidents. Furthermore, populations with pre-existing health conditions or compromised immune systems are more vulnerable to the health impacts of hazmat releases. Exposure to hazardous materials can exacerbate respiratory issues, allergies, and chronic illnesses. Individuals with limited access to healthcare or inadequate protective measures face additional challenges in managing their health during and after a hazmat incident. Schools, daycare centers, and healthcare facilities also have a heightened vulnerability to hazmat releases. These establishments often house a large number of people, including children, who may have limited ability to protect themselves or evacuate independently. 3.7.8.3.3 Impact on State Assets All state assets are vulnerable to impacts from hazardous material releases. Both the infrastructure (state assets) and people in and near areas where hazardous materials are released can suffer acute and chronic impacts.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 350 3.7.9 Infrastructure Incidents 3.7.9.1 Hazard Profile – Infrastructure Incidents Infrastructure failure refers to the partial or complete breakdown of critical systems, facilities, or networks that provide essential services to society. Infrastructure failures can have severe consequences, including economic losses, public safety risks, and disruptions to daily life. The following is a brief overview of some of the potential infrastructure incidents: • Structural failure occurs when the physical integrity of infrastructure such as bridges, buildings, or dams is compromised leading to collapse or significant damage. Structural failures can result from factors like poor design, construction flaws, material degradation, or natural hazards. • Utility failure occurs when systems such as power grids, water supply networks, and communication systems experience failures due to equipment malfunctions, natural disasters, cyberattacks, or inadequate maintenance. Utility failures can lead to power outages, water shortages, loss of communication, and disruptions to various sectors. • Transportation failures occur when roads, railways, airports, or ports suffer from failures that impede mobility and logistics. This includes road or bridge collapses, train derailments, airport closures, and disruptions to maritime operations. Severe weather, accidents, or inadequate maintenance can contribute to transportation failures. • Information technology failures occur from hardware or software malfunction, cyberattacks, network outages, or data breaches. These failures can disrupt communication, business operations, financial systems, and essential services dependent on technology. Natural disasters, aging infrastructure, insufficient maintenance, and human error/accidents all contribute to the hazard of infrastructure failure. Events like earthquakes, droughts, floods, storms, and extreme temperatures can overwhelm infrastructure systems, causing failures due to structural damage, power outages, and communication disruptions. Aging

Events like earthquakes, droughts, floods, storms, and extreme temperatures can overwhelm infrastructure systems, causing failures due to structural damage, power outages, and communication disruptions. Aging infrastructure that was built decades ago and is now in need of repair, retrofitting, or replacement is also an issue. Aging infrastructure can become more vulnerable to failures due to wear and tear, corrosion, and outdated design standards. Inadequate or deferred maintenance can weaken infrastructure over time, making it more prone to failure. These bridges play a crucial role in connecting different parts of the state and facilitating transportation. Tennessee has an extensive rail network that supports freight and passenger transportation and is served by all major Class I railroads. Railways in Tennessee are used for the transportation of foods and commodities including coal, agricultural products, and manufactured goods. Several navigable rivers pass through the boundaries of Tennessee including the Mississippi River, Tennessee River, Cumberland River, and the Clinch River. These waterways play a vital role in transportation, commerce, and recreational activities. A robust energy infrastructure is prevalent within the state that includes power generation plants, electrical transmission lines, and distribution networks. TVA is a public power corporation responsible for nearly all power generation and manages grid transmission in the state. Along with energy, Tennessee has a well-developed telecommunication infrastructure that includes landline and mobile networks, internet service providers, and fiber optic networks. These networks facilitate communication and data transfer across the state. Types of infrastructure vary across the regions within the state based on population density, economic activity, and geographical factors. Infrastructure also varies between urban, suburban, and rural areas. 3.7.9.2.2 Previous Occurrences/Probability Since the 2018 Hazard Mitigation Plan update, there have been several instances of infrastructure incidences within the state of Tennessee. Predicting infrastructure failure is challenging and difficult to quantify; however, based on historical records the annual chance of occurrence is calculated at 100% annually.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 358 Figure 170: Needs for Drinking Water Infrastructure Improvement per Person 2018251 3.7.9.3.1 Estimated Impact and Potential Losses Infrastructure failures can disrupt economic activities by causing delays, shutdowns, and reduced productivity. A bridge collapse, for example, can obstruct transportation routes, leading to the disruption of supply chains and increased costs for businesses. Failure of infrastructure can cause extensive damage to both public and private property while also disrupting the movement of people and goods. Industries reliant on transportation networks can suffer significant setbacks. These types of failures can also lead to communication breakdowns and utility outages while also adversely impacting the environment. Water bodies can be contaminated if a gas line ruptures, harming the ecosystem. Environmental damage can have long-term consequences for biodiversity, water quality, and natural resources. 3.7.9.3.2 Vulnerable Population One of the main impacts of infrastructure failure is the loss of life and injuries that could occur in the event of a bridge failure, building collapse, or transportation incident. These failures can cause immense grief and suffering for the families and loved ones of the victims. Injured individuals may require medical treatment, rehabilitation, and may experience long-term physical or psychological effects. Infrastructure failures erode public confidence in the reliability and safety of essential systems. They can damage the reputation of governing bodies, infrastructure managers, and engineering firms responsible for maintenance and management. Additionally, issues such as lack of 251 Ibid.

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 359 communication or utility outages can drastically impact the response efforts and make it challenging for affected individuals to receive aid. Infrastructure failures can also disrupt people’s daily routines and activities. Transportation failures can lead to delays, canceled trips, and difficulties in commuting to work, school, or other important engagements. In addition to disrupting daily routines, infrastructure failures can disrupt access to essential services such as clean water, electricity, healthcare facilities, and communication networks which can compromise people’s health, safety, and quality of life. Vulnerable populations such as the elderly, disabled individuals, and those with chronic illnesses may be particularly affected as they rely heavily on functioning infrastructure for their well-being. Populations residing in areas with aging or inadequate infrastructure are more vulnerable to infrastructure incidents. These communities may experience disruptions in essential services such as water, electricity, transportation, or communication systems. The lack of reliable infrastructure can hinder their access to resources, emergency services, and recovery efforts during and after an incident. Disadvantaged communities, including low-income neighborhoods and marginalized groups, often face greater vulnerability to infrastructure incidents. These communities may have limited access to well-maintained infrastructure, such as roads, bridges, and public transportation systems, increasing their exposure to risks. Inadequate infrastructure can exacerbate socioeconomic disparities, hinder economic opportunities, and impede access to essential services. Rural communities are also susceptible to the impacts of infrastructure incidents. Remote or isolated areas may have limited infrastructure and resources, making them more vulnerable to disruptions in transportation, healthcare services, or emergency response. The geographic challenges faced by rural communities can hamper their ability to recover from infrastructure incidents and access necessary support. Additionally, populations with disabilities or limited mobility face heightened vulnerability. Inaccessible infrastructure, such as lack of ramps, elevators, or accommodations for visual or hearing impairments, can hinder their ability to evacuate, access emergency services, or receive timely information during incidents. 3.7.9.3.3 Impact on State Assets All state assets are vulnerable to impacts from infrastructure incidences. Both the infrastructure (state assets) and people in and near areas where infrastructure incidences occur could be impacted.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 362 3.7.10 Severe Storms 3.7.10.1 Hazard Profile – Severe Storms Severe storms comprise the hazardous and damaging weather effects often found in violent storm fronts. They can occur together or separate; they are common and usually not hazardous, but on occasion they can pose a threat to life and property. The severe storms profile includes thunderstorms (convective), hail, lightning, high/strong winds (non-convective), and severe winter weather. 3.7.10.1.1 Thunderstorms A thunderstorm is a local storm produced by a cumulonimbus cloud and accompanied by lightning and thunder.252 A thunderstorm is a rain shower during which you hear thunder. Thunder is caused by lightning. Energy from lightning heats the air briefly to around 50,000 °F, much hotter than the surface of the sun (9,930 °F). A supersonic shock occurs that compresses the surrounding air and keeps it under intense pressure, the decay of the supersonic shock causes the air to explode outward. The huge pressure in the initial outward shock wave decreases rapidly with increasing distance and within ten yards or so has become small enough to be perceived as the sound we call thunder. Thunderstorms are capable of producing high winds, heavy rains, lightning, and hail. These events affect relatively small areas when compared with hurricanes and winter storms. A thunderstorm forms from a combination of moisture, rapidly rising warm air, and a force capable of lifting air such as a warm and cold front, a sea breeze, or a mountain. A thunderstorm is classified as “severe” when it contains one or more of the following: hail one inch or greater, winds gusting in excess

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: air, and a force capable of lifting air such as a warm and cold front, a sea breeze, or a mountain. A thunderstorm is classified as “severe” when it contains one or more of the following: hail one inch or greater, winds gusting in excess of 50 knots (57.5 mph), or a tornado. Typical thunderstorms are 15 miles in diameter and last an average of 30 minutes. An estimated 100,000 thunderstorms occur each year in the United States, with approximately 10% of them classified as severe. During the warm season, thunderstorms are responsible for most of the rainfall. Thunderstorms are monitored in real time using weather satellites and weather radars. Meteorologists watch these pictures over time to watch for rapidly growing clouds, a clue to a possible thunderstorm. Doppler radar sends out electromagnetic wave fields that can be reflected back to the radar by things in the air like precipitation. The amount of energy that is reflected back can tell us how heavy the rain might be. The NWS provides two levels of public notification for severe storms: watch and warning.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 363 Table 133: National Weather Service Levels of Public Notification Public Notification Required Action Area Coverage Severe Thunderstorm Watch Be prepared! Severe thunderstorms are possible in and near the watch area. Stay informed and be ready to act if a severe thunderstorm warning is issued. The watch area is typically large, covering numerous counties or even states. Severe Thunderstorm Warning Take action! Severe weather has been reported by spotters or indicated by radar. Warnings indicate imminent danger to life and property. Take shelter in a substantial building. Avoid mobile homes that can blow over in high winds. Warnings typically encompass a much smaller area. 3.7.10.1.2 Hail Hail is a form of precipitation consisting of solid ice that forms inside thunderstorm updrafts. Hailstones are formed when raindrops are carried upward by thunderstorm updrafts into extremely cold areas of the atmosphere and freeze. Hailstones then grow by colliding with liquid water drops that freeze onto the hailstone’s surface. If the water freezes instantaneously when colliding with the hailstone, cloudy ice will form as air bubbles will be trapped in the newly formed ice. However, if the water freezes slowly, the air bubbles can escape, and the new ice will be clear. The hail falls when the thunderstorm's updraft can no longer support the weight of the hailstone, which can occur if the stone becomes large enough or the updraft weakens. The size of hailstones is a direct function of the size and severity of the storm. The size varies and is related to the severity and size of the thunderstorm that produced it. The higher

The size varies and is related to the severity and size of the thunderstorm that produced it. The higher the temperatures at the earth’s surface, the greater the strength of the updrafts, and the greater the amount of time the hailstones are suspended, giving them more time to increase in size. Damage to crops and vehicles are typically the most significant impacts of hailstorms. Most lightning starts inside a thunderstorm and travels through the cloud. In the early stages of development, air acts as an insulator between the positive and negative charges in the cloud and between the cloud and the ground. When opposite charges build up enough, the air’s insulating capacity breaks down and there is a rapid discharge of electricity that is seen as lightning. Lightning can occur between opposite charges within the thunderstorm cloud (intra-cloud lightning) or between opposite charges in the cloud and on the ground (cloud-to-ground lightning). Intra-cloud lightning is the

text: capacity breaks down and there is a rapid discharge of electricity that is seen as lightning. Lightning can occur between opposite charges within the thunderstorm cloud (intra-cloud lightning) or between opposite charges in the cloud and on the ground (cloud-to-ground lightning). Intra-cloud lightning is the most common type of discharge. It transpires inside the cloud and looks from the outside of the cloud like a diffuse brightening that flickers. However, the flash may exit the boundary of the cloud, and a bright channel, similar to a cloud-to-ground flash, can be visible for many miles. In the United States, an average of 300 people are injured and 80 people are killed by lightning each year. Currently, cloud-to-ground and intra-cloud lightning flashes are detected and mapped in real-time by two U.S. networks: the National Lightning Detection Network (NLDN) and the Earth Networks Total Lightning Network (ENTLN). These two systems work by

This type of lightning has the potential for extreme fire activity and is normally highlighted in fire weather forecasts with a Red Flag Warning. 3.7.10.1.4 High/Strong Winds (Non-Convective Winds) High winds are defined as sustained wind speeds of 40 miles per hour or greater lasting for 1 hour or longer, or winds of 58 miles per hour or greater for any duration. They are often referred to as straight line winds to differentiate from tornado associated wind. Wind begins with differences in air pressures. It is a rough horizontal movement of air caused by uneven heating of the earth’s surface. Major damage directly caused by high winds is relatively rare, while minor damage is common and pervasive, and most noticeable when it contributes to power outages. These power outages can have major negative impacts such as increased tendency for traffic accidents, increased vulnerability to fire, food spoilage, and other losses that might be sustained by a loss of power. These high winds can also cause trees and limbs to fall, damaging cars and structures. Flying debris can also present a danger to those caught unsheltered during a storm. Three basic ingredients are necessary to make a winter storm: • Cold air: Below freezing temperatures in the clouds and near the ground are necessary to make snow and/or ice.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 367 • Lift: Something to raise the moist air to the clouds and cause precipitation. An example of lift is warm air colliding with cold air and being forced to rise over the cold dome. The boundary between the warm and cold air masses is called a front. Another example of lift is air flowing up a mountainside. • Moisture: To form clouds and precipitation. Air blowing across a body of water, such as a large lake or the ocean, is an excellent source of moisture. Winter storms include blizzards, snowstorms, and ice storms, which are described in Table 137. Table 137: Types of Winter Storms Winter Storm Description Blizzard Dangerous winter storms that are a combination of blowing snow and wind resulting in very low visibilities. While heavy snowfalls and severe cold often accompany blizzards, they are not required. Sometimes strong winds pick up snow that has already fallen, creating a ground blizzard. Ice Storm Storm which results in the accumulation of at least 0.25” of ice on exposed surfaces. They create hazardous driving and walking conditions. Tree branches and powerlines can easily snap under the weight of the ice. Lake Effect Storms As a cold, dry air mass moves over large lakes (e.g., the Great Lakes region), the air picks up lots of moisture from the lakes. This air, now full of water, dumps the water as snow in areas generally to the south and east of the lakes. Snow Squalls Brief, intense snow showers accompanied by strong, gusty winds. Accumulation may be significant. Snow squalls are best known in the

text: lakes. This air, now full of water, dumps the water as snow in areas generally to the south and east of the lakes. Snow Squalls Brief, intense snow showers accompanied by strong, gusty winds. Accumulation may be significant. Snow squalls are best known in the Great Lakes region. The aftermath of a winter storm can have an impact on a community or region for days, weeks, or even months; potentially causing cold temperatures, flooding, storm surge, closed and/or blocked roadways, downed utility lines, and power outages. Most deaths from winter storms are not directly related to the storm itself. People die in traffic accidents on icy roads, heart attacks while shoveling snow or hypothermia from prolonged exposure to cold. Accurately forecasting winter weather is a complicated process. It starts with a wide network of observing systems such as satellites, Doppler radars and automated surface observing systems. Computer forecast models take this information and estimate what will happen next. Forecasters then use their experience to write and issue forecasts.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 368 3.7.10.2 Risk Assessment – Severe Storms 3.7.10.2.1 Geographic Extent Tennessee experiences a range of severe weather conditions throughout the year including thunderstorms, hail, lightning, thunderstorm winds, non-convective winds, and winter weather. The entire state is vulnerable to this hazard. Thunderstorms are common in Tennessee, particularly during the spring and summer months. They can occur throughout the state but are more prevalent in the western and central regions. Severe thunderstorms with heavy rainfall, strong winds, and lightning can occur, leading to the possibility of flash floods and damaging winds. The eastern portion of Tennessee experiences a combination of atmospheric conditions influenced by the Appalachian Mountains which can contribute to the development of thunderstorms. Hailstorms, lightning, and thunderstorm winds are often localized within a thunderstorm and can affect the entire planning area of Tennessee. The exact extent of these phenomenon within a given area can be challenging to predict with precision, as it depends on the specific track and characteristics of the storm. The specific extent and impact of these phenomenon can vary from one storm to another. The following maps provide additional information about the extent of thunderstorms. Hail reports and wind reports are shown across the entire state. However, thunderstorm watches and lightning strikes follow a general west to east pattern, with West Tennessee seeing far more lightning strikes than East Tennessee. When a cold front or a low-pressure system moves through Tennessee, it can generate strong winds across the state. The extent of these winds can vary depending on the size and intensity of the system. In general, when a strong cold front sweeps across the state, it can bring gusty winds that impact a large geographic area. Mountainous regions, such as the Great Smoky Mountains, can experience enhanced wind speeds due to the influence of the terrain. Wind can funnel through valleys in the mountains causing them to accelerate and intensify. Elevated areas such as the Cumberland Plateau can experience slightly higher wind speeds due to the elevation when compared with the surrounding low-lying areas. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 371 Figure 176: Mean Number of High Wind Days per Year, 1986–2015255 Severe winter weather in Tennessee can encompass various conditions including snow, ice storms, and freezing rain. The geographic extent and severity of winter weather can vary from year to year. The eastern portion of the state typically experiences more significant winter weather when compared with other regions of the state due to the higher elevations and the influence of colder air masses. Snowfall in the eastern portion of the state can be more frequent and heavier, especially in the Appalachian Mountains and Cumberland Plateau. Middle and West Tennessee experience a mixture of winter weather conditions. Snowfall is generally less frequent and less substantial when compared with the mountainous regions of eastern Tennessee, but winter weather can still impact the region. Freezing rain and ice storms are typically more common in West and Middle Tennessee which can lead to hazardous road conditions and power outages. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 372 Figure 177: Average Annual Snowfall for Tennessee, 2008–2023 3.7.10.2.2 Previous Occurrences/Probability Since the 2018 Hazard Mitigation Plan update, the NCEI Storm Events Database indicates there have been 544 occurrences of hail which have impacted the state of Tennessee. Hail sizes for these events have ranged from 0.75 inches to 4 inches in diameter. These occurrences are responsible for $42,000 in damage and there have been no fatalities or injuries as a result during this time period. The annual chance of occurrence for severe storms in the state of Tennessee is calculated at 100% annually. Several notable hail events are described below: • June 19, 2019 – Large hail up to half dollar size fell in Brentwood (northern Williamson County). title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 388 Since the 2018 Hazard Mitigation Plan update, the NCEI Storm Events Database indicates there have been 1,812 occurrences of thunderstorm winds which have impacted the state of Tennessee. Thunderstorm wind speeds for these events have ranged from 45 mph to 96 mph. These occurrences are responsible for $54,572,830 in damage and there have been eight fatalities and 22 injuries as a result during this time period. Several notable events are described below: • June 2019 – A nine day stretch of near-daily severe storms across Middle Tennessee, with widespread damaging winds, scattered large hail, and five tornadoes impacting the area. The most damaging events occurred on Wednesday June 19, Friday June 21, and Thursday, June 27. During the first event in this severe storm sequence, scattered multicell and supercell thunderstorms affected much of Middle Tennessee during the afternoon and evening hours on June 19. • October 26, 2019 – Storms with high winds moved through the eastern edge of the rural West Tennessee region on Saturday. This resulted in extensive damage in multiple counties and multiple overturned 18-wheeler vehicles on Interstate 40, causing significant damage and slamming Hardin County west of the Tennessee River and Adamsville.269 Figure 181: Damages from Storm Winds on I-40, October 26, 2019 269 The Courier, “Storm causes heavy damage in Hardin County,” October 26, 2019, www.courieranywhere.com. https://www.courieranywhere.com/2019/10/26/storm-causes-heavy-damagein-hardin-county/

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 389 Figure 182: Severe Storms in October 2019 Caused Extensive Damage in Hardin County, Tennessee270 • January 11, 2020 – Severe storms and high winds rocked the Tennessee Valley which brought wind gusts over 60 mph and resulted in multiple damage reports. The National Weather Service in Huntsville issued Severe Thunderstorm and Tornado warnings as storms moved across the area.271 • March 29, 2020 – Thunderstorm winds of 83 mph occurred in Mt. Pisgah (White County) and Browntown (Cumberland County) and caused a combined damage of $7 million. This included hundreds of trees snapped and uprooted, roofs damaged or lost, barns and outbuildings destroyed, and a train blown partially off the tracks. • May 3, 2020 – Nashville Airport reported winds of 62 mph with gusts up to 71 mph, which is the fifth highest on record. That storm was classified as a derecho, the worst straight-line wind event since the derecho of July 2004. Total damage from the 2020 storm across Middle Tennessee was estimated at $16 million, with power lost to 130,000 customers for up to one week. • May 4, 2020 – Severe thunderstorms, called an MCS (Mesoscale Convective System), developed across western Tennessee in the afternoon hours then moved across southern Middle Tennessee during the evening hours. These storms once again produced widespread straight-line wind damage across Perry, Lewis, Wayne, Lawrence, and Giles counties. 270 Jackson Sun, “Storms damage multiple towns, shut down I-40,” October 26, 2019, www.jacksonsun.com. https://www.jacksonsun.com/story/news/2019/10/26/storms-damage-multipletowns-shut-down-40/2473965001/ 271 WHNT News, “January 11, 2020 Severe Weather Recap,” whnt.com. https://whnt.com/weather/liveblog-storm-reports-and-warnings-from-across-the-tennessee-valley-january-11-2020/

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan

Several notable events are described below: • January 23, 2019 – A 60 to 70 mph wind gusts tore part of the roof off a Greene County elementary school and sent metal debris flying through the parking lot. • February 20, 2019 – Areas of Greene County, Tennessee experienced a 123 mile-perhour wind gust in the Camp Creek area, according to the National Weather Service. Extremely high winds reportedly downed numerous trees and power lines.276 • April 14, 2019 – High winds in a storm downed trees and damaged trees across East Tennessee.277 • October 31, 2019 – A straight-line wind barreled across Claiborne County, snapping trees and power poles, and tossing roofs from buildings. • October 28, 2021 – High winds gusts of up to 70 mph were recorded in the Great Smoky Mountains National Park in Tennessee and North Carolina, forcing the closure of major thoroughfares in the park and creating dangerous conditions.278

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 416 3.7.10.2.3 Impacts of Climate Trends and Variations Climate trends and variations may lead to an increase in frequency and intensity of certain types of severe storms. Warmer air temperatures can contribute to more moisture in the atmosphere, providing fuel for stronger rainfall events and potentially more intense thunderstorms. The increased energy in the atmosphere can also contribute to the development of more powerful storms. Climate trends can also result in altered precipitation patterns influencing the distribution, timing, and intensity of rainfall during storms. Climate trends can also influence the paths and tracks of severe storms. Changes in atmospheric circulation patterns may lead to shifts in the regions where storms typically form or move, potentially affecting the areas that are historically vulnerable to specific types of storms. This can result in new areas being exposed to severe storms while other areas experience a decrease. Research by Ashley et al. (2023) into supercell thunderstorm formation compared historical data (1990–2005) and future climate models for the late 21st century (2085–2100), which indicate that the mid-South region of the United States (including West and Middle Tennessee) could see an increase in the number of supercell thunderstorms capable of producing severe thunderstorm hazards and tornadoes. These increases were mostly found in the late winter to early spring months of February, March, and April. Additionally, they found that an increasing number of supercell thunderstorms in this region could form in the late afternoon to overnight hours. Climate trends can contribute to compound events where multiple extreme weather events can occur simultaneously or in succession. These compound events can

Climate trends can contribute to compound events where multiple extreme weather events can occur simultaneously or in succession. These compound events can amplify the overall impacts on communities and ecosystems, making them more challenging to manage and recover from. For additional information about climate trends and variations that may impact severe storms, refer to the Extreme Temperatures and Flood sections. Changes in temperature can impact the timing, likelihood, and intensity of both thunderstorms and winter weather. Additionally, increases in extreme rainfall events in the future will often be associated with thunderstorms. Based on historical data, trends for thunderstorm winds, severe hail, lightning strikes, nonconvective winds, and winter weather were analyzed and mapped at the county level for Tennessee. For thunderstorm winds, Davidson and Overton counties had the most significant increasing trends, while a cluster of counties in southwest Tennessee had the most significant decreasing trends (Fayette, Haywood, Hardeman, Chester, and Henderson). Severe hail showed minimal counties with trends in either direction. Lightning showed very clear significant decreasing trends in most of East Tennessee and southern Middle Tennessee, along with Henry County in West Tennessee. No county showed an increasing trend in lightning strikes. Space-time cube analysis provides additional details of these trends at the county level. Sevier, Greene, and Davidson counties had the most significant increasing trends for non-convective winds. Camp Creek in Greene County has had many notable damaging non-convective wind events, also called mountain wind-wave events. Severe storm events such as winter weather can damage roads, bridges, railways, and airports. Heavy snowfall and ice can make roads impassable, causing delays and cancellations. These disruptions can affect not only local transportation but national and international logistics and supply chains. Severe storms, particularly storms with high winds, lightning, or ice accumulation can damage power lines, transformers, and other electrical equipment. Falling trees and branches can bring down power lines, leading to widespread outages. Prolonged power outages can have significant impacts on homes, businesses, and essential services like hospitals. High winds, heavy rainfall, and hailstorms associated with severe storms can damage buildings and structures. Roofs can be ripped off, windows shattered, and walls weakened. These storms can also disrupt communication systems such as telephone networks, internet connectivity, and broadcast services. Damaged transmission towers, downed power lines, and waterlogged underground cables can interrupt communication channels hampering emergency response efforts. 3.7.10.3.2 Vulnerable Population Severe storms can have a significant impact on the population in Tennessee. They can cause physical injuries and even fatalities. High winds, flying debris, falling trees, and structural collapses can pose immediate risks to people’s safety during a storm. These storms can displace individuals and families from their homes, either temporarily or permanently. In cases of extensive property damage, people may be forced to evacuate or seek emergency shelter. The displacement can result in temporary homelessness or the need for long-term housing solutions. Severe storms can disrupt critical infrastructure such as transportation systems, power grids, and water supply networks. Disruption in these services could lead to health issues or the inability to access essential services that are needed to meet basic needs. This can lead to not only physical issues but psychological effects as well. Everyone in the state of Tennessee is vulnerable to the impacts of severe storms; however, severe storms can have a disproportionate impact on vulnerable populations, exacerbating existing social, economic,

Acts of terrorism include threats of terrorism; assassinations; kidnappings; hijackings; bomb scares and bombings; cyber-attacks; and the use of chemical, biological, nuclear, and radiological weapons. The following is a brief overview of some of the potential terroristic actions: • Explosive devices have been used frequently by terrorists and is one of their more common weapons. Explosive devices are highly portable using vehicles and humans to transport them, and information on construction of these types of devices are readily available. They are also easily detonated from remote locations or by suicide bombers. • Biological threats are organisms or toxins that have the potential to kill or incapacitate people, livestock, and crops. The three basic groups of biological agents are bacteria, viruses, and toxins. Most biological agents are difficult to grow and maintain. Biological agents can be dispersed through aerosols, infecting animals that carry diseases to humans, or by contaminating food or water supplies. • Chemical threats are poisonous vapors, aerosols, liquids, and solids that have toxic effects on people, animals, or plants. They can be released by bombs or sprayed from aircraft, boats, or vehicles. They can be used as liquids to create a hazard to people and the environment. • Nuclear blasts are explosions with intense light and heat, a damaging pressure wave, and widespread radioactive material that can contaminate the air, water, and ground surfaces for miles around. • Radiological dispersion, often referred

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: liquids to create a hazard to people and the environment. • Nuclear blasts are explosions with intense light and heat, a damaging pressure wave, and widespread radioactive material that can contaminate the air, water, and ground surfaces for miles around. • Radiological dispersion, often referred to as a “dirty bomb,” combines a conventional explosive device with radioactive material. It is designed to scatter dangerous and sublethal amounts of radioactive material over a general area. The impact of terrorism on the United States has been significant. The most devastating act of terrorism in U.S. history was the September 11, 2001, attacks, when the extremist group AlQaeda hijacked four commercial airplanes and targeted prominent landmarks, resulting in the deaths of nearly 3,000 people. This event led to a paradigm shift in U.S. national security and foreign policy, as well as the creation of the Department of Homeland Security and the initiation of the "War on Terror." Types of terrorism can vary based on their motives and methods. Some common types include: • Religious Terrorism: Perpetrated by groups or individuals who claim to be acting in the name of a religious ideology. Examples include Islamic extremist groups like Al-Qaeda and ISIS. • Nationalist Terrorism: Conducted by individuals or groups seeking to promote the interests of a specific nationality or ethnic group. These terrorists often aim to create an independent state or gain autonomy.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 447 • Ideological Terrorism: Driven by a particular political ideology or belief system, such as communism, anarchism, or white supremacy. The motives may vary, but the aim is usually to challenge or overthrow an existing political or social order. • State-Sponsored Terrorism: In some cases, governments may sponsor or support terrorist activities as a means to achieve political or strategic objectives. However, this type of terrorism is relatively rare. • Cyberterrorism: Involves the use of technology and cyberspace to conduct attacks on computer systems, networks, and critical infrastructure, causing disruption and damage. It is important to note that these categories are not mutually exclusive, and individuals or groups may exhibit characteristics of multiple types of terrorism. Furthermore, the motivations behind acts of terrorism can vary significantly, making it a complex and evolving phenomenon to understand and combat. Predicting specific acts of terrorism is challenging. However, law enforcement agencies and intelligence organizations actively monitor potential threats and work to prevent attacks. Common targets for terrorist activities include crowded public places, transportation systems, government buildings, critical infrastructure, and symbolic landmarks. Efforts to counter terrorism in the United States involve a combination of intelligence gathering, law enforcement, border security, international cooperation, and public awareness campaigns. The aim is to prevent terrorist acts, protect citizens, and ensure the safety and security of the nation. 3.7.11.2 Risk Assessment – Terrorism 3.7.11.2.1 Geographic Extent A terroristic act could potentially occur anywhere in the state of Tennessee. This destruction disrupts normal functioning, causes economic losses, and can take considerable time and resources to repair. Infrastructure damage and disruption to businesses and services can lead to financial losses, decreased productivity, and increased unemployment. Tourism, trade, and investment may also suffer due to security concerns, further affecting economic growth and development. Terrorist attacks may target critical infrastructure, such as power grids, water supply systems, and communication networks. Damaging or disabling these services can have cascading effects, impacting daily life, businesses, emergency response capabilities, and public safety. The restoration of services often requires time and resources, further disrupting normal operations. 3.7.11.3.2 Vulnerable Population Terrorism aims to instill fear and panic in societies. The threat of future attacks can create a pervasive sense of insecurity and anxiety among the general population, altering people's behaviors and daily routines. Individuals may experience heightened stress, trauma, and longlasting psychological effects as a result of terrorism. Terrorism often results in the tragic loss of

These casualties generate immense grief and suffering for the victims' families and communities. Terrorism can also undermine social cohesion and harmony within communities. Attacks that target specific religious, ethnic, or cultural groups can exacerbate tensions and lead to divisions, discrimination, and even communal violence. Trust between different segments of society may be eroded, making reconciliation and unity more challenging. A vulnerable group subject to terrorism includes individuals belonging to minority or marginalized communities. Terrorist organizations may target specific ethnic, religious, or cultural groups, aiming to instill fear, promote division, or advance their extremist ideologies. This can lead to discrimination, persecution, and social unrest, placing these populations at heightened risk. Additionally, crowded and high-profile locations attract the attention of terrorists aiming to maximize casualties and media attention. Therefore, populations in urban centers, transportation hubs, tourist destinations, and places of symbolic significance may face increased vulnerability to terrorist attacks. The concentration of people in these areas can make them potential targets. Government officials, security forces, and infrastructure personnel are also vulnerable due to their roles in maintaining public safety and combating terrorism. These individuals may be specifically targeted by terrorist groups seeking to disrupt governance, intimidate authorities, or undermine security measures. 3.7.11.3.3 Impact on State Assets All state assets are vulnerable to acts of terrorism.

Power outages may occur due to explosives or attacks on nuclear plants, disrupting communication and fuel supply. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 452 3.7.12 Tornado 3.7.12.1 Hazard Profile – Tornado Tornadoes (also called twisters) are rapidly rotating funnels of wind extending between storm clouds and the ground. Tornadoes and waterspouts form during severe weather occurrences, such as thunderstorms and hurricanes, when cold air overrides a layer of warm air, causing the warm air to rise rapidly. This usually results in a counterclockwise rotation in the northern hemisphere. The updraft of air in tornadoes always rotates because of wind shear (differing speeds of moving air at various heights), and it can rotate in either a clockwise or counterclockwise direction; clockwise rotations (in the northern hemisphere) will sustain the system, at least until other forces cause it to die seconds to minutes later. Since February 1, 2007, the Enhanced Fujita (EF) Scale has been used to classify tornado intensity. The EF Scale classifies tornadoes based on their damage pattern rather than wind speed; wind speed is then derived and estimated. This contrasts with the Saffir-Simpson scale used for hurricane classification, which is based on measured wind speed. The following table shows the EF scale in comparison with the original Fujita (F) Scale, which was used prior to February 1, 2007. When discussing past tornadoes, the scale used at the time of the hazard is used. Damage and adjustment between scales can be made using the following tables. The National Weather Service (NWS) has the ability to issue advisory messages based on forecasts and observations. The following are the advisory messages that may be issued with definitions of each: • Tornado Watch: Issued to alert people to the possibility of a tornado developing in the area. A tornado has not been spotted but the conditions are favorable for tornadoes to occur. • Tornado Warning: Issued when a tornado has been spotted or when Doppler radar identifies a distinctive “hook-shaped” area within a thunderstorm line. Structures within the direct path of a tornado vortex are often reduced to rubble. Structures adjacent to the tornado’s path are often severely damaged by high winds flowing into the tornado vortex, known as inflow winds. It is here, adjacent to the tornado’s path, that the building type and construction techniques are critical to the structure’s survival. Although tornadoes strike at random, making all buildings vulnerable, mobile homes, homes with crawlspaces, and buildings with large spans are more likely to suffer damage. Although tornadoes strike at random, making all buildings vulnerable, mobile homes, homes with crawlspaces, and buildings with large spans are more likely to suffer damage. The major health hazard from tornadoes is physical injury from flying debris or being in a collapsed building or mobile home. Within a building, flying debris or projectiles are generally stopped by interior walls. However, if a building has no partitions, any glass, brick, or other debris blown into the interior is life threatening. Following a tornado, damaged buildings are a potential health hazard due to instability, electrical system damage, and gas leaks. Sewage and water lines may also be damaged. Tornadoes have historically impacted all areas of Tennessee. Peak tornado activity in Tennessee occurs during the spring, as it does in the rest of the United States. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 455 Figure 205: Annual Average Tornado Watches per Year296 3.7.12.2 Risk Assessment – Tornado 3.7.12.2.1 Geographic Extent Tennessee is located within an area of the United States commonly referred to as "Dixie Alley," which is known for experiencing a significant number of tornadoes. Tornadoes can occur throughout the state, but the frequency and severity tend to vary by region. The central and western portions of Tennessee, including cities such as Memphis, Jackson, and Nashville, are more susceptible to tornadoes compared to the eastern part of the state. This is due to the proximity of these regions to the warm, moist air masses from the Gulf of Mexico, which can interact with cool, dry air masses from the north and west, creating favorable conditions for tornado formation. There is no exact tornado season in Tennessee, as tornadoes can occur in any month, but the highest likelihood for tornadoes typically spans from late winter through early summer, with the peak occurring in April and May. A second, smaller peak occurs again in November. During this time, atmospheric conditions, such as the clash of warm and cold air masses and the presence of strong wind shear, contribute to the development of severe thunderstorms and tornadoes. 296 Ibid.

Based on historical events, the annual chance of occurrence for tornadoes in the state of Tennessee is 100%. Several notable tornado outbreaks are described below: • June 21, 2019 – Statewide (Specific Examples include Davidson County, Macon County, and Fentress County): Four tornados touch down across three counties with two being a EF0 and two being EF1 on the Enhance Fujita scale. The longest of the four tornados stayed on the ground for 2 minutes and 24 seconds and, fortunately, caused minimal damage and no fatalities. The tornados were part of an extremely dangerous storm called a Derecho. A Derecho is a line of fast-moving windstorms and sometimes thunderstorms that move across a great distance accompanied by powerful straight-line winds that may cause widespread destruction and/or produce Tornadoes.297 297 National Weather Service, “June 21, 2019, Derecho & Tornadoes.” June 21, 2019, Derecho & Tornadoes (weather.gov)

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 478 Figure 223: Number of Tornadoes in Tennessee by Strength 3.7.12.2.3 Impacts of Climate Trends and Variations It is uncertain how climate trends will impact the overall frequency of tornadoes, with convective storms (from which tornadoes form) being the least well understood extreme events when it comes to attributing future changes to climate trends and variations. However, some studies suggest that the number of days conducive to severe thunderstorms, which can spawn tornadoes, may increase in certain regions. Additionally, warmer temperatures can provide more energy to storms, potentially leading to more intense tornadoes. Tornado formation depends on the interaction of multiple atmospheric factors, including temperature, humidity, wind shear, and instability. While climate trends may alter some of these factors, the precise impact on tornado formation remains uncertain. Warmer temperatures and increased moisture content in the atmosphere can contribute to more favorable conditions for tornado formation, but other factors like wind shear patterns may also change and reduce the chances for tornado formation. Climate trends could also affect the geographical distribution and tracks of tornadoes. Changes in large-scale weather patterns, such as shifts in the jet stream or alterations in atmospheric circulation patterns, may influence where tornadoes form and how they move. This could lead to changes in the regions that are most susceptible to tornado activity. The following figures display emerging hotspot analysis for tornadoes as well as trends at the county level. There are several sporadic and new hot spots in Middle Tennessee, especially surrounding and east of the Nashville metro area. Obion County in northwest Tennessee shows the strongest increasing trend in tornadoes and is additionally identified as a new hot spot along with neighboring Lake County.

These violent storms, characterized by powerful winds and immense forces, have a profound impact on buildings, roads, utilities, and other essential elements of a community's infrastructure. The immediate aftermath of a tornado is marked by the devastation of homes and structures, leaving behind debris and ruins. Critical infrastructure, such as hospitals, schools, and public facilities, often suffer severe damage or complete destruction, resulting in the disruption of vital services and compromising the community's functionality. Transportation becomes a challenge as roads and bridges are heavily impacted, rendering them impassable or unsafe. The tornado's immense power uproots trees, topples power lines, and damages electrical grids, leading to widespread power outages that can persist for days or even weeks. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 489 3.7.12.3.2 Vulnerable Population Tornadoes have a profound impact on the population of the affected areas, leaving behind a trail of devastation, loss, and disruption. These violent storms, characterized by swirling winds and destructive forces, pose a significant threat to the safety, well-being, and livelihoods of people in their path. The immediate impact of a tornado on the population is the loss of life and injuries. Tornadoes can cause fatalities and inflict severe harm on individuals caught in their path. The sudden and unpredictable nature of these storms often leaves little time for evacuation or sheltering, putting people at risk. The loss of loved ones and the physical injuries sustained can have long-lasting emotional and physical effects on the survivors. Tornadoes also result in population displacement and homelessness. The destruction of homes and buildings leaves many individuals and families without a place to live. Evacuation orders and damaged infrastructure may force people to seek temporary shelter in emergency centers or with friends and family. The disruption of normal life and the uncertainty of housing can create immense stress and hardship for those affected. The impact of tornadoes on the population extends beyond immediate physical harm and displacement. There are significant psychological and emotional effects as well. Survivors may experience trauma, grief, and anxiety in the aftermath of a tornado. Witnessing the destruction of their homes and communities can lead to feelings of loss, fear, and vulnerability. The recovery process can be emotionally challenging as individuals and communities try to rebuild their lives and regain a sense of normalcy. The economic impact of tornadoes on the population is also substantial. Many people lose their sources of income due to the destruction of businesses and disruption of local economies. The cost of rebuilding damaged infrastructure, homes, and public facilities adds to the financial burden. In some cases, entire communities may struggle to recover economically for years after a tornado event. Mobile homes, due to their lightweight construction, can be particularly susceptible to damage or destruction during tornado events. Individuals living in these structures may face challenges in finding safe shelter or have limited time to evacuate, increasing their risk of injury or fatality. Schools, daycare centers, and other educational facilities house a significant number of children and staff members, making them vulnerable during tornado events. Adequate tornado preparedness measures, including robust shelter plans and regular drills, are crucial to ensure the safety of these populations. Individuals with limited access to safe shelter, such as those experiencing homelessness or living in substandard housing, are also at increased risk during tornadoes. Their ability to seek shelter or find suitable protection may be compromised, heightening their vulnerability to severe weather events. Additionally, individuals with disabilities or limited mobility may face specific challenges during tornado events. Accessible shelters and evacuation plans, as well as inclusive emergency communication systems, are crucial for ensuring their safety and well-being. 3.7.12.3.3 Impact on State Assets All state assets are vulnerable to tornadoes. However, wooden structures, mobile structures, sheds, and other similar types of buildings are most vulnerable. Additionally, state assets in northeast Tennessee are generally less vulnerable since far fewer tornadoes occur in this region. These assets are still vulnerable to tornadoes, even with their lower frequency in the region.

These natural disasters can travel long distances on the ground and their path and intensity are unpredictable. Unfortunately, Tennessee is at a disadvantage regarding early tornado detection due to its terrain and the prevalence of nocturnal tornadoes. This puts more residents at risk compared to similarly sized states. Tornadoes can cause delays in affected areas, as trees and powerlines may fall, impacting safety and security, communication systems, and energy-reliant items. Power outages can also pose a risk to those who rely on medical equipment at home. Additionally, the Browns Ferry and Joseph M. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 494 3.7.13 Wildfire 3.7.13.1 Hazard Profile – Wildfire Wildfires are uncontrolled fires that spread through wildlands, consuming natural vegetation such as forests, grasslands, and brush lands. They may cause structure fires when they spread into human-developed areas containing buildings and other human-made objects. Wildlands are sometimes intentionally burned through prescribed fires. A wildfire, by definition, is unintentional, uncontrolled, and located in wildlands. Wildfires often go unnoticed until they produce enough smoke to be apparent to nearby observers or detected through wildfire monitoring programs. Wildfires can be intentionally or accidentally started by humans through arson or campfires, for example, or can be caused by natural events such as lightning. Wildfires are categorized into three types based on how they spread: • Ground fires burn organic matter in the soil beneath surface litter and are sustained by glowing combustion. • Surface fires spread with a flaming front and burn leaf litter, fallen branches, and other fuels located on the ground surface. • Crown fires burn through the tree canopy. These are the most intense fire type and are often the most difficult to contain. Three factors contribute significantly to wildfire behavior: • Topography. Mountainous terrain is more prone to wildfire than areas that are flat or have low relief. South-facing slopes are more prone to wildfires because they receive more solar radiation than flat areas and slopes facing in other directions. Greater solar radiation tends to dry vegetation and make it more prone to catching fire and burning. Steep slopes also allow fire to spread rapidly uphill, which typically slows or stops at ridgelines because

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: solar radiation than flat areas and slopes facing in other directions. Greater solar radiation tends to dry vegetation and make it more prone to catching fire and burning. Steep slopes also allow fire to spread rapidly uphill, which typically slows or stops at ridgelines because fire spreads more slowly downhill. • Fuel. Fuel is classified by size, moisture content, and volume. As fuel volume increases, fires become more intense and produce longer flames, making it more difficult to control and extinguish. Fuel with low moisture content ignites more easily than wet fuels. The size and continuity of fuels both horizontally and vertically are also important factors. • Weather. The most dynamic factor affecting wildfire behavior is weather. Temperature, humidity, wind, and lightning all contribute significantly to wildfire ignition and spread. Weather events ranging from small storms to major systems, and extreme conditions such as drought, heat, humidity, and wind lead to increased wildfire activity. Cool weather, higher humidity, and increased precipitation, on the other hand, reduce wildfire occurrence and improve controllability. The National Wildfire Coordinating Group (NWCG) classifies incidents as either natural caused, human caused, or undetermined. Specific causes of natural wildfires are lightning, volcanoes, “unknown,” or “other.” Specific causes of human-caused wildfires are: (1) debris and open burning, (2) equipment and vehicle use, (3) firearms and explosives use, (4) fireworks, (5) power generation/transmission/distribution, (6) railroad operations and maintenance,

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 495 (7) recreation and ceremony, (8) smoking, (9) misuse of fire by a minor, (10) arson, and (11) “other causes.”318 Table 176 identifies the fire intensity scale utilized to determine risk to wildfires. Table 176: The Southern Group of State Foresters Fire Intensity Scale Level Definition 1 Lowest Intensity: Minimal direct wildfire impacts. Location has a minimal chance of being directly impacted by wildfire. 2 Low Intensity: Small flames usually less than two feet long; small amount of very short-range spotting possible. Fires are easy to suppress. 3 Moderate Intensity: Flames up to eight feet in length; short-range spotting is possible. 4 High Intensity: Large flames up to 30 feet in length; short-range spotting common; medium-range spotting possible. 5 Highest Intensity: Very large flames up to 150 feet in length; profuse short-range spotting, frequent long-range spotting; strong fire-induced winds. Wildfires occur in or adjacent to wildlands, including forests, national and state parks, and wildlife management areas. As such, the impact of wildfire on the local population is higher in areas where development occurs near or within wildlands. The wildland-urban interface (WUI) land cover surface, first identified and developed by the SILVIS Lab at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, may be used to determine areas at risk (see Figure 231). Intermix WUI are those areas where housing and wildfire fuel (vegetation) intermingle. Interface WUI are areas that have housing within 0.5 mile of vegetation. The Federal Register defines WUI areas as those containing at least one housing unit per 40 acres. Both intermix and interface areas are at risk of wildfires.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 509 3.7.13.2.3 Impacts of Climate Trends and Variations Climate has a profound impact on wildfires, significantly altering their behavior and increasing the risks associated with them. Rising global temperatures and changing weather patterns have created a conducive environment for more frequent, intense, and widespread wildfires. As temperatures increase, vegetation dries out more quickly and becomes more flammable, providing ample fuel for fires to ignite and spread rapidly (refer to the Extreme Temperatures section for additional information). Prolonged periods of drought, exacerbated by climate trends, further intensify this situation by creating drier conditions across larger areas, making ecosystems more susceptible to ignition. Changes in precipitation patterns also play a role, with some regions experiencing longer periods of reduced rainfall and increased aridity, resulting in parched landscapes and heightened fire risk (refer to the Drought section for additional information). Stronger and more erratic winds associated with climate trends and variations can intensify fire behavior, making it more challenging to control and contain wildfires. Rapid arctic warming has more recently resulted in a narrower temperature difference between the middle latitudes and Arctic, slowing down the jet stream and creating more ridges and troughs. Specifically for Canadian wildfires, troughs can push more smoke down into the United States and Tennessee. Because of these changes, Tennessee may experience increased air quality issues from wildfires in other parts of North America in the future. Additionally, the longer wildfire seasons, caused by shifting climate patterns, extend the window of fire risk, increasing the likelihood of multiple fires occurring simultaneously and straining firefighting resources. The release of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases during wildfires also contributes to climate trends and variations, creating a feedback loop where fires contribute to further warming. Addressing the impact of climate trends on wildfires requires comprehensive efforts to implement effective fire management strategies, promote sustainable land practices, and enhance community preparedness and resilience to minimize the devastating consequences of wildfires. 3.7.13.3 Vulnerability Analysis – Wildfire The National Risk Index (NRI) includes data on the expected annual losses to individual natural hazards, historical loss, and overall risk at a county and Census tract level. One of the most immediate and visible effects is the damage inflicted on transportation networks. Wildfires can render roads and highways impassable, either due to the destruction of bridges and overpasses or the presence of debris and fallen trees. This hampers emergency response efforts, impedes evacuation routes, and disrupts the flow of goods and services.

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 513 Another critical aspect affected by wildfires is the electrical infrastructure. Power lines and transformers can be damaged or destroyed by the intense heat and flames, leading to power outages that can last for extended periods. This not only affects the functionality of homes and businesses but also impacts essential services such as hospitals, schools, and communication networks that rely on electricity. The loss of power can disrupt daily life, exacerbate emergency situations, and hinder recovery efforts. Water and sewage systems are also vulnerable to wildfires. The intense heat can damage or melt water pipes, leading to leaks, ruptures, or a complete loss of water supply. In addition, the destruction of infrastructure may result in contamination of water sources, making it unsafe for consumption or causing difficulties in treating and distributing water. Similarly, sewage systems can be impacted, leading to the release of untreated wastewater into the environment, posing health risks and further environmental damage. Furthermore, telecommunications infrastructure can suffer severe consequences from wildfires. The destruction of cell towers and communication lines can disrupt connectivity and impede emergency communication channels. This makes it challenging for affected communities to receive timely updates, request assistance, or coordinate relief efforts. Beyond these immediate impacts, wildfires can also have long-term consequences for infrastructure. The loss of vegetation due to wildfires increases the risk of soil erosion, leading to potential slope collapse and damage to roads, buildings, and other structures. Increased runoff during heavy rain events can also cause flooding and mudslides, further compromising infrastructure and exacerbating the recovery process. 3.7.13.3.2 Vulnerable Population Wildfires in the state of

Increased runoff during heavy rain events can also cause flooding and mudslides, further compromising infrastructure and exacerbating the recovery process. 3.7.13.3.2 Vulnerable Population Wildfires in the state of Tennessee have a profound impact on the population, particularly on vulnerable groups within the state. The direct consequences of wildfires can lead to the displacement of residents, causing temporary or even permanent relocation. As fires encroach upon residential areas, people are forced to evacuate their homes, leaving behind their belongings and sometimes their entire communities. This displacement disrupts the lives of individuals and families, creating emotional distress and uncertainty about their future. Vulnerable populations are especially affected by wildfires in Tennessee. These include the elderly, children, individuals with disabilities, and those with limited mobility or pre-existing health conditions. The evacuation process can be particularly challenging for these groups, as they may require specialized transportation or medical assistance. Accessible shelters and healthcare facilities that can cater to their specific needs are essential but may be strained during times of widespread wildfire emergencies. Moreover, adverse health effects of wildfires can be particularly severe for vulnerable populations. Smoke and poor air quality resulting from wildfires can exacerbate respiratory conditions such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Children and the elderly are especially susceptible to these health risks. Wildfires within and outside of Tennessee can have substantial impacts on air quality and, consequently, vulnerable

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 3: Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment 514 populations. The stress and trauma associated with the evacuation and loss of homes can also impact mental health, further affecting vulnerable populations who may already be at risk. In rural areas of Tennessee, where wildfires are often more prevalent, vulnerable populations may face additional challenges. Limited access to healthcare services and resources in these areas can make it more difficult for individuals to receive the necessary medical attention and support during and after wildfires. Disruption of local infrastructure, including road closures and damage to healthcare facilities, further compounds these difficulties. Populations vulnerable to wildfires encompass various groups that face increased risks in such situations. One particularly vulnerable group includes individuals residing in areas with a high wildfire risk, such as regions with dry climates, dense vegetation, or proximity to forested areas. These populations may be directly in the path of a wildfire or subject to rapid spread, increasing their exposure to smoke, flames, and the potential for property damage or loss. Rural communities located in or near wildland-urban interface areas are also vulnerable to wildfires. These areas represent the intersection of urban development and natural landscapes, posing unique challenges for fire management. Limited access to resources, lack of fireresistant infrastructure, and limited evacuation routes can heighten vulnerability in these communities. Elderly individuals, individuals with disabilities, and those with pre-existing health conditions may face increased vulnerability to wildfires. These individuals may have limited mobility or require specialized assistance during evacuations, making it more challenging to reach safety. Additionally, exposure to smoke and poor air quality can have significant health impacts, exacerbating respiratory conditions and compromising well-being. Low-income communities may face heightened vulnerability due to socioeconomic factors. Limited resources, inadequate housing conditions, and reduced access to transportation can impede their ability to evacuate safely during wildfires. These communities may also lack insurance coverage or financial means to recover from fire-related damages. 3.7.13.3.3 Impact on State Assets A total of 958 state assets are located within wildland-urban interface (WUI) areas. [44 CFR § 201.4(c)(3)(ii)] 4.1 Introduction A thorough evaluation of the state’s existing capabilities for risk reduction measures and developing community resilience is an essential step in the hazard mitigation process. After the risk assessment, the capability assessment helps inform the state about which mitigation actions are feasible. A deeper understanding of state and local hazard mitigation capabilities helps the state develop risk-based, capability-informed mitigation actions that are comprehensive and feasible given current capabilities. Mitigation capabilities are traditionally divided into four categories: • Planning and Regulatory: State plans, policies, statutes, or regulations that could affect the state’s resilience to future hazard events and other future conditions, including climate change. This includes plans and regulations that guide growth and development. • Administrative and Technical: State staff, skills, and tools that can be utilized for hazard mitigation planning and reducing risk through mitigation projects. These capabilities can belong both to state agencies and departments as well as academic partners, county and regional quasigovernmental or nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), non-profits, private organizations, and community-based organizations. • Financial: Resources to fund mitigation actions. This includes state, federal, private, or non-profit resources that may be able to support risk reduction. • Education and Outreach: Programs and methods of communication that communicate risk, support mitigation actions, and encourage risk reduction. This includes technical assistance, training, and education and awareness campaigns that build capacity. Capabilities can also be classified as pre-disaster and post-disaster mitigation capabilities. Predisaster capabilities include activities such as training staff, educating the public about their risk and how to mitigate it, and successfully applying for annual mitigation grants. Post-disaster capabilities include adhering to substantial damage assessment requirements, educating the public on how to build back better, and successfully applying for grants that are available only after a disaster. Due to the nature of disaster events, both types of capabilities are often needed

Silver Jackets teams in states across the United States bring together multiple state, federal, and sometimes tribal and local agencies to learn from one another. By applying their shared knowledge, the teams enhance mitigation, response, and recovery efforts related to such events. No single agency has all the answers, but leveraging multiple programs and perspectives can provide a cohesive solution. Silver Jackets teams represent an important opportunity to bring partners together. Why “Silver Jackets”? Traditionally, people from different agencies wear differentcolored shirts or jackets when responding to emergencies. FEMA personnel wear blue, and USACE personnel wear red.
