title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 4: Capability Assessment 555 Figure 249: Tennessee Firewise Communities Map 4.3.2 The National Flood Insurance Program Congress established the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) in 1968 due to a lack of available private insurance and increased federal costs to repair flood damage. Many homeowners may be unaware that, to this day, most private home insurance policies do not cover flood losses. The NFIP allows people in participating communities to purchase insurance coverage for potential property damage because of flooding. To qualify for flood insurance, a community must join the NFIP and agree to enforce sound floodplain management standards. In return for a local community adopting and enforcing local floodplain management regulations, flood insurance is available in the community. Currently, 402 Tennessee communities participate in the NFIP. Only eight are non-participating, and none of them have a designated Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA). Flood insurance is an important tool that communities can use to support post-disaster recovery. On average, between 1996 and 2019, the average claim paid out by the NFIP in Tennessee was $29,600, compared to only $6,000 for FEMA’s Individual and Households Program from 2006 to 2016.327 327 FEMA, “Historical Flood Risk and Costs,” October 21, 2022. https://www.fema.gov/datavisualization/historical-flood-risk-and-costs

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 4: Capability Assessment 556 TEMA is the designated state agency for administering the NFIP in Tennessee. Local communities are responsible for adopting and enforcing NFIP minimum standards. The State NFIP Coordinator supports local communities in implementing the program through training, technical assistance, office hours, a newsletter, and local community assessments. Community officials are encouraged to join monthly webinars on the second Tuesday of each month from 9 a.m. to 11 a.m. These webinars cover original topics tailored to the needs of the State of Tennessee. Two courses are routinely offered: a three-day virtual Introduction to Floodplain Management and a Certified Floodplain Surveyor Class, making Tennessee only the second state in the nation to have surveyors certified in doing elevation certificates. The Tennessee Association of Floodplain Managers also offers recorded training through their YouTube channel.328 Additional resources, including the Tennessee Floodplain Management Permitting Guide (FMPG), can be found online or by request. To participate in the NFIP, communities must adopt and enforce a floodplain management ordinance. TEMA, in conjunction with FEMA Region 4, developed the Tennessee Flood Damage Prevention Model Ordinance for participating Tennessee communities. This statespecific model ordinance includes higher standards than the NFIP minimums, demonstrating Tennessee’s commitment to reducing flood risk. Those higher standards include the following: • A requirement for a Finished Construction Elevation Certificate. • Freeboard requirements. “Freeboard” refers to a measure of safety expressed in feet built above a flood level for purposes of floodplain management. In SFHAs that have Base Flood Elevations (BFEs), the minimum freeboard elevation requirement is the BFE plus 1 foot. In SFHAs where the BFE has not been established, the elevation requirement is at least 3 feet above the highest adjacent grade. • A requirement for stream encroachments to comply with the regulations for Zone AE with floodway, Zone AE without floodway, and Zone A streams to undergo engineering analysis and submit a conditional letter of map revision (CLOMR). • Standards for unmapped streams where areas of special flood hazard are neither indicated nor identified.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 4: Capability Assessment 557 As part of adopting this ordinance, each participating jurisdiction also commits to administering substantial damage requirements. “Substantial damage” refers to a home or structure in the SFHA that has repair costs equal to or exceeding 50% of the market value of the structure before the disaster event, regardless of the cause of the damage. Repairs to substantially damaged structures are, by definition, substantial improvements. Substantial improvement refers to any reconstruction, rehabilitation, addition, or other improvement to a structure that would equal or exceed 50% of the market value of the structure. Structures with these designations are required to be rebuilt in accordance with local floodplain management regulations. Typically, this means either flood-proofing, elevating, demolishing, or relocating a structure to reduce its likelihood of receiving damage from a future flood. NFIP-insured property owners may be eligible for Increased Cost of Compliance (ICC) funding to help with these projects. Multiple resources and technical assistance are available to support communities in administering these substantial damage requirements. TEMA and FEMA offer trainings, including three in the last year on topics such as FEMA’s Substantial Damage Estimator Tool and developing a substantial damage plan. Furthermore, the state has a post-disaster guide for community officials conducting inspections. Communities can receive funding to support substantial damage estimates through FEMA’s PA program under Section 1206: Building Code and Floodplain Management Administration and Enforcement. Under this section, FEMA can “provide assistance to state and local governments for building code and floodplain administration and enforcement, including inspections for substantial damage compliance.”329 Although this section is relatively new, the City of Waverly has already been able

One challenge in administering the NFIP within the state is encouraging nonparticipating communities to join the NFIP. Previously, many of the nonparticipating communities joined following the flooding in 2010. In 2021, however, when the state again experienced heavy rainfall and flooding, and two (2) additional communities were interested in joining the NFIP including Houston and Humphreys counties. The importance of joining the NFIP was evident after the 2021 flood as, due to being sanctioned by the program and no longer participating, some affected areas were ineligible to receive Individual Assistance (IA) nor PA from FEMA due to being sanctioned. The challenges facing the remaining communities with joining include resistance to land use codes and operating in a rural environment, which limits the likelihood that the remaining communities will join at any time. Still, the State continues to support outreach and is available to support these communities if they are interested. Outreach is an important goal moving forward. Over the years, there have been multiple updates to the NFIP and its guiding legislation. Recently, FEMA implemented the Risk Rating 2.0: Equity in Action initiative. This update included significant changes to the NFIP’s risk rating methodology. Under Risk Rating 2.0, insurance premiums are intended to be more financially sound and better reflect the insured property’s flood risk. Previously, FEMA acknowledged that policyholders with lower-value homes were paying for more of their share of the risk while policyholders with higher-value homes were paying less.330 Now, FEMA intends to distribute the cost of risk more equitably across policyholders and use industry best practices to reflect each individual property’s flood risks more accurately. All new policies after October 2021 and those renewed after April 2022 use this updated pricing methodology. The Association of State Floodplain Managers (ASFPM) and the Pew Charitable Trust developed a dashboard using FEMA premium data from May 2020 and October 2021 to show the estimated differences in premium rates. As shown in Figure 250, most Tennessee policyholders experienced an increase in their premium rate, with most seeing an increase of only $10 or less.331 Furthermore, 28.7% of NFIP policy premiums decreased. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 4: Capability Assessment 559 The NFIP works closely with private insurance companies to offer flood insurance to property owners and renters. As of February 2023, there were 25,649 NFIP policies in force in the state. Between February 2022 and February 2023, the number of NFIP policies across the state was reduced by 1,398.332 This reflects an ongoing trend of a slow decline in NFIP policies in force since the last plan update, when 29,285 were recorded. This trend is not unique to Tennessee. A 2022 report from the FEMA Flood Insurance Advocate indicates that the most common reasons for policies lapsing include the following:333 • Policyholder’s inability to pay due to personal financial hardship • Renewal bills not received because of mail delays • Renewal bills sent to the incorrect mailing address • Payment processing discrepancies • Lender servicing confusion The expense of flood insurance significantly contributes to the downward trend of individual NFIP policies in Tennessee. Education and outreach are also challenges. Often, homeowners and renters are unaware that their traditional home insurance does not include flood coverage. Insurance agents also need to be informed. Risk Rating 2.0 represents a significant change for the industry, and many agents are not familiar with the new policies and requirements, such as whether they need an elevation certificate or not. Further coordination between TEMA and the Tennessee Department of Commerce & Insurance is necessary in order to educate insurance agents and promote flood insurance publicly. NFIP data also helps the state track high-risk areas through historical flood loss estimates. Mitigating losses in Severe Repetitive Loss (SRL) and Repetitive Loss (RL) structures

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: Tennessee Department of Commerce & Insurance is necessary in order to educate insurance agents and promote flood insurance publicly. NFIP data also helps the state track high-risk areas through historical flood loss estimates. Mitigating losses in Severe Repetitive Loss (SRL) and Repetitive Loss (RL) structures is a priority for FEMA. FEMA defines an RL structure as an NFIP-insured structure with at least two paid flood losses of more than $1,000 each in any 10-year period since 1978.334 An SRL structure is defined as any NFIP-insured building that has at least four or more separate claim payments for flood damage, with the amount of each such claim exceeding $5,000 and the cumulative amount exceeding $20,000, or at least two separate NFIP claim payments with the cumulative amount exceeding the fair market value of the insured building on the day before each loss.335 A summary of these structures in the state is included in the Flood Profile in Section 2. The state supports reducing the number of SRL and RL structures through hazard mitigation grant programs by focusing on projects that address repetitive issues and awarding additional points for projects that address RL/SRL properties. Further information on how the state prioritizes local projects to address repetitive flood losses is included in Section 5 (Mitigation Strategy), Appendix C, and Appendix E.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 4: Capability Assessment 560 Another big change coming from Risk Rating 2.0 is how premium discounts can now be applied uniformly across the community, regardless of whether the structure is inside or outside of the SFHA. This may increase community interest in participating in the CRS. The CRS, originally instituted by FEMA in 1990, is an incentive program designed to promote higher standards and differentiate between those communities that are making a notable effort at risk reduction and those that are not. It incentivizes those in the NFIP to meet 18 specific goals and objectives, which then qualify them for insurance rate reductions. These goals are in addition to the primary objectives of the NFIP, which are to reduce flood damage to insurable properties, provide flood insurance, and encourage adopting and enforcing comprehensive floodplain management policies. Credit is awarded for eligible activities that result in a CRS community ranking between Class 1 and Class 10. Communities that join the CRS without meeting any additional higher standards are recorded as Class 10 and receive no insurance premium discount. For each lower class, the community receives a 5% insurance premium discount. Community officials can refer to the CRS Coordinator’s Manual for more details. Communities that are interested in participating in the CRS program can reach out to the State NFIP Coordinator for more information. The Tennessee communities that participate in the CRS are listed below. Of those, four are classified as Class 9, which affords them a 5% reduction in their insurance rates. The highest-ranking jurisdiction, the City of Knoxville, Class 6, qualifies for a 20% premium rate reduction. Currently, the state has 45 open CAVs, which have documented various levels of deficiencies. To join and remain in the CRS program, communities need to be responsible for their own floodplain management administrative procedures. Challenges arise when communities still refer members of the public to the state for assistance. Communities that do not meet CRS standards can be put on probation from the program and even suspended from the NFIP. To avoid these consequences, communities must also address issues identified in their CAV and ensure that violations have been remedied to the maximum extent possible. The state has a CRS User Group that has met quarterly over the last two years. This group is preparing to undertake a comprehensive assessment of the credits Tennessee CRS communities are receiving. Understanding where communities currently receive credits could serve two purposes. First, the group will be able to assess if there are any other steps that could be easily taken for the current CRS communities to receive a better score and move up a class. Further, the state can identify and address why communities are not participating in the program and if there is anything that can be done to support them in joining. For example, sometimes it is challenging for local municipalities to garner interest from other departments outside of floodplain management. By recording what other neighboring jurisdictions are doing, best practices can be compiled and shared to make the process as clear and easy as possible. Another recorded challenge with participating in CRS is the lack of staffing and identifying what can be done with the local or regional resources available. Overall, the state has made significant efforts to advance the NFIP program in Tennessee in recent years. FEMA’s Community Assistance Program—State Support Services Element (CAPSSE)—helps fund the NFIP Coordinator’s office. This grant program helps ensure that the goals of the NFIP are met, promotes floodplain management expertise and local capability, and provides for state efforts to work with communities.336 The CAP-SSE Tiered State Framework (TSF) helps FEMA identify and incentivize state efforts to develop and maintain the capabilities necessary to carry out the duties of a State NFIP Coordinating Agency.337 It also helps to more fairly and consistently evaluate state strengths and areas for improvement. State floodplain management programs are ranked as follows: Foundational, Proficient, and Advanced. Three years ago, Tennessee would have ranked below the foundational level. Today, thanks in large part to a concentrated effort to document all of the ongoing work being accomplished, Tennessee is ranked as “Proficient.” Since these tiers directly relate to the amount of funding the program may receive, that enabled the program to double the funding received in only three years.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 4: Capability Assessment 562 4.3.2.1 Flood Hazard Mapping Flooding is the most common natural disaster in the United States, but this risk is not stagnant. Flood risk can change over time due to changes in development, climate, and other factors. It is important to understand the current flood risk to be able to identify effective mitigation measures. FEMA and its partners are responsible for developing flood maps that visually detail this risk. Risk Mapping, Assessment and Planning (Risk MAP) is a process administered by FEMA that involves analyzing historical flood data, including stream gauge records, satellite imagery, and aerial photographs, to understand the patterns and extent of previous flood events. It also considers topographic data, such as elevation models and land use information, to evaluate the vulnerability of different areas. By combining these data sources and sophisticated modeling techniques, flood maps are produced that delineate areas at various levels of flood risk, enabling communities and individuals to make informed decisions regarding reducing risk, managing the floodplain, and purchasing flood insurance. In Tennessee, these floodplain maps are unique in that they include parcel lines directly on the maps. The cooperating technical partner is responsible for developing these parcel lines and coordinating with FEMA to incorporate them into the flood maps. Tennessee and its partners are actively involved in the flood hazard mapping process. A map partners meeting is held prior to the annual Tennessee Floodplain Managers Conference, during which time FEMA and the mapping contractor present on the status of ongoing mapping projects and upcoming initiatives. Participants in the Map Partners Meeting include FEMA, TEMA, TDOT, TDCI, TVA, USACE, the

text: partners meeting is held prior to the annual Tennessee Floodplain Managers Conference, during which time FEMA and the mapping contractor present on the status of ongoing mapping projects and upcoming initiatives. Participants in the Map Partners Meeting include FEMA, TEMA, TDOT, TDCI, TVA, USACE, the SHMO, the NFIP Coordinator, and the State Dam Safety Program. Together, these partners can leverage their resources for mapping projects around the state. This meeting is also an opportunity to ensure there is no duplication of effort and that each applicable agency focuses on acquiring new information. Participants who are unable to attend the conference still have an opportunity to participate in the flood hazard mapping process. The State NFIP Coordinator is responsible for ensuring that the presentation is shared with all 402 floodplain administrators. The State NFIP Coordinator also accepts a list of identified areas that communities think need to be studied or restudied on an ongoing basis. Ultimately, FEMA, in conjunction with the map partners, is responsible for making the final decision on what areas will be studied and incorporating new data into the effective Flood Insurance Rate Maps (FIRMs).

In Tennessee, local governments have broad discretionary power when making zoning decisions. T.C.A. Title 13, Chapter 7, contains several zoning provisions. Of most relevance here are the parts dealing with county and municipal zoning. T.C.A. § 13-7-101 and 201 are already quoted above, showing the scope of authority given to counties and municipalities. This includes the authority to regulate land use related to flood hazards and flood insurance. State environmental authorities regulate sensitive environmental areas such as wetlands. The agencies and individual municipal planning commissions have broad power over what can be built or redeveloped. The process for obtaining planning permission varies depending on the size of the project, location, municipality, and whether a state government agency is involved. If a special exception is needed, the local board of zoning appeals may make the decision, and the board may be required to hold a public hearing. Denials of building permits are appealed to the board of zoning appeals, while county planning commission decisions are appealed to the county board of zoning appeals. If one fails to comply with planning decisions or regulations, cities and counties can exercise their police powers and obtain injunctive relief. Table 189 describes the laws that relate to state building commercials. State commercial building codes include the 2012 edition of the International Building Code (IBC). In 2020, the state adopted the 2018 edition of the International Residential Code with amendments.341 The State Fire Marshal’s Office is responsible for setting the minimal commercial building codes and codes for state-owned facilities. The state is in the process of updating its codes to the 2021 edition with amendments; however, rulemaking must occur before it becomes effective. The State Fire Marshal’s Office is also responsible for code enforcement, along with local fire and building code offices. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 4: Capability Assessment 590 4.6 Changes in State Capabilities Since 2018, the State of Tennessee has seen multiple changes to the hazard mitigation program. Some programs, like the mitigation grants team, are fortunate enough to have retained their staff and avoided common challenges like staff turnover. Many capabilities, including GIS, planning, and the NFIP program, have expanded. The following is a short summary of some of the significant changes that have occurred. 4.6.1 Changes in Agency Capabilities Interagency coordination has increased through regular meetings of the SHMPC. TEMA’s Planning Branch has conducted successful outreach and engagement, widely promoting the mitigation message across the state through planning regions. Since FEMA’s new planning policy guidance was released in 2022, the Planning Branch and Safe Dams Program have increased their collaboration capabilities. While there has been relatively little local increase in interest in profiling dam failure largely due to the lack of significant historical events, the state stands ready to support any local mitigation plans seeking to successfully complement the HHPD planning requirements. Further details of the Planning Branch’s activities and its critical efforts with local communities can be found in Appendix C. Other partners are also more actively engaged. State hazard mitigation representatives participated in a Central United States Earthquake Consortium (CUSEC) and are looking for possible ways to address seismic vulnerability moving forward. Additionally, since the last plan update, there has been an increase emphasis on interagency coordination within the State Emergency Operations Center (SEOC). The Tennessee Department of Transportation (TDOT) and the Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation (TDEC) are now integrated in the SEOC, enhancing overall capabilities. Grants

The Tennessee Department of Transportation (TDOT) and the Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation (TDEC) are now integrated in the SEOC, enhancing overall capabilities. Grants for community safe room projects are being applied for and awarded around the State. Multiple safe rooms have been successfully funded. These safe rooms will help protect communities in Tennessee that are at-risk from tornadoes and high winds. The State has a strong capability to support further safe room grant applications. Further integrating safe rooms into schools will benefit numerous Tennessee communities. 4.6.2 Changes in Roles and Responsibilities Since the last update, the state has formally identified a State Climate Office. The office was originally established by the Tennessee Valley Authority; however, it stopped operating in 2006 and did not return until the Tennessee Climate Office was established in 2016 at ETSU. In 2021, in coordination with the American Association of State Climatologists, the office was officially designated as the state’s official climate office. Since then, the State Climatologist has provided weekly input to the U.S. Drought Monitor, monthly reports on climate/weather patterns, and information on disasters, and representatives of the State Climate Office were actively involved in the plan update, including the writing process and meetings.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 4: Capability Assessment 591 4.6.3 Changes in Funding Sources Since the last plan update, there have been multiple changes to the available mitigation funding sources, including FEMA’s introduction of two new mitigation funding programs. The Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC) program significantly expands the amount of pre-disaster mitigation funding available for mitigation project. Previously, most mitigation funding opportunities, such as HMGP, were available on a post-disaster basis. While BRIC funding is determined by the total amount of overall disaster spending for a given year. Grant funding is not state-specific, and each state receives an allocation. As such, each year the state will receive funding even if no disaster has been declared during the year. This gives eligible applicants more opportunity to plan and prepare for a grant application, knowing that there will be funds available annually. Additionally, since there is both an allocation, which can be used for projects at the state’s discretion, and a competitive pool of funding, both smaller projects such as hazard mitigation plan updates and larger, community-based projects can potentially be awarded funding. FEMA has also recently established the STORM (Safeguarding Tomorrow through Ongoing Risk Mitigation) revolving loan fund. The STORM Act, which became law in January 2021, authorized FEMA to provide capitalization grants to eligible entities, including the State of Tennessee, to establish revolving loan funds for hazard mitigation efforts. These loan funds are intended to provide low-interest loans to jurisdictions to enhance community resilience by reducing the loss of life and property, the cost of insurance, and the need for federal disaster payments. text: Local Capacity and the Grant Application Process One misconception about the State of Tennessee is its local capacity. Despite having multiple major metropolitan areas, the state has a lot of different counties, including many small local jurisdictions. These local jurisdictions face additional hurdles when applying for mitigation funding, particularly when it comes to staff time and capacity. This is a challenge for other states as well. A consistent message repeated at the National Emergency Management Association conference every year is the need to simplify and streamline the process. During the Capability Assessment Workshop, plan participants repeatedly identified the beginning of the grant application process as a significant hurdle to small, rural participation. FEMA says that mitigation projects must be cost-effective, technically feasible, and environmentally sound. Many local government officials may identify a need but not be sure how to effectively mitigate it or fund the mitigation project. It is important to make the application process—particularly the front end, when all eligible applicants must be made aware of funding opportunities and understand the application requirements—as least cumbersome as possible. This issue is exacerbated by limited staff capacity at the state level. Having more state staff dedicated specifically to supporting local communities throughout the mitigation process—especially at the beginning of the application process—may help reduce this challenge. The state is currently in the process of hiring additional staff with this goal in mind. 4.7.4 Awareness, Education, and Outreach Overall, education and outreach are strengths of the state. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 5: Mitigation Strategy 600 5. Mitigation Strategy Effective hazard mitigation requires the collective effort of many agencies, organizations, communities, and individuals working together to lessen the impact of disasters. During the mitigation planning process, the state secured input from organizations across many disciplines that share one goal: promoting community resiliency. This section of the plan outlines the state’s approach to addressing short- and long-term risks that is aligned with the mitigation mission statement, goals, objectives, and mitigation actions established by the State Hazard Mitigation Planning Committee (SHMPC). After completing the hazard risk assessment, the SHMPC identified potential strategies to reduce or eliminate those risks in ways that address the needs of Tennesseans and state agencies that manage elements of, and actions included in, the mitigation strategy. The results of the risk assessment informed planning participants how to best manage three essential tasks, the completion of which would enable the SHMPC to develop an effective mitigation strategy. The committee: • Reviewed the goals, objectives, and mitigation strategy included in the 2018 SHMP to assess their effectiveness and relevance and to identify potential gaps in mitigation needs that must be addressed. • Asked state agencies responsible for mitigation actions to review each action to determine whether it is an ongoing initiative or whether the action has been completed, deferred, or deleted because it is no longer relevant. Agencies were also asked to provide information supporting the status of each action, including how it may be implemented in the future. • Members of the SHMPC also identified new strategies to improve capabilities and mitigate risks identified in statewide as well as the local risk assessments, so that mitigation priorities are based upon loss reduction. Overall, this strategy reflects the state’s goal to reduce and/or eliminate the adverse effects of natural, technological, and human-caused hazards on the state’s built and natural environments and the population, especially vulnerable socioeconomic groups. The mitigation strategy was also developed to comply with the required provisions of the Emergency Management Accreditation Program (EMAP) in order for Tennessee to maintain its accreditation, which the state first received in 2007.

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 5: Mitigation Strategy 601 5.1 Program Mission “The Tennessee Mitigation Program supports and makes effective long-term investments to lessen the impact of disasters.” The state’s mitigation program was designed to practically implement the vision, goals, and objectives of its mitigation program by identifying and implementing specific initiatives that further community resilience. The program supports the development of effective, long-term investments by providing state agencies, counties, and stakeholders with tools, technical assistance, data, and information about best practices; promotes information sharing; and coordinates planning and decision-making across the public and private sectors. Shared tools include, but are not limited to, federal and state grant funding opportunities, tools used to analyze and map hazard-related data, and subject matter expertise about specific hazards to which the state is vulnerable. The Tennessee hazard mitigation program is inclusive and welcomes input from Tennessee’s diverse communities. The program’s impact is felt beyond state borders since hazard incidents are often regional and not confined to a given area. For example, earthquake occurrences may affect more than one state, and the effects to hazard events are felt nationally and worldwide. A well-managed mitigation program fosters widespread resiliency among the people, organizations, businesses, governments, and communities that work cooperatively toward mutually shared goals. A comprehensive review has been conducted of all local hazard mitigation plans to ensure the integration of local risk assessments and mitigation actions that will be updated alongside the SHMP as needed. By supporting local mitigation planning efforts, the state mitigation strategy takes into consideration the individual strategies, capabilities and needs of local governments. Appendix C provides more details on how the state supports and integrates with these planning processes. The state’s mitigation program also makes effective long-term investments, both directly and indirectly. Some resources, such as Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) funding, may be used only for hazard mitigation projects that directly lessen disaster impacts. Other resources, such as staff time and state-funded grants, may be used to support the overall emergency management mission of the Tennessee Emergency Management Agency (TEMA) and its communities. Benefits from mitigation planning and investments enable the state and its mitigation partners to make well-informed decisions about how to lessen the impact of disasters. A thorough approach to planning includes ongoing environmental scanning to systematically survey and interpret relevant data and circumstances to identify opportunities and threats that may influence decision-making. Such efforts will enable state and local government to identify communities that are not well equipped to respond to and recover from disasters. The state identifies opportunities to allocate increased resources to help such communities achieve their mitigation goals.

Cost-effectiveness FEMA provides a tool to determine the cost effectiveness of a mitigation project, known as the Benefit-Cost Analysis (BCA) Toolkit. While there are many ways of determining the cost effectiveness of any given mitigation project, the BCA Toolkit is the current, official method utilized by FEMA when reviewing Hazard Mitigation Assistance projects for funding consideration. FEMA deems a project to be cost-effective when the Benefit Cost Ratio (BCR) is 1.0 or greater. This figure indicates that for each dollar spent to fund a mitigation action will result in one dollar of loss avoidance. The higher the BCR calculation for a proposed mitigation project or action, the more cost-effective it will be in avoiding post-disaster losses. 4. Environmental impacts When conducting mitigation actions, it is imperative to consider the interconnectedness of the built and natural environments and the ways in which the community interacts with both. Being environmentally sound requires individuals, communities, and governments to be mindful of their actions and their impact on the environment. Mitigation projects may include unintended environmental impacts such as those discussed here, which may further trigger environmental justice concerns, such as:362 ▪ Health and safety (e.g., hazardous air pollutants, odor, sewage systems, noise, or vibration) ▪ Aesthetics (e.g., visual impacts) ▪ Social (e.g., siting issues; concerns about and use of consistency in implementing policies to relocate displaced existing communities; changes in access to and/or location of community facilities or social services; additional traffic; and potential impacts on those who may consume potentially tainted fish, vegetation, or wildlife) ▪ Economic efforts that may change the population’s access to employment opportunities Overall, an effective and environmentally friendly mitigation action will take into consideration the need to create a healthier and more sustainable planet for future generations, while simultaneously implementing protection measures against immediate risks.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 5: Mitigation Strategy 608 5.2.2.1 Mitigation Action Prioritization Mitigation actions will be reviewed considering the criteria discussed above and assigned a priority ranking of high, medium, or low. High priority actions are those considered to have the greatest potential to improve community resiliency, have a high probability of being fully funded, and are likely to be fully executed. Medium priority actions are those that have a strong BCR and will provide solid community benefits but will not meet priority community needs if completed. Low priority actions are those that may be feasible and have the potential to benefit the community but lack an identified funding source or have inadequate staff time to effectively complete the project. The Safe Dams Programs assess dams around TN on an annual basis, which becomes the basis for prioritizing projects related to HHPDs, including grant applications to the HHPD program and the National Dam Safety Program (NDSP) State Assistance grant programs. Any dam that fails this conditional assessment will be considered “marginal” status and will receive priority to receive grant funding before any other monitored structure. By ensuring that conditions are captured in real-time, funding can be allocated in the areas of highest vulnerability. 5.2.3 Funding Sources for Mitigation Actions Both annually and following a Presidential Disaster Declaration, mitigation funding is available to support projects and programs designed to promote community resiliency and reduce response and recovery times in future disasters. There are several different resources, each with its own guidelines and eligibility requirements. Additional State and Federal funding sources are described in Section 4: Capability Assessment. 5.2.3.1 FEMA Hazard Mitigation Assistance Funding Sources 5.2.3.1.1 Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities Grant Program Established by FEMA in 2020, the Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC) grant program prioritizes large-scale infrastructure projects to increase the resiliency of community lifelines and gives a higher level of consideration to mitigation projects in underserved and disadvantaged communities. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 5: Mitigation Strategy 609 5.2.3.1.2 Flood Mitigation Assistance Grant Program The Flood Mitigation Assistance (FMA) grant program focuses on reducing the loss of life and property as a result of flooding. Projects addressing Repetitive Loss (RL) and Severe Repetitive Loss (SRL) properties are the focus and priority, particularly projects to acquire and remove the properties from the floodplain. This program also supports flood mitigation planning efforts at the local level. FMA in Tennessee is housed with TEMA, which coordinates application submissions to FEMA from state and local government agencies. 5.2.3.1.3 Hazard Mitigation Grant Program The Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) makes funding available to institute critical mitigation measures designed to reduce the risk of loss of life and property damage during future disasters. HMGP is available when authorized after a Presidential Major Disaster Declaration. The amount of HMGP funding available to eligible applicants is based on the estimated total federal assistance to be provided by FEMA for disaster recovery under the Presidential major disaster declaration. Once approved, Tennessee will be eligible to apply for up to 15% of the cost of recovery for the declared disaster. Up to 7% of available HMGP funding can be allocated to mitigation planning activity grants, and up to 5% can go toward initiative projects that do not require a BCA. 5.2.3.1.4 HMGP Post Fire States, federally recognized tribes, and territories affected by fires resulting in a Fire Management Assistance Grant (FMAG) declaration on or after October 5, 2018, are eligible to apply. The funding amount available will be provided by FEMA and is a national aggregate calculation based on an average of historical

The funding amount available will be provided by FEMA and is a national aggregate calculation based on an average of historical FMAG declarations from the past 10 years. This amount will be recalculated at the beginning of every fiscal year. The total HMGP funding available for each FMAG declaration for FY22 is $786,552 for applicants with a standard hazard mitigation plan and $1,048,736 for applicants with an enhanced hazard mitigation plan.363 HMGP Post Fire differs from the standard HMGP in the following ways: • A Fire Management Assistance declaration rather than a Presidential major disaster declaration activates FMAG assistance. • Assistance is first available for counties and tribal lands that receive Fire Management Assistance declarations. Funded projects also reduce the need for federal funding to rebuild communities after a disaster occurs. FEMA provides funding to states, territories, and tribal nations as outlined in the Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) and program guidance. PDM grants are nationally competitive and provide a fixed set-aside of funding to each state for eligible projects. Many of the PDM projects are still in progress even though the program itself has been sunset by FEMA. BRIC serves as its effective replacement by providing an annual funding source for pre-disaster mitigation projects. 5.2.3.1.7 Public Assistance 406 Mitigation Following a Presidential disaster declaration under Section 406 of the Stafford Act, certain eligible public assistance projects may conduct mitigation measures that restore a facility to beyond its pre-disaster state. These loans have low interest rates and provide coverage for damages incurred that will not be reimbursed by a FEMA Presidential disaster declaration. In Tennessee, this program is administered federally by the SBA Tennessee District Office and by TNECD at the state level. SBA loans can provide mitigation assistance pre- and post-event to make property improvements to reduce potential future losses. In recent years, the legislature has allocated funds to TNECD to promote community resilience activities, including $28 million to the West Tennessee River Basin Authority for the construction of the Water Education Training (WET) Center, which will provide a unique opportunity to floodplain administrators and emergency managers from around the state to increase their knowledge of detailed flooding situations in a controlled environment. In Fiscal Year 2023, the state allocated TDEC $500,000 to hire a consultant to model State Park Dams and modernize the Emergency Action Plan (EAP) template for each dam owner. title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 5: Mitigation Strategy 615 This collaboration between state agencies ensures the fair and equitable implementation of post-disaster mitigation programs and the allocation of funding for project work. TEMA, through the Mitigation Evaluation Panel, chaired by the State Hazard Mitigation Manager, objectively reviews eligible grant applications/proposals for programmatic merit using the Mitigation Application Ranking System (MARS). Only applications meeting federal and state eligibility requirements for financial consideration and support will be evaluated. A summary of the MARS Panel evaluations will be provided to the Hazard Mitigation Council for review, questions, comments, discussion, and concurrence on the final prioritization of grant application proposals.369 5.2.5 Monitoring Progress of Mitigation Actions TEMA tracks the progress of mitigation projects statewide to ensure that mitigation projects are providing the intended loss avoidance from hazards. To do so, TEMA utilizes a dashboard known as MARS which documents project location, type, funding amount, and current progress for federally funded mitigation projects. Dashboards have also been established for both proposed and approved projects, and the implementation and maintenance of local hazard mitigation plans. The Approved Hazard Mitigation Projects dashboard provides the status of all FEMA HMA projects via the OpenFEMA dataset. Project status and funding sources are represented visually to display how much funding comes from particular sources, and show the amount of open, obligated and closed projects. Projects are also recorded by type, providing a representation of the most sought-after projects by FEMA project code, and by location to show which counties have received the most HMA funding, with statewide included as a separate category. Local Hazard Mitigation Plans are tracked in a separate dashboard to display current status of all county hazard mitigation plans statewide, and the status of their timeline to expiration. 5.2.5.1 Approved Federal Hazard Mitigation Funding Statewide, 2018–2023 Table 193: Approved HMGP Funding Sub applicant Approval Date Type of Project Total Eligible Funding Federal State City of Kenton 6/15/2021 Flood Control $125,000.00 $93,750.00 $15,625.00 Metro NashvilleDavidson 8/13/2021 Acquisition/ Demolition $1,149,645.00 $862,233.75 $143,705.62 Bedford County 4/29/2021 Warning Sirens $60,000.00 $45,000.00 $7,500.00

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 5: Mitigation Strategy 617 Figure 255: Belle Forest Community School Tornado Safe Room 5.2.5.2.2 Gibson County Special School District Tornado Safe Rooms All schools within the Gibson County Special School District have constructed tornado safe rooms. These structures are open to students and staff during the day and are available to the surrounding residential communities in the evening. These projects have been funded by HMGP and the Tennessee Department of Education (TDOE), with plans to continue the construction of safe rooms at the majority of schools across Tennessee. 5.2.5.2.3 Middle Fork Bottoms Recreational Area Middle Fork Bottoms Recreational Area is a floodplain restoration project that began in 2016 when the National Disaster Resilience Competition awarded funds for flood risk management. The heart of this project aids in flood resiliency and provides the opportunity for community members and visitors to the area to experience nature and learn about the natural habitats that the area encompasses. This project highlights the importance of nature-based solutions in order to mitigate future flooding events.

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 5: Mitigation Strategy 618 Figure 256: Middle Fork Bottoms Recreational Area Located just outside of Jackson in the City of Three Way, this 850-acre formerly undeveloped property added over 300 acres of practical flood storage. It boasts 5 miles of paved trails that may be used for walking, running, and biking; a wetland observation overlook; and five lakes, ranging from 2 to 10 acres, for guests to fish on or paddle around in with kayaks, canoes, or paddleboards. In addition to attracting outdoor enthusiasts, the Middle Fork Bottoms Recreational Area has been restored to also double as complex bottomland hardwood forests, marshes, and other wetland habitats, which are key to retaining and slowly filtering floodwaters that previously inundated the property and farmland further downstream. Guests may access the wetlands via the observation overlook that allows for viewing waterfowl, birds, spring peepers, and other wildlife. Future plans for more wetland observation and viewing experiences include installation of a 1-mile boardwalk that will meander through the forested wetlands. 5.2.5.2.4 Shelby County Greenprint for Resilience Three resilience projects are underway in Shelby County to mitigate against inland flooding. Following a large-scale severe storm and flooding event in 2011, the county utilized CDBG-DR funding to establish floodways, re-establish wetlands, and perform stream restoration in three separate waterways in Memphis: Big Creek Millington, Wolf River Memphis, and South Cypress Creek Memphis. This project also includes a regional resilience plan to address future climate and flooding considerations within the county and the tristate region, which is funded through a HUD Sustainable Communities Regional Planning Grant.371 371 FEMA, “Mitigation Action Portfolio.” https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/2020-08/fema_mitigationaction-portfolio-support-document_08-01-2020_0.pdf

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 5: Mitigation Strategy 619 Figure 257: Flooding at Riverside Blvd. and Beale St. in Downtown Memphis, 2011372 5.2.5.2.5 West Tennessee River Basin Authority – Water Education Training Center In response to the severe rain and flooding events that occur across the state of Tennessee every year, the West Tennessee River Basin Authority, TDEC, and the University of Tennessee Institute of Agriculture have partnered to develop and operate the Tennessee Water Education and Training (WET) Center at Lone Oaks Farm in Middleton. The WET Center offers the opportunity for professionals from related sectors to receive hands-on training in floodplain management, and to learn how to mitigate the impacts of stormwater on people and property. The initial concept design for the facility includes the following:373 • The Water Shed: The main building structure for the facility includes an indoor classroom, laboratory, and public restrooms on the Upper Level, with offices, storage, and equipment storage on the Lower Level. • The Upper Reservoir: A one-million-gallon storage tank used to release flows to simulate anything from a minor rain to a major flood for the areas below. Participants will be able to operate gates and view the events from walkways. • The Flumes: Concrete canals used to teach flow measurement, sediment movement, and demonstrate culvert performance. Each will be gated so they can be isolated from flows and multiple demonstrations can take place at the same time. 372 “2001 Memphis Flooding,” May 2011. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:2011_Memphis_flooding.jpg 373 Bauer Askew Architecture | Design, “Programming Study for Tennessee Water Education and Training (WET) Center,” 2023.

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 5: Mitigation Strategy 620 Figure 258: The WET Center’s Upper Reservoir (2021 Project Rendering, Bauer Askew Architectural Design) • The Lower Basin: A 60,000-square-foot area with a 24-inch-thick layer of soil underlain by concrete that can be moved and shaped with heavy equipment to simulate a variety of conditions, from levees and roadways to streams and entire watersheds. Participants will create infrastructure and v it in active flows. Water will be recirculated from the lower reservoir to the upper reservoir with a pumping system or released slowly through an approved outfall point. The WET Center is funded entirely by the State of Tennessee, which includes a $28 million allocation from the Office of the Governor. Once the Center has been built, its capabilities and functions may be improved with additional HMGP, FMA, and BRIC grant funding. The site will provide an educational forum for professionals across the state to understand how to apply for and allocate mitigation funding from these and other sources to initiate or advance programs that reduce damage from flood events. 5.3 Mitigation Grant Application Priorities HMGP grant applications are ranked using the Mitigation Action Ranking System (MARS) form. Application reviewers at the state level will review all submitted applications and provide a numerical score for each project in each of the below categories. • Effective Mitigation Project (up to 26 points) • Community Impacted by a Disaster in the Past Year (25 points) • Demonstrated Hazard Mitigation Planning and Capability (up to 20 points) • Repetitive Loss, Severe Repetitive Loss, Floodplain, or Floodway (up to 15 points)

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 5: Mitigation Strategy 621 • Critical Facility or Economic Benefit (up to 15 points) • Disadvantaged Area (up to 10 points) In the first three scored categories, the State of Tennessee prioritizes rural and low-income counties that have demonstrated the capability to successfully plan or implement hazard mitigation projects. The next three scored categories focus on an applicant’s risk, vulnerability, and commitment to implementing hazard mitigation. If a community was part of a Presidentially Declared Disaster within the last year, it is given an additional 25 points. This is intended to prioritize communities currently recovering from a major disaster. The next three scored categories give priority to high-risk hazards and high-priority hazards, as listed in the applicant’s own mitigation plan, as well as the number of people benefited by the project. The next four categories focus on high-flood-risk properties, giving a very significant number of points for repetitive loss, severe repetitive loss, floodplain, and floodway properties. It is possible to get as many as 15 points from this section for a single project. The next two scored categories focus on critical facilities and economic benefit. The last two scored categories provide points for permanently solving the issue, saving lives, or addressing more than one issue. See Appendix E for a sample MARS form.

text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Section 6: Plan Maintenance 639 6. Plan Maintenance The plan maintenance process consists of three distinct steps: monitoring, evaluating, and updating the plan. All plans are living documents that reflect the diverse population and organizations that they support. The State Hazard Mitigation Plan (SHMP) should be reviewed and revised at least annually to ensure that all information remains current. The plan should also be reviewed following a major disaster or emergent event to evaluate the accuracy of the information presented and the effectiveness of its proposed mitigation actions, goals, and objectives to ensure they are still relevant and applicable to current priorities. To support the dynamic nature of maintaining the SHMP, the SHMPC and relevant stakeholders will meet at least once per year to reaffirm the accuracy of all information as presented. Should revisions need to be made, all changes will be logged and communicated to the SHMPC and FEMA Region 4. Annual reviews may be relatively straightforward and include a basic review of plan contents, but the five-year update, on which the state will begin work in 2027, will provide a comprehensive update and multistage process similar to that of developing the initial SHMP. The ESHMP should be re-evaluated when one of the following situations occurs: • At the request of the Governor • At the request of the TEMA Director • After a hazard event • After a training exercise • Following a tabletop exercise or drill • When the scope of a proposed project or mitigation action has changed significantly or has been completed Reviews of the strategy should take place following the months in which severe storms and flooding occur to assess the impact to the population and damage to the built and natural environment. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Appendix A: Assurances of Continued Compliance with Federal Requirements 645 Appendix A: Assurances of Continued Compliance with Federal Requirements The Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan (SHMP) was prepared pursuant to the requirements of the Disaster Mitigation Act of 2000 (DMA or DMA 2000) (Public Law 106-390) and the implementing regulations outlined in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) set forth by the Interim Final Rule published in the Federal Register on February 26, 2002 (44 CFR Sections 201.4 and 201.5) and finalized on October 31, 2007. (Hereafter, these requirements, and regulations will be referred to collectively as the Disaster Mitigation Act, or DMA 2000.) While the Act emphasizes the need for mitigation plans and coordinated mitigation planning and implementation between state and local authorities, new regulations established requirements that hazard mitigation plans must meet in order for a state jurisdiction to be eligible for certain federal disaster assistance and hazard mitigation funding under the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (Public Law 93-288). The Tennessee SHMP falls under the assurances proclaimed in this plan: Tennessee assures that it will comply with all applicable federal statutes and regulations in effect with respect to the periods for which it receives grant funding in compliance with 44 CFR Part 13.11(c). The state will amend the SHMP whenever necessary to reflect changes in state or federal laws and statutes, as required in 44 CFR Part 13.11(d). The adoption of this SHMP demonstrates the state’s commitment to fulfilling the mitigation objectives outlined in the SHMP. Likewise, the state authorizes the agencies identified in the SHMP to execute their responsibilities associated with implementing this plan.

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Appendix B: References 661 Financial Capability Lead/ Responsible Organization Description of Capability Flood Mitigation Assistance (FMA) Program FEMA This provides funding to assist states and communities in implementing measures to reduce or eliminate the long-term risk of flood damage to buildings, manufactured homes, and other structures insurable under the NFIP. The grant program is competitive and funded annually. Hazard Mitigation Grant Post Fire (HMGP-PF) FEMA This program is designed to help communities recover from a wildfire. Eligible project types include wildfire mitigation, infrastructure retrofit, soil and slop stabilization, post-wildfire flood prevention, sediment reduction, and items that qualify for the 5% initiative, such as installing warning signs. Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP) FEMA The purpose of the program is to reduce the (longterm) loss of life and property due to natural disasters and enable mitigation measures to be implemented during the immediate recovery from a disaster declaration. Pre-Disaster Mitigation (PDM) Grant Program FEMA The PDM grant program makes federal funds available to state, local, tribal, and territorial governments to plan for and implement sustainable, cost-effective measures designed to reduce the risk to individuals and property from future natural hazards while also reducing reliance on federal funding from future disasters. Public Assistance (PA) Program FEMA The program provides emergency assistance to save lives and protect property and assists with permanently restoring community infrastructure affected by a federally declared incident. Rehabilitation of High Hazard Potential Dam (HHPD) Grant Program FEMA This grant is available through FEMA’s Dam Safety Program for technical, planning, design, and construction grants for eligible dams. Eligible dams needed to be documented as “high hazard potential” in the USACE’s National Inventory of Dams. Additional requirements include being in a state with a dam safety program, being classified as “high hazard potential” by the state, having an Emergency Action Plan (EAP), located in a jurisdiction with a FEMA-approved hazard mitigation plan that includes dam risk, and failing to meet minimum standards, which constitutes an unacceptable risk to the public. The non-federal cost share requirement is no less than 35%.

The Planning Branch is responsible for the State Hazard Mitigation Plan (SHMP) and reviews local hazard mitigation plans (LHMPs) to ensure they are compliant with federal and state hazard mitigation guidance. TEMA’s four regional offices provide mitigation planning assistance to all 95 counties. Each regional office is staffed by a full-time planner who supports local jurisdictions in their development of LHMPs. The regional planners prioritize assisting counties with the planning process through meetings, by helping them understand the new FEMA planning requirements, and through internal documentation. The planners also support the counties with other planning initiatives, such as special event planning and basic emergency operations planning.

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Appendix C: Coordination of Local Planning 685 TEMA sets statewide mitigation priorities and shares risk assessment data, all of which are included in the SHMP. Local jurisdictions can access the updated plan and related information and planning resources in TEMA’s digital Planning Library. The Planning Library can be accessed with the following link: https://plans-tnema.hub.arcgis.com/ Planning resources in the Planning Library include the LHMP template, which has been updated in accordance with FEMA’s 2023 Local Mitigation Planning Policy Guide. The template was first developed in 2010 to allow a single TEMA planner to efficiently produce approvable LHMPs. It has evolved along with the state’s mitigation program and has been proven to enhance the planning process and integration of all hazard mitigation plans. This template fosters a sense of cohesion between the local plans and the state’s hazard mitigation program. All county plans follow the template’s format, making them easy to understand. LHMPs are not subject to any additional requirements from the state. To be approved at the state level, county plans must simply meet the planning requirements set forth by FEMA in Title 44 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 201. The content of the LHMP template helps local planners meet the required elements for a FEMA-approved hazard mitigation plan. Additionally, the template includes guidance on helpful language, provides graphics illustrating Tennessee’s common hazards, and outlines a simple hazard identification and risk assessment process. The state reviews the plan

text: a simple hazard identification and risk assessment process. Local Plan Review and Integration TEMA follows a designated review process for all local plans. Once a jurisdiction has completed its plan, it can submit it to TEMA for a preliminary review. The state reviews the plan following FEMA’s Local Mitigation Planning Handbook and Local Mitigation Plan Review Guide. TEMA will review the plan within 30 to 45 days. If the plan meets all of FEMA’s planning requirements, it will be forwarded to FEMA for review. TEMA may recommend revisions to the plan, especially if the plan does not meet all FEMA planning requirements. In this case, the state agency will provide detailed feedback with the required revisions. Once the jurisdiction has incorporated the feedback, TEMA will forward the revised plan to FEMA for official review. In cases where FEMA requires revisions for final approval, the state will work with the county to make revisions. A new five-year planning cycle will begin with the approval and adoption of the 2023 SHMP update. The state intends to update the plan annually, and updates may include revisions to the plan’s mitigation goals, mitigation actions, funding resources, state and local capabilities, or any other part of the plan affected by changing community or hazard elements. This is further detailed in Section 6, Plan Maintenance. Through these updates, TEMA shares the most recent risk assessment data and mitigation priorities with the local governments. Risk assessments from LHMPs are linked with the State Hazard Mitigation Plan as part of the regular five-year update cycle, rather than annually. Most local plans are also updated on a five-year cycle, ensuring that all information is up to date. If there

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Appendix C: Coordination of Local Planning 688 TEMA works with local jurisdictions to identify potential funding sources and administers federal funding as it becomes available. More information and contact information for each funding source can be found on the state website at: https://www.tn.gov/tema/emergency-community/mitigation/mitigation-grantprograms.html Available non-federal funds are used as matching funds for federal grants and are prioritized using the Mitigation Action Ranking System (MARS) described in the Prioritizing Local Assistance section below. Prioritizing Local Assistance and Funding The State of Tennessee has established an application procedure for the prioritization of grant funding according to the Mitigation Application Ranking System (MARS). A copy of this application is provided in at the end of these minutes for inclusion Appendix E of this SHMP, Planning Process Documents. Tennessee authorities use this system to assess the eligibility of a funding request by evaluating its qualifications against specific criteria, which are then scored. The state’s evaluation follows three phases: (1) application eligibility; (2) project eligibility; and (3) the Tennessee Hazard Mitigation Council (THMC) review. The state provides an application to local jurisdictions requesting funding and requires the applicant to include a project proposal that discusses the project duration, scope of work, estimated budget, and a cost-benefit analysis (CBA). TEMA will assist the jurisdiction during the application process as needed. The State Hazard Mitigation Officer (SHMO) serves as the Federal Mitigation Grant Administrator and is responsible for screening applications, monitoring, and evaluating the progress of approved mitigation projects. The SHMO will also review each application to ensure it complies with the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) program guidance. This may include a preliminary environmental assessment. FEMA

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: Grant Administrator and is responsible for screening applications, monitoring, and evaluating the progress of approved mitigation projects. The SHMO will also review each application to ensure it complies with the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) program guidance. This may include a preliminary environmental assessment. FEMA will conduct an independent environmental compliance review, but the state will ensure that all required documentation and support materials are included in the application package for submission to FEMA. The project will be assessed for eligibility and ranked based on the following criteria: • The proposed project must align with the SHMP. • The project must solve a hazard- or risk-related problem. Projects that merely identify or analyze hazards or problems are not eligible. • The project should have a beneficial impact on the designated disaster area. • The project must comply with 44 CFR Part 9, Floodplain Management and Protection of Wetlands, and 44 CFR Part 10, Environmental Considerations. • The project must address a repetitive problem or a problem that poses a significant negative risk if left unsolved.

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Appendix C: Coordination of Local Planning 689 • The project must be cost-effective and reduce the risk of future damage and loss resulting from a major disaster in that it: ▪ Has been determined to be the most practical, effective, and environmentally compliant option. ▪ Contributes to a permanent or long-term solution to the problem addressed. ▪ Accommodates long-term changes in the area it affects. • The project has manageable routine maintenance requirements. After the ranking of all eligible applications, the SHMO will prepare a summary of all proposals which will be presented to the THMC for review. The TNHMC consists of ten members from various state departments, each possessing unique mitigation experience. These departments include the following:  Department of Agriculture  Department of Commerce & Insurance  Department of Economic & Community Development  Department of Environment & Conservation  Department of Finance & Administration  Department of Health  Department of Safety – Homeland Security  Department of Safety – Highway Patrol  Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency  Department of Transportation  TEMA (State Hazard Mitigation Officer) Once the THMC review is complete, formal recommendations will be submitted to the Governor’s Authorized Representative (GAR). The SHMO will submit the application summaries, rankings, and final prioritization decisions of the Council to the GAR for review by FEMA. FEMA will have final approval authority for all funding projects. Should a project be rejected, the SHMO will advise sub applicants and inform them of their right to appeal the decision using the designated appeals process. Each component of the Mitigation Application Ranking System (MARS) application will receive a rating between

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: for all funding projects. Should a project be rejected, the SHMO will advise sub applicants and inform them of their right to appeal the decision using the designated appeals process. Each component of the Mitigation Application Ranking System (MARS) application will receive a rating between 1 and 5, with 1 representing the lowest capability rating and 5 the highest. The MARS application components are as follows: • The capability of the applicant to complete the activity based on prior project performance and regional assessments of those activities • The population of the area in question • The median income of that population • The community’s participation in the Community Rating System (CRS), adoption of International Building Code (IBC)/building codes, history of mitigation efforts, identification of IDS (Intense Developmental Stress), or involvement in a declared disaster within the past year • If involved in a declared disaster, whether the proposal directly addresses said disaster • The number of presidentially declared disasters in the area for the previous 10 years • Whether the proposed activity mitigates a high-risk hazard for the project’s geographic area

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Appendix C: Coordination of Local Planning 690 • The priority of the project/strategy being mitigated in the applicant’s plan • The number of people benefiting from the proposed activity • Whether the proposal includes Repetitive Flood Claim structures (e.g., NFIP structures with a history of one or more claims for damage or loss) • Whether the proposal includes properties located in a floodplain or floodway • Whether the proposal consists of a critical facility or function • Whether the proposal provides economic benefit to the local community through the following: ▪ Private sector (residents) ▪ Public sector (business) ▪ Government (local) ▪ Minority (National Environmental Policy Act [NEPA]) ▪ Partnering (between the public and government) • Whether the proposed activity will permanently eliminate the problem being addressed • Whether the proposed activity will accomplish the following: ▪ Save lives ▪ Mitigate more than one hazard ▪ Accomplish multiple objectives Additional Considerations This state monitors areas of intense developmental pressure to ensure that communities comply with the IBC as adopted by the state. According to U.S. Census data, Tennessee experienced population growth of over 9% between 2010 and 2020 and this figure is expected to increase in future years.374 An expanded built environment may increase pressure for more housing and business development. The state and local communities will need to ensure that development is aligned with the requirements set forth in local building codes, zoning regulations, and comprehensive plans. Areas of intense development pressure are considered in the funding process. These areas are identified in the MARS application and are scored accordingly. Please note that the funding process does not currently account for areas impacted by climate change, but this will be addressed in the upcoming MARS process update. Concerns arise when high-risk communities are included in a presidential disaster declaration or when there is a funding request to remove severe repetitive loss structures that house vulnerable populations. The MARS criteria address properties located in floodplains and floodways as well as areas of high population density where disasters have historically occurred. The MARS application asks applicants to identify any existing Repetitive or Severe Repetitive Loss properties in the project area, or any Repetitive Flood Claim structures.
