text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Appendix C: Coordination of Local Planning 691 The MARS scoring requirement also incorporates components regarding social vulnerability and underserved communities. The applicant and the state will gather the materials needed to conduct an environmental review of the proposed project. This review addresses areas of concern, including, but not limited to, waterways, floodplains, historical and cultural elements, as well as low-income and minority populations. The MARS application also asks applicants to identify how the proposed project will benefit the local community, specifically minority populations. This component is scored accordingly and is a consideration in the prioritization of project funding. Funding for projects regarding High Hazard Potential Dams (HHPDs) is prioritized based on a conditional assessment. This assessment is conducted annually by the Tennessee Safe Dams Program and identifies the most vulnerable dams in the state. The dams identified during this assessment are then given funding priority over any grant opportunities that may arise. The state wants to ensure that the highest risk dams are addressed first. These projects are focused on repair that will limit and mitigate the risk to dam failure. A limitation of this process is that HPPD prioritization is not currently integrated into the MARS system, though there is an opportunity to address this limitation in the next MARS system update by incorporating HHPD scoring elements. The prioritization of funding methodology for FEMA’s Rehabilitation of HHPD Grant Program is currently limited, since the program is so new, and TEMA has not yet applied for the grant. TEMA will address this limitation by capitalizing on future HPPD funding opportunities and refining their prioritization methodology. TEMA will utilize the existing

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: Rehabilitation of HHPD Grant Program is currently limited, since the program is so new, and TEMA has not yet applied for the grant. TEMA will address this limitation by capitalizing on future HPPD funding opportunities and refining their prioritization methodology. TEMA will utilize the existing conditional assessment, or an adapted version of it, as long as it meets FEMA’s HHPD prioritization criteria. TEMA may also elect to utilize FEMA’s Risk Based Prioritization Method. FEMA’s method includes the following elements: • Step 1: Identify static, hydrologic, and seismic failure modes for each dam. • Step 2: Determine qualitative risk values for each failure mode for each dam and plot them in the Risk Prioritization matrix. • Step 3: For dams with similar risk values, apply differentiators (e.g. PAR, value of the dam as an asset, critical infrastructure at risk, impact to Community Lifelines, etc.) to rank the dams. • Step 4: Evaluate potential projects using the same methodology/matrix to determine which projects reduce risk reduction to acceptable levels. This step justifies the project priority list from which projects are selected. Barriers to Developing, Adopting and Implementing Local Hazard Mitigation Plans Hazard mitigation planning is a complex process that crosses many disciplines. It includes community planning, infrastructure design, capital improvement budgeting, floodplain management, and emergency management. Barriers may be present at several points during the planning process. For example, emergency management professionals and planners often

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Appendix C: Coordination of Local Planning 692 rely on outside expertise in order to produce an effective plan. The planning process requires a high level of coordination and collaboration among planning participants and stakeholders. This requirement may present challenges because representatives from all organizations, including TEMA, may have competing priorities. TEMA itself may be trying to lead the plan update process while managing the Emergency Operations Center and coordinating disaster response and recovery. Counties and other local planning groups may also be limited by their available resources. The tables presented in the Local Capabilities section of this appendix were developed based on a recent analysis of each county’s local capabilities. The tables show that there are few planners working for Tennessee cities and counties. It may be difficult for a jurisdiction with a limited number of staff—and without a staff member familiar with community or mitigation planning—to manage a complex project like updating the LHMP. Limited resources and capabilities present a challenge, even with significant support from TEMA’s Regional Planning Offices. The U.S. Census Bureau’s 2019 Community Resilience Estimates for Equity and Disasters reported that 41% of the Tennessee population is affected by at least one social risk factor.375 Underserved communities include people living in poverty, persons with disabilities, minority populations, and more. Additionally, much of Tennessee is rural, and there are unique challenges in understanding the full scope of rural community needs, especially since they have fewer community resources.376 While the local planning team may do all in its power to reach out to a diverse group of stakeholders and residents, certain population groups may be hard to reach,

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: understanding the full scope of rural community needs, especially since they have fewer community resources.376 While the local planning team may do all in its power to reach out to a diverse group of stakeholders and residents, certain population groups may be hard to reach, and the planning team may not fully understand the challenges that need to be addressed. Disasters are occurring more frequently and with greater intensity. This can make it difficult to identify and develop a plan to mitigate potential hazards, particularly as weather patterns and plan for potential hazards, particularly since weather patterns and climate are changing. Most LHMPs do not currently address the increasing frequency of extreme hazard events, the occurrence of which may impair how local communities develop and implement mitigation strategies to address hazard impacts. Similarly, most local mitigation plans do not address high hazard potential dam (HHPD) risks, mostly because there is not an extensive hazard history regarding dam failure, and most jurisdictions do not feel the threat is imminent. With hazards or conditions that are relatively new, such as climate change, and hazards that occur infrequently, such as dam failure, there may be gaps in how local jurisdictions are addressing and profiling these hazards. More information regarding the challenges of addressing HHPDs are detailed in the Local Capabilities section of this Appendix. Another barrier to local mitigation planning is the accessibility of accurate and timely data, especially in rural areas. Even when there is sufficient data for hazard events such as flooding, it may not be well documented. Some sources may provide inaccurate, incomplete, or

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Appendix C: Coordination of Local Planning 693 conflicting information about a specific event. For hazards that occur infrequently, there may be little to no data available. It can also be difficult to obtain precise data about non-natural hazards, such as infrastructure failure. There are several factors that also make it challenging to adopt the local hazard mitigation plans, especially for the smaller jurisdictions and rural cities. Due to limited resources, including staff, time, and revenue, these smaller cities and towns must carefully allocate their budget and time resources. In addition, it can be challenging for smaller communities to perceive the longterm benefits of adopting hazard mitigation plans. While these plans are intended to reduce the impact of future disasters, the initial investment may seem significant, leading to hesitation or reluctance to commit resources. For these reasons, a lot of smaller jurisdictions will not fully adopt their plan, or will opt out of participating in the county-wide, multijurisdictional plan. As grant and federal funding are on very long timelines, and the funding is not always guaranteed, the jurisdictions may also be disincentivized to participate. State representatives and the regional planners are working to help these communities understand the importance of having an adopted hazard mitigation plan by emphasizing potential grant funding opportunities and the long-term risk reduction benefits. TEMA recognizes these challenges and works with its counties to overcome them. Its priorities include strengthening intergovernmental relationships and improving the quality and accessibility of hazard data. For example, to address the challenge of obtaining accurate and sufficient data, TEMA has partnered with East Tennessee State University (ETSU) in the 2023 SHMP update

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: counties to overcome them. Its priorities include strengthening intergovernmental relationships and improving the quality and accessibility of hazard data. For example, to address the challenge of obtaining accurate and sufficient data, TEMA has partnered with East Tennessee State University (ETSU) in the 2023 SHMP update to develop the plan’s hazard profiles. Also, for the 2023 plan update, the agency collaborates with governmental and non-governmental organizations to promote equity in the mitigation planning process to ensure all vulnerable populations and underserved communities are fully represented. TEMA will continue to develop and implement strategies, including, but not limited to, developing outreach programs, and conducting hazard studies, as identified in the SHMP. Local Capabilities An analysis was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of existing capabilities and the opportunity to implement mitigation actions. Currently, only ten local jurisdictions address high hazard potential dams (HHPDs) in their local mitigation plans. This is mainly because the risk of dam failure is not perceived as immediate, given the lack of previous dam failure incidents. This is challenging because it means that the local jurisdictions are not eligible for HHPD grant funding and are not actively building working relationships with local dam owners and state dam safety representatives. An opportunity exists to implement mitigation actions to reduce the risk of high hazard potential dams as more jurisdictions address this element in their LHMPs. The state is working with local Emergency Management Agencies (EMAs) to help them become more involved in the HHPD process. The state plans to hold regional meetings with local jurisdictions to provide them with additional data and explain the presence of dams in their respective areas, along with the associated risks. The

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Appendix C: Coordination of Local Planning 694 goal of these meetings is to create more awareness among local jurisdictions and implement more mitigation opportunities that reduce the risk to and from HHPDs. Local jurisdictions also perform a breach analysis prior to issuing a new building permit that informs the applicant of how the new construction, or alteration to existing construction, may be affected by the potential failure of any surrounding dams, as outlined by Tennessee Code Title 69, Chapter 11. However, a challenge exists in how many jurisdictions are actually enforcing this legislation or have the ability to do so. Additionally, many areas view their flooding capabilities as an extension to their HHPD capabilities. Others participate in the National Flood Insurance Program and have a Certified Floodplain Manager on staff This is shown in the following tables. Ninety-nine per cent of local jurisdictions profile flood hazards in their LHMP and already have mitigation projects and actions aimed at reducing flood risk. While the state does not have much authority over how local jurisdictions implement mitigation actions regarding HHPDs, the state will continue working with the EMAs and developing tools, such as the High Hazard Potential Dam Dashboard, which is in early stages of development. Regarding other local capabilities, with the adoption of local hazard mitigation plans, comprehensive plans, and capital improvement plans, jurisdictions are positioned to implement and integrate mitigation strategies, especially as these local plans are updated or developed. The jurisdictions that have implemented regulatory capabilities such as zoning ordinances and building codes have an opportunity to expand on these regulations and address new mitigation strategies. text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Appendix D: SHMP Feedback from TEMA and FEMA Region 4 738 Agency Requesting SHMP Revision/Update Revision/Update Requested Correction Made Section Number Page Number FEMA Element HHPD2.b.2 asks for Location and size of PARs from high hazard potential dams, as well as potential impacts to institutions and critical infrastructure/facilities/community lifelines. The plan explains as a limitation that not all high hazard potential dams have modeled and digitized inundation zones. Some dams, however, do have current inundation zones, and these were analyzed for impact to state owned facilities. Required Revision – For high hazard potential dams for which data exists, provide the location (i.e. inundation zone) and size of the Population at Risk, as well as potential impacts to the specific institutions and critical infrastructure/facilities/community lifelines within the hazard area. If there are additional limitations to performing the analysis, describe these and describe the approach to addressing the deficiencies. Addressed on page 137-138; data deficiency described 3.7.2.3.1 137–138 FEMA Element HHPD7 asks for a description of the method of funding actions that are prioritized differently from action for other hazards. The HHPD grant program has a different and specific risk-based prioritization method for ranking eligible high hazard potential dams and deciding which activities to fund. “The prioritization method compares projects based on common failure modes, potential consequences resulting from a dam incident, and the expected risk-reduction and other benefits of potential projects.” (page 5-22 of the HHPD Grant Program Guidance (https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/202008/fema_hhpd_grant-guidance.pdf). Required revision - Describe the HHPD method for funding prioritization. Since TEMA has not yet applied for HHPD grants and since changes to the methodology requirements are expected, a statement of limitations and/or a general description is acceptable. Described the method of prioritizing funding for the HHPD grant, addressing limitation. Appendix C 692

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Appendix E: Planning Process Documentation 773 Tennessee State Capability Assessment Worksheet The Capability Assessment is an important component of the State Hazard Mitigation Planning process. Types of Capabilities There are typically four capability types: 1. Planning and Regulatory: state plans, policies, statutes, or regulations that could affect your state’s resilience to future natural hazard events and other future conditions, including the potential effects of climate change. These are the plans and regulations that guide development and manage growth in your state. These tools can shape risk reduction in the built and natural environment. 2. Administrative and Technical: staff, skills and tools that can reduce the risk of hazards in your state. These may be those of state agencies and departments, academic partners, regional planning, non-profit and private organizations. 3. Financial: potential funding resources to support hazard mitigation. These may be state funds and programs, FEMA or other federal programs, and private and non-profit resources. Consider how these resources work together to advance mitigation. Think about how to set the criteria for prioritizing mitigation investments. (See Review of Requirements below.) 4. Education and Outreach: existing programs that support mitigation and communicate risk. These could include technical assistance, training and education and awareness campaigns that build capacity. Additionally, state capabilities can be thought of in terms of community lifelines. Community lifelines are the most fundamental services in the community that, when stabilized, enable all other aspects of society to function. FEMA’s National Response Framework, 4th Edition, identifies seven critical community lifelines that are the most fundamental services in the community. Additional information can be found here: Lifelines Toolkit v2.0 (fema.gov). Community lifelines can help find and leverage important mitigation capabilities to conduct your state’s plan.

title: Tennessee State Hazard Mitigation Plan
text: State of Tennessee Standard State Hazard Mitigation Plan August 2023 Appendix E: Planning Process Documentation 798 Community Input during the Planning Process While public comment is not required during the state hazard mitigation planning process, TEMA created two public surveys to create awareness about, and secure input on, hazards and mitigation actions discussed in the 2023 SHMP. Another survey was developed to secure input on the draft plan. First Survey: Input about Hazards and Mitigation Actions TEMA posted the first online survey using the SurveyMonkey took and asked partner agencies and residents about their experience with hazards of concern, and mitigation actions respondents thought would be the most effective in limiting or avoiding damage to property and harm to people. TEMA posted notices on social media sites to promote widespread community response. The survey was available for public review and response for four weeks, from July 18 to August 15, 2023. Each site included a link to the survey posted on the SurveyMonkey website. The survey generated 373 responses from all stakeholders, with a solid 78.28% of answers coming from the general public, versus employees of state and county government. Survey results provided practical insights about what are seen as the hazards of highest concern; hazards that have most affected the community; and mitigation actions seen as most effective in reducing hazard impacts. Participants were asked to provide their zip code, and a list of zip codes shown indicates contributors from across the state shared their input about hazards affecting them. Second Survey: Feedback on the Draft Plan A follow-up survey was developed to secure input on the completed draft 2023 SHMP. TEMA stakeholders, in particular, recommended additions and changes that were incorporated into the plan. Appendix D includes a list of changes made in the plan as a result of feedback received.
